memory.abstract: The Simplicity Principle for Polymer Graph Learning: Across two days of experiments, simple, well-tuned baselines consistently beat complex mechanisms imported from molecular GNN literature. This integration formalizes the pattern, identifies its domain boundaries, and surfaces implications for Day 3-4 experimental design.
memory.keyword: simplicity-principle polymer-graph-learning over-engineering static-vs-learned baseline-first molecular-to-polymer-transfer

content.consensus: Across all experiments spanning Day 1 and Day 2, a consistent meta-pattern has emerged: simple, well-executed baselines outperform complex architectural mechanisms imported from the molecular GNN literature. Day 1: Rich features + pure 3-RU training with standard GAT (mean aggregation) decisively beat GRIN-inspired {1,3}-RU mixed augmentation requiring max-aggregation and L1 sparsity (mem_080, mem_081). Day 2: Static RWPE at input (35.94K) substantially outperforms LSPE decoupled learnable positional encoding (37.96K), and the LSPE paper's core claim — that decoupled position-structure learning amplifies PE signal — reverses for polymers (mem_094 vs. mem_089). Architecture scaling (4 layers, 256 hidden, AdamW, 2-layer MLP) alone delivered 4.75K improvement (mem_093), dwarfing the contribution of SPSE edge encodings (+1.14K worse) and max-aggregation (+1.42K worse) combined (mem_091). The pattern is unambiguous: for polymer Tg prediction, complexity adds noise, not signal.
content.conflicts: This finding conflicts with the molecular GNN literature's dominant narrative — that sophisticated structural encodings (SPSE, LSPE, ELENE) and advanced aggregation mechanisms (max, GRU, PNA) are necessary for strong performance. The resolution is domain-specific: molecular graphs (ZINC, Peptides) have diverse topologies with cycles, branches, and varying local structures, making learned encodings and complex aggregations genuinely valuable. Polymer graphs, even at 3-RU, are essentially linear chains where the topological signal is simple and static encodings suffice. The transfer of molecular GNN innovations to polymers must be gated by a domain-appropriateness check that has been missing from our hypothesis generation.
content.alignment: This principle aligns with the MetaMethod's 'match algorithms to physical reality' directive (mem_002): models suited for topologically diverse molecular graphs may not fit polymer datasets. It also aligns with the anti-self-deception rule: honest reporting of negative results (SPSE, max-aggregation, LSPE) is precisely what enables this meta-insight to emerge. The principle also aligns with the LSPE paper's own finding that sparse GNNs outperform Transformer GNNs on molecular benchmarks where local structure dominates (mem_089) — the polymer case takes this further: local structure so dominates that even within sparse GNNs, simpler > complex.
content.key_insight: The Simplicity Principle for polymer graph learning: before deploying any complex mechanism, first exhaust simple baselines — deeper/wider architectures, better training (AdamW), richer features, and static domain-appropriate encodings. Complexity is warranted only when there is evidence that the task requires the specific inductive bias the mechanism provides. For polymers, static node-level positional encodings (RWPE) capture the primary structural signal (position along chain); edge-level path encodings (SPSE) and learned positional evolution (LSPE) address problems that don't exist for tree-like graphs. This principle should guide Day 3-4 experimental design: prioritize graph-level encodings (SPD histograms, global descriptors), static injection at input, and pretraining — not more complex message-passing mechanisms.

memory.abstract: The Topological Simplicity of Polymer Graphs as a Fundamental Design Constraint: Polymer graphs (even 3-RU) are essentially 1D chains with sparse branching. This topological simplicity explains the asymmetric success of node-level vs. edge-level encodings, the reversal of the LSPE finding, and why the scale mismatch between molecular and polymer graphs matters.
memory.keyword: topological-simplicity polymer-graph tree-like 1D-chain node-vs-edge-encoding scale-mismatch encoding-degeneracy design-constraint

content.consensus: Polymer graphs, even with 3 repeat units, are fundamentally tree-like 1D chains with sparse branching — a topological reality that has systematically invalidated encoding strategies designed for topologically diverse molecular graphs. Three independent lines of evidence converge on this: (1) SPSE edge path counts are 100% degenerate at k=2 — there are simply no alternative paths between adjacent nodes in a linear chain (mem_091). (2) Node-level RWPE has 0% degenerate graphs and strong 2D PCA separability (PC1=68.5%, PC2=29.1%) — even linear chains have well-defined node positions (chain-end, interior, branch-point) that random walks can distinguish (mem_094). (3) The LSPE finding reverses for polymers: on ZINC molecules (mean 23 nodes, diverse cycles and branches), learned PE evolution helps (0.090 vs 0.122 MAE); on polymer graphs (mean 104 nodes, largely linear), learned PE evolution hurts (37.96K vs 36.29K static) — because there is nothing topologically complex for the learned evolution to disambiguate (mem_094 vs mem_089).
content.conflicts: The SPSE paper (mem_087) proposes simple path counts as a universal improvement over RWSE for graph transformers, validated on molecular benchmarks (ZINC, Peptides, PCQM4Mv2). Our finding that SPSE is 100% degenerate for polymer edges does not invalidate SPSE — it reveals that SPSE's core advantage (distinguishing cycles from paths, enabled by Proposition 3's cycle-counting property) is irrelevant for graphs that lack cycles entirely. SPSE is solving a problem that polymer graphs don't have. This is not a failure of SPSE but a domain mismatch — the same domain mismatch that made static ELENE k=1 fail on polymers (mem_084), though for different reasons.
content.alignment: This principle aligns with and extends the periodic polymer graph literature (mem_052): polymers are fundamentally 1D periodic structures, and representations should reflect this. The success of node-level RWPE can be understood through this lens: the random walk landing probability of node i returning to itself after k steps is essentially encoding the node's position along the 1D chain — chain-end nodes have lower return probability than interior nodes. This is why higher k helps (k=32 > k=16): for larger polymer graphs (104 nodes), longer random walks are needed to distinguish chain-ends from deep-interior nodes. The scale mismatch (ZINC: ~23 nodes, polymer: ~104 nodes) compounds the topological simplicity: not only are polymer graphs simpler topologically, they are 4-5x larger, requiring proportionally longer positional encoding ranges.
content.key_insight: Polymer graph topology is a first-order design constraint that invalidates encoding strategies relying on topological diversity (edge-level path counts, learned positional evolution) while amplifying the value of simple positional encodings (node-level RWPE with sufficiently high k). The design implication for Day 3-4: (a) avoid any encoding that requires alternative paths or topological diversity — these are dead ends; (b) embrace encodings that capture position along 1D chains — RWPE works, and polymer-specific variants (distance-to-chain-end, monomer-index) may work even better; (c) the optimal encoding dimension k should scale with graph size, not be set by molecular benchmarks; (d) pretraining on PI1M may provide the topological diversity (across different polymer structures) that supervised learning on Tg alone cannot, which is why PerioGT's contrastive pretraining reaches 30.8K.

memory.abstract: The Undertraining-to-True-Ceiling Trajectory: The Day 1 "preprocessing ceiling" of 41.6K RMSE was actually an undertraining artifact. Architecture scaling (+4.75K) and static RWPE (+0.91K) have reduced the gap from 10.8K to 5.14K. This integration maps the improvement trajectory, identifies what remains, and frames Day 3-4 pretraining exploration as the likely path to SOTA.
memory.keyword: undertraining-ceiling architecture-scaling improvement-trajectory pretraining-necessity gap-to-SOTA cumulative-progress

content.consensus: The Day 1 conclusion that a 'preprocessing ceiling' existed at 41.6K RMSE was incorrect — it was an undertraining ceiling. The evidence is unambiguous: simply scaling the GAT architecture (3→4 layers, 128→256 hidden, 1→2 layer MLP predictor, Adam→AdamW) improved from 41.6K to 36.85K — a 4.75K (11.4%) improvement with zero change to preprocessing, features, or data (mem_093). Adding static RWPE k=32 further improved to 35.94K — another 0.91K (mem_094). The cumulative improvement from Day 1 best to Day 2 best is 5.66K (41.6K → 35.94K), representing 52% of the original 10.8K gap to SOTA. The true ceiling for GAT-based architectures without pretraining is likely in the 33-35K range, still 2-5K above PerioGT's 30.8K, indicating pretraining is the likely remaining lever.
content.conflicts: The trajectory reveals an important tension: architecture scaling alone delivered 4.75K improvement, while sophisticated encoding mechanisms (SPSE, LSPE, max-aggregation) delivered zero or negative improvement (mem_091, mem_094). This reverses the implicit prioritization in our Day 2 planning — we expected architectural innovation (encodings, aggregation) to dominate, but capacity expansion dominated. The MetaMethod's 'never under-train' directive (mem_002) was violated on Day 1, and the cost was a misdiagnosed ceiling that could have prematurely steered us toward pretraining. This does not mean pretraining is unnecessary — PerioGT's 30.8K was achieved with pretraining (mem_078, mem_079) — but it means we should first establish the true supervised ceiling before concluding pretraining is required.
content.alignment: This trajectory aligns with well-known deep learning principles: (a) model capacity must be sufficient before architectural innovations can be fairly evaluated — a principle violated in Day 1's 3-layer/128-hidden GAT; (b) regularization (AdamW's decoupled weight decay) matters more as models grow — the Day 2 baseline uses AdamW while Day 1 used Adam; (c) the gap that remains after capacity expansion and simple encodings (~5.14K) is the signal that pretraining is genuinely needed. This also aligns with PerioGT's design: PerioGT uses periodicity-aware contrastive pretraining on ~1M unlabeled polymers (PI1M), which is precisely the approach we should explore on Days 3-4. The alignment is reinforced by the fact that TransPolymer (mem_039) also demonstrated that MLM pretraining on PI1M-scale polymer data yields SOTA across multiple benchmarks.

cumulative_progress.day_2_spse_maxgat: 36.85K (no improvement from SPSE edge paths or max-aggregation)

content.key_insight: Every ceiling is provisional until capacity is saturated and simple encodings are exhausted. The 5.14K residual gap to SOTA — after capacity expansion, better optimization, and static positional encoding — is the genuine signal that a qualitatively different approach (pretraining) is needed. Day 3-4 should pursue: (a) further architecture scaling (5-6 layers, 384-512 hidden) to establish the true non-pretraining ceiling, ideally reaching 33-35K; (b) polymer-specific positional encodings (distance-to-chain-end, monomer-index) that may outperform generic RWPE; (c) graph transformer architectures (GPS-style, mem_088) with static RWPE + SPD biases as the non-pretraining architecture baseline; and (d) self-supervised pretraining on PI1M — either contrastive (PerioGT-style periodicity contrast) or MLM (TransPolymer-style masked polymer modeling) — as the primary mechanism to close the remaining gap. The 30.8K SOTA is reachable if pretraining captures the polymer-specific structural priors that supervised learning on 7170 samples cannot.

memory.abstract: MoMuCon: Monomer-vs-Multimer Contrastive Pretraining on PI1M — converting the Day-1 multimer effect (3-RU > 1-RU) into a self-supervised signal that teaches the GAT encoder polymer-specific scale invariance, then finetuning on Tg
memory.keyword: contrastive-pretraining PI1M monomer-multimer GAT-encoder NT-Xent polymer-scale-invariance

H: MoMuCon Hypothesis: The multimer effect discovered on Day 1 — where 3-RU graphs consistently outperform 1-RU graphs for Tg prediction — reflects a fundamental polymer property: the same polymer expressed at different repeat-unit resolutions carries the same chemical identity but reveals different structural detail. This can be converted into a self-supervised contrastive pretraining signal on PI1M (1M unlabeled polymers). By training the GAT encoder to map 1-RU and 3-RU graph embeddings of the same polymer close together in representation space (positive pair) while pushing apart embeddings of different polymers (negative pairs), the model learns a polymer-specific representation that captures backbone identity invariant to RU scale. When finetuned on Tg, this pretrained representation should close a significant portion of the 5.14K gap to SOTA without requiring architectural changes — the same GAT+RWPE architecture that reached 35.94K is used, only with pretrained weights.

Pretraining Necessity Hypothesis: The 5.14K residual gap after architecture scaling (+4.75K) and static RWPE (+0.91K) represents structural information that cannot be learned from 7170 labeled Tg samples alone — the sample complexity of polymer chemical space is too high. However, PI1M's 1M unlabeled polymers sample this space broadly, and self-supervised pretraining can extract general polymer structural priors that transfer to Tg. If MoMuCon closes ≥2.5K (reaching ≤33.4K), pretraining is confirmed as the key missing ingredient. If it closes <1K, the 1-RU→3-RU contrastive signal may be too weak, and masked polymer modeling (node/edge masking on graphs) should be explored as an alternative pretraining objective.

pretraining_phase.dataset: 200K polymers randomly sampled from PI1M (scalable to full 1M if resources permit). For each polymer, construct both 1-RU and 3-RU graphs with rich node features (atomic number, hybridization, aromaticity, degree, formal charge, ring membership, chirality, hydrogen count). Static RWPE k=32 precomputed and concatenated to node features at input.
pretraining_phase.encoder: GAT (4 layers, 256 hidden, 4 attention heads, mean aggregation) — the proven Day-2-best architecture. This is the encoder whose weights will be transferred to finetuning.
pretraining_phase.projection_head: 2-layer MLP (256→128→64) with BatchNorm and ReLU, producing the contrastive embedding z. Only encoder weights are transferred; projection head is discarded after pretraining.
pretraining_phase.contrastive_loss: NT-Xent (normalized temperature-scaled cross entropy) with temperature τ=0.1. For each batch of B polymers, the 2B graphs (B×1-RU + B×3-RU) form B positive pairs (same polymer, different RU) and 2B×(2B−2) negative pairs. Loss = −(1/2B) Σ log[exp(sim(z_i, z_j)/τ) / Σ_{k≠i} exp(sim(z_i, z_k)/τ)] where (i,j) are positive pairs.
pretraining_phase.training: AdamW optimizer (lr=1e-3 pretraining, weight_decay=1e-4), batch size 128 (effective 256 graphs), cosine decay, 200 epochs. GPU memory: ~8GB for batch size 128 with 104-node graphs.

finetuning_phase.predictor: 2-layer MLP (256→128→1) with ReLU, same as Day 2 best
finetuning_phase.training: AdamW (lr=1e-4, lower than Day 2's 3e-4 to avoid catastrophic forgetting, weight_decay=1e-4), linear warmup 5 epochs, cosine decay to 1e-6. Early stopping patience=50 on validation RMSE. Batch size 64, max 200 epochs.
finetuning_phase.data: Full Tg dataset (7170 polymers, 3-RU graphs, rich features, static RWPE k=32), 72/8/20 split (seed=71)

ablation_plan: A: No pretraining baseline = 35.94K (Day 2 best)
B: Pretrain with SimCLR-style augmentations on 1-RU graphs only (node dropout, edge perturbation) — tests whether contrastive learning on graph augmentations suffices without multimer signal
C: MoMuCon with 1-RU→2-RU pairs — tests whether 2-RU provides sufficient scale difference
D: MoMuCon with 1-RU→3-RU pairs (primary)
E: MoMuCon with 2-RU→3-RU pairs — tests whether larger RU difference helps
F: Pretrain on 200K vs 500K vs full 1M PI1M — tests data scale sensitivity
G: Frozen encoder finetuning vs full finetuning — tests whether pretrained features are directly transferable

Y: H1 confirmation — MoMuCon closes ≥2.5K of the 5.14K gap: If finetuning the MoMuCon-pretrained GAT achieves 32-33.4K RMSE (1.9-3.9K improvement over 35.94K baseline), the MoMuCon hypothesis is strongly supported. This would represent the single largest Day-over-Day improvement and confirm that the multimer effect generalizes as a pretraining signal. The remaining 1.2-2.6K gap to PerioGT's 30.8K would likely require PerioGT's specific periodicity-aware augmentations (which explicitly contrast periodic vs. non-periodic graphs) rather than our simpler monomer-vs-multimer contrast.

H1 partial — MoMuCon closes 1-2K: If finetuning achieves 34-35K (1-2K improvement), MoMuCon provides a meaningful but incomplete signal. This would suggest that 1-RU→3-RU contrast captures some polymer identity but misses the explicit periodicity signal that PerioGT's pretraining captures. Masked polymer modeling (masking nodes/edges and reconstructing them, analogous to TransPolymer's MLM but on graphs) should be explored next.

H1 disconfirmation — MoMuCon closes <1K: If finetuning achieves ≥35K, the monomer-vs-multimer contrastive signal is too weak to provide useful pretraining. Possible reasons: (a) 1-RU and 3-RU graphs of the same polymer are already very similar structurally — the contrastive task may be too easy and the model learns trivial features; (b) PI1M polymers may not overlap sufficiently with Tg dataset polymers in chemical space; (c) graph-level contrastive learning may need very large batch sizes (≥512) for effective negatives, and our batch size 128 may be insufficient. In this case, pivot to masked polymer modeling on graphs or node-level contrastive objectives.

H2 confirmation — 1-RU→3-RU > 1-RU→2-RU > 1-RU augmentations only: If the multimer-based contrastive pairs (D, E) outperform SimCLR-style graph augmentations (B), the multimer signal specifically carries useful pretraining information beyond generic graph augmentation. This would validate the Day 1 finding that multimer degree matters.

Critical diagnostic — t-SNE of pretrained embeddings: After pretraining, 1-RU and 3-RU embeddings of the same polymer should cluster tightly while different polymers are well-separated. If all embeddings collapse to a single cluster, the contrastive loss has failed (temperature too low, insufficient negatives). If embeddings are scattered randomly, the model hasn't learned meaningful features.

Negative result contingency — if MoMuCon fails completely: PerioGT's periodicity-aware contrastive learning (which explicitly contrasts periodic polymers with non-periodic or different-periodicity variants) may be necessary because it captures a stronger signal — the repeating structure itself, not just scale invariance. This would not invalidate the pretraining direction but would narrow it to periodicity-specific objectives. Additionally, TransPolymer's masked language modeling approach (mem_039) applied to polymer SMILES sequences rather than graphs could be a fallback.

memory.abstract: GPS-Lite: GAT Encoder + Single Global Attention Layer with SPD Bias — a minimal hybrid architecture that adds exactly one global attention layer after the proven GAT+RWPE encoder to capture long-range backbone periodicity without the complexity of interleaved GPS layers
memory.keyword: GPS-lite hybrid-architecture GAT-encoder global-attention SPD-bias periodicity polymer-Tg

H: GPS-Lite Hypothesis: The GPS framework (mem_088) demonstrated that hybrid MPNN+global-attention architectures achieve SOTA across 11 of 16 graph benchmarks. However, full interleaved GPS layers may be unnecessarily complex for polymer graphs, which are topologically simple (tree-like). A minimal hybrid — keeping the proven 4-layer GAT+RWPE encoder intact and adding exactly one global attention layer with SPD bias before readout — can capture the long-range backbone periodicity that local message-passing misses, without introducing the complexity that caused LSPE and SPSE to fail. This should provide 1-3K improvement over the 35.94K GAT+RWPE baseline while respecting the Simplicity Principle (only +1 layer added).

SPD-Periodicity Hypothesis: Shortest-path distances on a 3-RU polymer graph encode the repeating-monomer structure: atoms within the same repeat unit have small SPDs (1-5), atoms in adjacent repeat units have medium SPDs (5-15), and atoms in far repeat units have large SPDs (15-30+). A learned attention bias b_ij = MLP(one_hot(clip(SPD_ij, 0, 32))) per attention head allows the global attention mechanism to learn distance-dependent attention patterns that reflect backbone periodicity — atoms separated by exactly one monomer length receive characteristic bias values. This is a simpler, non-pretraining path to periodicity awareness: the SPD bias provides the structural prior that PerioGT's contrastive pretraining learns from data. If SPD bias alone provides ≥1K improvement, periodicity can be partially captured architecturally.

Simplicity-Compatibility Hypothesis: GPS-Lite is architecturally compatible with the Simplicity Principle because: (1) it adds only 1 layer to a proven architecture; (2) the SPD bias is a static, precomputed encoding (consistent with our finding that static RWPE > learned LSPE); (3) edge features are restricted to the GAT encoder (not the global attention), following GPS's design principle that decouples edge features from global attention to avoid O(N²E) complexity; (4) no learnable positional evolution, no max-aggregation, no edge-level path encodings — all mechanisms that failed on Days 1-2 are avoided.

architecture.encoder: GAT (4 layers, 256 hidden, 4 attention heads, mean aggregation) with static RWPE k=32 concatenated to rich node features at input. This is the proven Day-2-best architecture, frozen as a module. The encoder produces node representations H ∈ R^(N×256).
architecture.global_attention_layer: Single multi-head self-attention (8 heads, head_dim=32, total 256) with SPD attention bias. For each head h: Attention_h(Q,K,V) = softmax((QK^T)/√d + B_h) · V, where Q,K,V = Linear projections of H, and B_h[i,j] = MLP_h(one_hot(clip(SPD[i,j], 0, 32))) with MLP_h being a tiny 2-layer network: 33→16→1 (33 = 0..32 clipped SPD values). The per-head MLPs learn head-specific distance sensitivities.
architecture.residual: H' = LayerNorm(H + GlobalAttn(H)) — residual connection with layer normalization preserves the GAT encoder's representations while allowing the global attention to refine them.
architecture.readout: Mean pooling over H' → 2-layer MLP predictor (256→128→1) with ReLU, same as Day 2 best.
architecture.parameter_count: GAT encoder: ~1.2M (unchanged). Global attention: ~0.3M (QKV projections + output projection). SPD bias MLPs: ~1.1K per head × 8 = ~9K. Total: ~1.5M — only 25% increase over the 1.2M GAT baseline.

X.training_strategy: AdamW optimizer (lr=3e-4, weight_decay=1e-4), linear warmup 10 epochs, cosine decay to 1e-6. Gradient clipping at 1.0. Dropout 0.1 on attention weights, 0.2 on FFN. Early stopping patience=50 on validation RMSE. Batch size 64, max 300 epochs. Same Tg dataset: 7170 polymers, 3-RU, rich features, RWPE k=32, 72/8/20 split (seed=71).
ablation_plan: A: GAT+RWPE baseline (35.94K) — Day 2 best, no global attention
B: A + global attention WITHOUT SPD bias (plain self-attention) — tests whether global receptive field alone helps
C: B + SPD bias (primary GPS-Lite) — tests whether SPD-encoded periodicity specifically helps
D: C with Laplacian PE bias instead of SPD (b_ij = MLP(|λ_i − λ_j|) for top-8 eigenvectors) — tests whether general positional bias works as well as SPD
E: C with 2 global attention layers instead of 1 — tests whether more global processing helps or overfits
F: C with Performer linear attention instead of full quadratic attention — tests scalability to larger graphs
G: C where global attention uses only a subset of nodes (top-k by RWPE variance, k=32) instead of all ~104 nodes — tests whether sparse global attention suffices

Y: H1 confirmation — GPS-Lite achieves 33-35K (0.9-2.9K improvement): If adding the single global attention layer with SPD bias improves over the GAT+RWPE baseline by ≥0.9K, the GPS-Lite hypothesis is supported. This would demonstrate that even minimal global attention captures long-range structural signals that local GAT message-passing misses — likely backbone periodicity and chain-end effects. The improvement magnitude indicates how much of the 5.14K gap is addressable through architecture alone without pretraining.

H1 partial — GPS-Lite achieves 35-35.9K (0-0.9K improvement): If the improvement is marginal, global attention provides limited benefit for polymer Tg. This would align with the LSPE paper's finding (mem_089) that sparse GNNs outperform Transformers on molecular tasks where local structure dominates — polymer Tg may be predominantly determined by local chemistry (functional groups, ring structures) rather than global chain topology.

H1 disconfirmation — GPS-Lite degrades performance (>35.94K): If global attention worsens performance (as LSPE did: 37.96K vs 36.29K static), it would further strengthen the Simplicity Principle and the finding that global mechanisms overfit on limited polymer data. Global attention's O(N²) receptive field may introduce noise from distant, irrelevant atom pairs that drowns out the local chemical signal.

H2 confirmation — SPD bias provides ≥0.5K over plain global attention: If C (with SPD) > B (without SPD), the SPD-Periodicity hypothesis is supported — the shortest-path distance structure of polymer graphs encodes periodicity that the attention mechanism can exploit. This would provide a partial architectural path to periodicity awareness without PerioGT-level pretraining. Critical sub-test: attention weight analysis should reveal that atoms separated by ~1 monomer length receive systematically different attention than atoms at other distances.

H3 (Simplicity-Compatibility) confirmation: If GPS-Lite succeeds where LSPE and SPSE failed, it validates a design principle: simple architectural additions (one static layer) work, while complex learned mechanisms across all layers (LSPE, SkipRWPE) fail. This would refine the Simplicity Principle: 'add one simple thing at a time' rather than 'replace the learning paradigm.'

SPD diagnosticity check: Compute SPD histograms for 3-RU polymer graphs. If SPD distributions are highly similar across different polymers (e.g., all vinyl polymers have nearly identical SPD patterns), the SPD bias may provide limited discriminative signal. If SPD distributions vary meaningfully across polymer classes (vinyl vs. polyether vs. polyamide), the bias should help.

Expected performance range: GPS-Lite is expected to achieve 33-35.5K. Combined with architecture scaling to 5-6 layers and/or wider hidden dim (384-512), the non-pretraining ceiling may reach 32-34K. The remaining gap to 30.8K would then be closed by pretraining (Idea 1 — MoMuCon). If both GPS-Lite and MoMuCon succeed independently, combining them (pretrained GAT encoder + global attention layer, finetuned jointly) becomes the Day 4 integration experiment.

memory.abstract: SelfGNN proposes a contrastive self-supervised GNN framework that avoids explicit negative sampling by leveraging Batch Normalization for implicit contrastive terms, introduces four O(1) feature augmentation techniques competitive with O(N³) topological augmentations, and achieves performance comparable to supervised GNNs while consistently outperforming semi-supervised and unsupervised baselines on node classification across seven real-world datasets.
memory.keyword: ["self-supervised learning", "graph neural networks", "contrastive learning", "graph data augmentation", "batch normalization"]

content.background: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm bridging unsupervised and supervised methods, driven largely by contrastive learning (CL). CL works by maximizing similarity between augmented views of the same object while pushing them apart from negative samples. In computer vision, recent methods (BYOL, SimSiam) have shown that explicit negative samples can be dropped entirely — implicit contrastive terms from Batch Normalization suffice, and performance matches or exceeds supervised pretraining. However, in graph representation learning, virtually all SSL methods — including DGI, MvGRL, and GCC — rely on explicit negative sampling: they construct corrupted graph views or sample negative nodes from other graphs. Whether implicit negative sampling can work for GNNs remains an open question. Furthermore, graph data augmentation is underdeveloped compared to CV: most work focuses on topological augmentation (e.g., higher-order graph diffusion via PageRank or heat kernel), which incurs O(N³) matrix inversion and dramatically increases edge counts, causing GPU memory issues. Feature augmentation — standard in CV — has been largely neglected or even argued against for graphs. SelfGNN addresses both gaps: (1) it is the first contrastive SSL method for GNNs that uses only implicit negative samples via BatchNorm, and (2) it introduces four novel feature augmentation strategies that are O(1) and competitive with expensive topological augmentations.
content.method: SelfGNN adopts a Siamese network architecture with two parallel branches: a student network (left) and a teacher network (right). Both branches share the same structure — a GNN encoder f (representation block) that is agnostic to GNN type (GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, etc.) and produces node embeddings. The student additionally has a prediction block g (an MLP) on top. Given two augmented views G₁ and G₂ of the same graph G, the student encodes G₁ → f_θ(G₁) → g_θ(f_θ(G₁)), and the teacher encodes G₂ → f_φ(G₂). The loss is a cosine-similarity-based MSE: L_θ = 2 − 2·⟨g_θ(X₁), X₂⟩ / (||g_θ(X₁)||_F · ||X₂||_F). Critically, gradients flow only through the student (θ); the teacher's parameters φ are updated via exponential moving average (EMA) of θ: φ ← τφ + (1−τ)θ. This stop-gradient + EMA design, combined with BatchNorm layers in the network, introduces implicit negative samples that prevent representational collapse — the model cannot trivially output a constant vector. The authors empirically drop the projection head common in CV SSL (e.g., SimCLR, BYOL), finding it adds no gain for graphs. Four feature augmentation (FA) techniques are introduced: (1) Split: split features along the dimension into two halves X[:, :F/2] and X[:, F/2:]; (2) Standardize: z-score normalization across features; (3) Local Degree Profile (LDP): construct 5-statistic node features from local degree distributions, zero-padded to match original dimension; (4) Paste: concatenate LDP features to original features with reciprocal zero-padding. Three topological augmentations (TA) based on graph diffusion are used: PPR (personalized PageRank), Heat Kernel PageRank, and Katz-index — all involving matrix inversion. For scalability, a CLUSTERSELFGNN variant uses METIS clustering to partition the graph into subgraphs, applies TA per-subgraph, and trains in mini-batches.
content.experiment: Seven real-world datasets from PyTorch Geometric are used: three citation networks (Cora: 2,708 nodes, 5,278 edges, 1,433 features, 7 classes; Citeseer: 3,327/4,552/3,703/6; Pubmed: 19,717/44,324/500/3), two Amazon co-purchase networks (Photo: 7,487/119,043/745/8; Computers: 13,381/245,778/767/10), and two Arxiv author collaboration networks (CS: 18,333/81,894/6,805/15; Physics: 34,493/247,962/8,415/5). Citation networks use the Planetoid public split; others use 70/10/20 random stratified split. All models train for 1000 epochs with validation-based early stopping. SelfGNN uses a 2-layer GNN encoder (512→128 units), dropout 0.2, learning rate 0.0001, representation size 128. TA hyperparameters: α=0.15 (PPR), t=3 (HK), β=0.1 (Katz). Baselines include three supervised GNNs (GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE) trained with partial labels, and two self-supervised methods (DGI, MvGRL with three TA variants: PPR, HK, Katz). Evaluation: logistic regression classifier on frozen embeddings, 5-fold CV for Experiment 1; 50-run mean ± std for Experiment 3. Ablations study BatchNorm necessity (with vs. without), projection head effect, and Split perturbation sensitivity (random feature permutation before splitting).
content.result: Experiment 1 (vs. supervised GNNs): SelfGNN achieves comparable or better accuracy than supervised GCN/GAT/GraphSAGE on citation networks. On Cora, SelfGNN-SPLIT reaches 85.0% (GAT original: 79.1%); on Citeseer, 72.3% (GCN: 65.7%); on Pubmed, 82.7% (GAT: 77.5%). On fully-supervised Amazon and Arxiv datasets, supervised methods outperform SelfGNN, but the SSL gap narrows with feature augmentations. Among feature augmentations, Split and Standardize consistently perform best; LDP underperforms. Among topological augmentations, PPR and HK outperform Katz. For large graphs (CS, Physics), full-batch TA runs out of GPU memory. Experiment 2 (CLUSTERSELFGNN): The subgraph-sampling variant on Physics achieves results comparable to full-batch FA methods, solving the OOM problem with minimal accuracy loss. Experiment 3 (vs. self-supervised GNNs): SelfGNN's best FA variant (SELFBFA, typically Split) outperforms MvGRL across all datasets and matches or exceeds DGI — e.g., on Photo: 90.86% vs. DGI 92.6% vs. MvGRL-PPR 91.0%. Ablation: removing BatchNorm causes severe performance instability, confirming it as the critical implicit contrastive mechanism. LayerNorm fails similarly. The projection head adds no significant gain and increases variance. Random permutation before Split has negligible impact, showing robustness. A practical insight: TA methods need strong dropout (0.65–0.8) and few epochs (200–400), while FA needs mild dropout (0.2–0.35) and many epochs (1500), likely because higher-order TA graphs accelerate feature propagation. Limitations: SelfGNN loads two parallel GNNs in memory, doubling the memory footprint for full-batch training. The CLUSTERSELFGNN remedy is preliminary. Future work: principled scalable training for the dual-encoder architecture.
content.dataset: Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, Amazon Photo, Amazon Computers, Arxiv CS, Arxiv Physics
content.topic_relation: SelfGNN directly informs the Day 3-4 primary hypothesis on self-supervised pretraining for polymer Tg prediction. It provides a contrastive SSL framework that avoids explicit negative sampling — a design choice that simplifies pretraining on PI1M by removing the need for careful negative pair construction. The finding that BatchNorm alone prevents collapse (without negative samples, projection heads, or momentum encoders beyond EMA) offers a minimalist SSL recipe testable on polymer graphs. The feature augmentation techniques (Split, Standardize) are O(1) and could be adapted to polymer node/edge features. The paper also demonstrates that simple augmentations can match complex topological ones, aligning with the Simplicity Principle from Day 2.
content.topic_contribution: Actionable contributions for polymer SSL: (1) The Siamese student-teacher + EMA + BatchNorm architecture provides a concrete, simple SSL blueprint for PI1M pretraining — no negative pair mining needed, just two augmented views and MSE loss. (2) Feature augmentation strategies (especially Split and Standardize) can be directly adapted to polymer graphs as O(1) augmentations, sidestepping the O(N³) cost of topological diffusion augmentations on large polymer datasets. (3) The ablation evidence that BatchNorm is necessary and sufficient for collapse prevention, while projection heads are unnecessary for graphs, guides architecture decisions for polymer SSL implementations. (4) The CLUSTERSELFGNN subgraph-sampling strategy offers a template for scaling SSL to large PI1M-scale pretraining.

memory.abstract: MoCL proposes knowledge-aware contrastive learning for molecular graphs, introducing bioisostere-based substructure substitution (230 rules) as local-level augmentation that preserves molecular semantics, and ECFP-based global similarity contrast to encode inter-graph structural relationships, achieving SOTA on 7 molecular benchmarks under both linear and semi-supervised evaluation.

content.background: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become state-of-the-art for molecular property prediction but suffer from data hunger — task-specific labels in the biomedical domain (e.g., drug responses from biological experiments) are expensive and time-consuming to obtain. Self-supervised pretraining has thus been actively explored. Among pretraining paradigms, graph contrastive learning — which maximizes mutual information between paired graph augmentations — has shown effectiveness on downstream tasks. However, the existing graph contrastive learning framework has two critical limitations. First, augmentations (node dropping, edge perturbation, subgraph extraction, attribute masking) are designed for general graphs and can severely alter molecular semantics: dropping a carbon atom in a phenyl ring breaks the aromatic system, perturbing connections may introduce entirely different functional groups, and subgraph extraction yields arbitrary fragments not representative of molecular functionality. Only attribute masking preserves biological validity. Second, standard contrastive schemes only learn representations invariant to local perturbations, neglecting global dataset structure — some molecules should be closer in embedding space due to genuine structural or biological similarity. Additionally, accurately estimating mutual information in high dimensions is difficult, and the connection between MI maximization and contrastive learning success remains unclear, with metric learning potentially sharing deeper connections. These gaps motivate infusing domain knowledge into both augmentation design and contrastive schemes for molecular graphs.
content.method: MoCL leverages domain knowledge at two levels. **Local-level domain knowledge**: Instead of random corruption, MoCL proposes *substructure substitution* — replacing a valid substructure in a molecule with a bioisostere, a chemical group known to preserve similar physical/chemical properties. The authors compile 218 substitution rules from domain resources (covering 36 unique source substructures across 8 groups: carboxylic acid, ester, ketone, phenyl, tbutyl, disubstituted amide, monosubstituted amide, non-substituted amide), each represented as SMARTS string transformations. Since these rules mostly target heteroatom and aromatic ring positions, 12 additional rules for adding/dropping general carbon groups are appended, totaling 230 rules. The augmentation can be applied multiple times sequentially (MoCL-DK1 through MoCL-DK5), with rule availability dynamically updated as the molecule changes. **Global-level domain knowledge**: Extended Connectivity Fingerprints (ECFPs) encode substructure presence as binary vectors; Tanimoto coefficient between ECFP vectors quantifies structural similarity between molecules. MoCL incorporates this global similarity through two alternative objectives: (a) least-square loss directly matching embedding cosine similarity to fingerprint similarity, or (b) contrastive loss treating fingerprint-nearest neighbors as positive pairs. **Double contrast objective**: The full loss is L = L^local + λ·L^global, where L^local is the standard InfoNCE contrastive loss between two augmented views of the same graph, and L^global is the global similarity loss. The encoder is GIN (3 layers, 512 hidden dim), chosen for its expressiveness and ability to incorporate edge features. A 2-layer MLP projection head (128 dim) maps representations before contrast, using cosine similarity as the critic. The authors provide a theoretical lemma connecting the objective to metric learning: under simplifying assumptions (identity projection head, inner product similarity, 1-nearest neighbor, λ=1), the full objective decomposes into three triplet losses — two local (pulling augmented views together vs. pushing apart other molecules) and one global (pulling fingerprint-similar molecules together vs. pushing dissimilar ones apart). This unifies local transformation-invariance and global structure encoding within a single metric learning framework.
content.experiment: Evaluation uses 7 benchmark molecular datasets spanning diverse tasks: **bace** (1,513 molecules, binding affinity), **bbbp** (2,050 molecules, blood-brain barrier penetration), **clintox** (1,483 molecules, FDA clinical toxicity, 2 tasks), **mutag** (188 molecules, mutagenicity), **sider** (1,427 molecules, adverse drug reactions, 27 tasks), **tox21** (7,831 molecules, in vitro toxicity, 12 tasks), **toxcast** (8,597 molecules, in vitro toxicity, 617 tasks). Two evaluation protocols: **linear** (freeze pretrained representations, train linear classifier on top) and **semi-supervised** (initialize with pretrained weights, finetune all layers with limited labels; ~100 labeled molecules per dataset). Baselines include: Vanilla GNN trained from scratch, traditional graph pretraining methods (InfoGraph, EdgePred, ContextPred, Attribute Masking), and graph contrastive learning with four general augmentations (node dropping, edge perturbation, subgraph extraction, attribute masking). MICRO-Graph (motif-based contrastive) is also compared where reported results exist. All methods use 3-layer GIN (512 hidden), 128-dim embeddings, Adam optimizer (lr=0.001), dropout 0.5, batch size 32, 100 pretraining epochs. For domain augmentation, different repeat times {1,2,3,5} are tested. For global knowledge, λ ∈ {0.5, 1.0, 5.0, 10.0} and dataset-dependent neighbor sizes (e.g., {50,100,150,300} for most datasets, smaller for mutag, larger for tox21/toxcast). ECFP dimension 1024 with Tanimoto similarity. AUC is the primary metric for classification tasks. Data split: 80/10/10 train/val/test, 5 runs with different splits, early stopping via validation set.
content.result: **Local-level domain knowledge (Q1)**: Substructure substitution augmentation (MoCL-DK) consistently outperforms general augmentations. Representations from MoCL-DK plus a linear classifier achieve on-par or better accuracy than a fully-trained deep GNN. Combining MoCL-DK with attribute masking yields further improvements — this is the strongest augmentation pair because neither violates biological assumptions. Harder contrast via different augmentation combinations generally benefits more than same-augmentation pairs. Augmentation strength follows an inverted-U pattern: MoCL-DK3 (3 successive substitutions) usually achieves best results, with performance declining at MoCL-DK5. **Global-level domain knowledge (Q2)**: Adding global similarity information improves all augmentation schemes, but the gain is substantially larger for MoCL-DK than for general augmentations. The contrastive global loss (CL) consistently outperforms the least-square regression loss (LS). MoCL-DK-G(CL) achieves state-of-the-art: e.g., bace 0.845 (vs. scratch 0.785), bbbp 0.905 (vs. scratch 0.861), clintox 0.750 (vs. scratch 0.647), mutag 0.969 (vs. scratch 0.918), tox21 0.768 (vs. scratch 0.820), under linear protocol. Under semi-supervised protocol, improvements are also observed but with weaker margin. **Sensitivity analysis (Q3)**: A relatively small but not too small neighbor size combined with moderately large λ yields optimal results. **Key observations**: (1) Strong linear evaluation performance does not guarantee semi-supervised gains — finetuning all layers may override delicate initialization. (2) Single-property prediction tasks (mutag, bbbp) benefit more from pretraining than multi-task toxicity prediction (tox21, toxcast), as toxicity depends on cellular context beyond molecular structure. (3) Global similarity contrast is more effective when paired with domain-specific augmentation, suggesting synergistic effects between local and global domain knowledge. **Limitations**: Transfer learning across datasets was not evaluated; the approach depends on curated bioisostere rules; effectiveness varies by task nature.
content.dataset: bace, bbbp, clintox, mutag, sider, tox21, toxcast
content.topic_relation: Directly relevant to Day 3-4 primary hypothesis on self-supervised pretraining for polymer Tg. MoCL demonstrates that domain-knowledge-infused contrastive learning substantially outperforms generic graph augmentations — a finding that strengthens the case for polymer-specific pretraining design. The substructure substitution paradigm (chemically valid transformations) maps naturally to polymer-specific augmentations like monomer substitution or chain-length variation. The global similarity contrast using domain fingerprints (ECFP) can be adapted using polymer-specific fingerprints. The double contrast objective and theoretical connection to triplet loss provide a clean framework that can be ported to polymers.
content.topic_contribution: Provides three actionable design principles for polymer pretraining experiments: (1) **Domain-knowledge-guided augmentation**: Replace generic augmentations with chemically/physically valid transformations (for polymers: substitute one monomer with a chemically similar one, vary chain length while preserving backbone chemistry, add/drop repeat units). MoCL's 230 bioisostere rules are a template for compiling polymer-specific substitution rules. (2) **Global similarity contrast**: Use fingerprint-based similarity (e.g., polymer-specific ECFP variants or monomer-composition fingerprints) to define positive pairs beyond same-molecule augmentations, enabling the model to learn inter-polymer structural relationships. (3) **Double contrast objective with tunable λ**: Jointly optimize local invariance and global structure — the λ sensitivity analysis provides guidance for balancing these objectives. These principles are directly testable on PI1M pretraining → Tg finetuning and align with the Simplicity Principle (start with simple, well-motivated augmentations before complex frameworks).

memory.abstract: This paper applies Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) — a self-supervised learning method that predicts target graph embeddings from context graph embeddings in latent space rather than reconstructing input features — to stochastic polymer molecular graphs, demonstrating improved downstream property prediction in label-scarce scenarios, with particular benefit for transfer learning across different polymer chemical spaces.
memory.keyword: JEPA, self-supervised learning, polymer graphs, graph pretraining, contrastive learning, joint embedding, subgraphing
memory.content:
{
  "background": "Polymer informatics holds great promise for accelerating materials discovery through virtual screening and property prediction, yet progress is fundamentally bottlenecked by the scarcity of high-quality labeled polymer datasets—a consequence of the time- and cost-intensive nature of experimental synthesis and characterization. While transfer learning and multitask learning have been explored as mitigation strategies, self-supervised learning (SSL) offers a particularly appealing path by enabling pretraining on vast unlabeled polymer datasets before fine-tuning on limited labeled data. Prior SSL work on polymers has focused predominantly on text-based approaches operating on SMILES/pSMILES representations (polyBERT, TransPolymer), with limited exploration of graph-based SSL. The only prior graph-based SSL study for polymers (Gao et al., 2024) used node/edge masking and pseudolabel prediction on stochastic polymer graphs, finding that combining node-level and graph-level SSL tasks was most effective—consistent with broader findings in graph SSL literature. However, conventional graph SSL methods operate in input space, attempting to reconstruct masked node/edge features directly. This approach forces the model to predict every noisy, hard-to-predict detail of the input, which in high-dimensional molecular domains can lead to overfitting. The recently proposed Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), developed originally for image SSL, addresses this by operating in embedding space: rather than reconstructing raw inputs, JEPA predicts the embedding of a target view from the embedding of a context view. This embedding-space prediction encourages learning semantically rich representations that abstract away from low-level details. JEPA had been extended to graph-level tasks (Skenderi et al., 2023) but had not been applied to molecular graphs, particularly not to the unique structural characteristics of stochastic polymer graphs—which include weighted edges describing monomer ensembles, topologies, and stochasticity beyond simple repeat-unit graphs. This paper bridges that gap by studying JEPA-based SSL pretraining on stochastic polymer molecular graphs, investigating whether this embedding-space approach improves downstream property prediction when labeled data is scarce.",

  "method": "The polymer-JEPA framework operates on stochastic polymer graphs as introduced by Aldeghi & Coley (2022), where monomer graphs are connected through weighted edges indicating connection probabilities that reflect the polymer chain architecture. The core JEPA idea for graphs involves three stages: (1) **Subgraph partitioning**: the polymer graph is decomposed into a set of subgraphs using one of three algorithms—random walk subgraphing, motif-based subgraphing (via BRICS algorithm), or METIS clustering. From this set, a larger context subgraph and one or more smaller target subgraphs are selected or constructed. Context and target subgraphs must satisfy several constraints: the context must include elements from both monomers in copolymers, every edge and node must appear in at least one subgraph, context must be larger than targets, targets should minimally overlap with context, and the subgraph compositions must change at each training iteration to prevent overfitting. (2) **Dual-encoder architecture**: Two GNN encoders are employed—a context encoder and a target encoder. The GNN backbone is a variant of the weighted directed message passing neural network (wD-MPNN) from Aldeghi & Coley, but modified to use node-centered rather than edge-centered message passing (shown in Appendix B to not affect performance while being easier to implement in PyTorch Geometric). The context encoder processes only the context subgraph to produce a context embedding s_x via pooling of node embeddings. The target encoder processes the ENTIRE polymer graph (not just the target subgraph), enabling effective exchange of global information during message passing for contextualization of target embeddings. Target subgraph embeddings s_y are obtained by pooling only the node embeddings belonging to the target subgraph from the target encoder's full-graph output. (3) **Embedding-space prediction**: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) predictor h_φ takes as input the context embedding s_x summed with a linearly transformed positional encoding token p̃_i that encodes the relative position of each target subgraph: ŝ_y(i) = h_φ(s_x + p̃_i T̃). Positional encoding uses random-walk structural encoding (RWSE) at two levels: node-level (to maintain positional information when working with subgraphs) and subgraph/patch-level (encoding connectivity between context and target subgraphs). The loss is the average L2 distance (MSE) between predicted ŝ_y and true s_y across all m target subgraphs. (4) **Optional pseudolabel objective**: Motivated by prior work showing that transferring pseudolabel predictor weights improved downstream performance, the authors jointly train the encoder with both the JEPA objective and a molecular weight prediction task (weighted sum of monomer molecular weights), using an additional MLP predictor on top of the target encoder's polymer graph embedding. (5) **Training procedure**: The dataset (42,966 conjugated copolymer photocatalysts) is split 40% for pretraining, 40% for finetuning scenarios, and 20% for testing. After pretraining, only the trained target encoder is retained for finetuning; an MLP predictor is added on top, and finetuning is done end-to-end, updating both the target encoder and the MLP predictor.",

  "experiment": "**Dataset**: The primary dataset is the conjugated copolymer photocatalyst dataset from Aldeghi & Coley (2022), containing 42,966 polymers composed of 9 A monomers and 862 B monomers, classified by three chain architectures (alternating, random, block) and three stoichiometry ratios (1:1, 1:3, 3:1). Two downstream tasks are tested: (Task 1) predicting electron affinity (EA, regression) on the same conjugated copolymer dataset but held-out splits, and (Task 2) predicting phase behavior (classification into lamellae, cylinders, gyroid, spheres, or disordered) on a diblock copolymer dataset (Arora et al., 34) containing 4,780 labeled polymer samples across 49 diblock copolymers—representing a transfer learning scenario since this is a different polymer chemical space.

**Data split**: 40% pretraining (17,186 entries), 40% finetuning scenarios, 20% test. For the finetuning data scarcity study, labeled data availability is varied from 0.4% (192 polymers) to 24% (10,311 polymers) for Task 1, and from 4% (191 polymers) to 80% (3,824 polymers) for Task 2.

**Baselines**: (1) Supervised wD-MPNN without pretraining; (2) The input-space SSL method by Gao et al. (2024) using node/edge masking and pseudolabel prediction; (3) Random forest model using count-vector ECFP fingerprints (size 2048, radius 2) with polymer fingerprints obtained by averaging across an ensemble of 32 oligomer sequence fingerprints, following Aldeghi & Coley; (4) For the Gao et al. comparison, a 5-fold cross-validation with three repetitions and different splits is used for robustness due to small finetune dataset size. Both methods use wD-MPNN with 3 layers and hidden dimension 300.

**Metrics**: R² and RMSE for regression (EA prediction); AUPRC (area under Precision-Recall curve) for classification (phase behavior).

**Ablation study on subgraphing hyperparameters**: Each experiment pretrains on 40% of the conjugated copolymer dataset and finetunes on 0.4% (192 data points) to simulate label-scarce conditions. Parameters varied: (a) context subgraph size (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, 95% of total graph); (b) target subgraph size (5%, 10%, 15%, 20%); (c) number of target subgraphs (1-5); (d) subgraphing algorithm (random-walk, motif-based/BRICS, METIS). Random-walk subgraphing is used for size/number ablations due to its direct control over subgraph sizes. The default configuration for these ablations uses 3 target subgraphs of ~15% size with context size varying, or 60% context with target size varying.",

  "result": "**Downstream performance (Task 1—same chemical space)**: JEPA pretraining improves EA prediction performance especially in low labeled data scenarios. Improvements are observed for finetuning dataset sizes up to 4% (1,728 polymers); beyond ~8% labeled data, pretraining benefits plateau as supervised learning on available labels becomes sufficient. At the smallest scenario (0.4% labeled), pretraining yields substantial R² improvement; the improvement varies from 39.8% in the smallest labeled data scenario to 0.4% at 8% labeled data.

**Transfer learning (Task 2—different chemical space)**: Pretraining on conjugated copolymers consistently improves phase behavior classification on diblock copolymers across ALL labeled data scenarios (improvement of ~0.02–0.1 in AUPRC), even up to 80% labeled data. This demonstrates that the knowledge acquired during pretraining is not overfitting to the training chemical space but rather learning general chemical knowledge about polymers that transfers across different polymer types. The authors expect this to be especially advantageous for small datasets with complex structure-property relationships.

**Comparison to input-space SSL (Gao et al., 2024)**: Overall performance is comparable between embedding-space (JEPA) and input-space (node/edge masking) SSL. JEPA performs slightly better in very low data scenarios, while Gao et al.'s method performs better with more labeled data available. The pseudolabel objective provides consistent improvement for input-space SSL but smaller, less consistent improvement for JEPA—suggesting that JEPA's embedding-space prediction may already implicitly capture molecular-weight-relevant information.

**Comparison to random forest baseline**: The random forest model with expert-engineered ECFP fingerprints outperforms the pretrained wD-MPNN in very low labeled data regimes (0.4% and 0.8%), and on the diblock dataset it outperforms throughout all data scenarios—likely because the mole fraction alone is highly informative for determining copolymer phase behavior (an atypical case). However, JEPA's advantage is that it eliminates reliance on handcrafted descriptors, learning directly from polymer graph structure.

**Subgraphing ablation findings**: (a) Optimal context subgraph size: 60% (~10-15 atoms of the ~20-25 atom polymer graph). The model is robust to context size changes, with a suggested broadly effective range of 50-75%. (b) Optimal target subgraph size: 10% of total graph (~2-3 atoms). The ideal range balances effective learning without oversimplification. A target size of 10-20% is hypothesized to be effective across different molecular sizes. (c) Number of targets: a single target provides best performance, though the model is not highly sensitive to this parameter. Fewer targets may increase exposure to diverse subgraphs per epoch. (d) Subgraphing algorithm: all three algorithms perform similarly, with random-walk subgraphing showing the best performance and stability. Motif-based (BRICS) subgraphing underperforms slightly despite producing chemically meaningful subgraphs, likely because it produces a small, deterministic set of subgraphs, limiting variability. METIS generates more subgraphs on average than motif-based, introducing more variability. Random-walk subgraphing generates different subgraphs at every epoch and allows greater control over sizes.

**Key principles**: (1) Variations in subgraphs and subgraph sizes play a more crucial role in determining model performance than the chemical meaningfulness of subgraphs themselves. (2) The embedding-based nature of JEPA offers promising opportunities for integrating multimodal data in pretraining.",

  "dataset": "Conjugated copolymer photocatalyst dataset (42,966 polymers, 9 A monomers × 862 B monomers, 3 chain architectures × 3 stoichiometry ratios) from Aldeghi & Coley (2022); Diblock copolymer dataset (4,780 samples, 49 diblock copolymers) from Arora et al. (34)",

  "topic_relation": "This paper directly addresses the 'Self-Supervised Pretraining' primary hypothesis in TopicState, providing a concrete SSL framework (JEPA) that operates on polymer graphs rather than text-based representations. It is complementary to PerioGT (mem_078, mem_079), which uses periodicity-aware contrastive pretraining with a graph transformer, while JEPA uses embedding-space prediction with wD-MPNN encoders. The finding that embedding-space SSL captures general polymer knowledge transferable across chemical spaces supports the pretraining direction. The paper also relates to the 'Data Centric Foundation' hypothesis through its use of stochastic polymer graph representations (Aldeghi & Coley) and the finding that subgraph construction strategy (random-walk vs. motif-based vs. METIS) significantly affects pretraining quality—analogous to how multimer construction affected supervised GAT performance in mem_080. The comparison showing that JEPA slightly outperforms input-space SSL in very low data regimes but underperforms with more data provides nuanced evidence about when embedding-space vs. input-space SSL is preferable.",

  "topic_contribution": "Provides several actionable contributions for Day 3-4 pretraining experiments: (1) JEPA offers an alternative SSL paradigm to contrastive learning—rather than contrasting positive/negative pairs, JEPA learns by predicting target embeddings from context embeddings in latent space, which may be simpler to implement and tune than contrastive methods requiring careful negative pair construction. (2) The dual-encoder design with a target encoder that processes the full graph (for global context) while only pooling target nodes provides a template for polymer SSL architectures. (3) The finding that subgraph construction strategy matters more than chemical meaningfulness of subgraphs suggests that simple random-walk subgraphing with controlled sizes is sufficient—this aligns with the Simplicity Principle (mem_096). (4) The transfer learning result (pretraining on one polymer space improves prediction in another) provides evidence that PI1M-scale pretraining should generalize to Tg prediction even if PI1M and Tg datasets cover somewhat different polymer chemistries. (5) The pseudolabel finding that JEPA already captures molecular-weight-relevant information suggests that polymer-specific SSL may not need explicit auxiliary objectives if the SSL task itself is well-designed. (6) The subgraphing hyperparameter guidelines (context: 50-75%, target: 10-20%, single target, random-walk subgraphing) provide concrete starting points for adapting JEPA to polymer Tg prediction."
}

memory.abstract: KPGT introduces a novel self-supervised learning framework that combines a Line Graph Transformer (LiGhT) emphasizing chemical bonds via line graph representation with path/distance encodings, and a knowledge-guided pre-training strategy that leverages molecular descriptors and fingerprints through a virtual knowledge node to guide masked node prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 11 molecular property prediction benchmarks.
memory.keyword: ["self-supervised learning", "graph transformer", "molecular property prediction", "line graph", "knowledge-guided pre-training"]

content.background: Molecular property prediction is central to drug and material discovery. Molecules are naturally represented as graphs with atoms as nodes and chemical bonds as edges, and GNNs have been widely adopted for learning molecular representations. However, due to the scarcity of labeled molecules and the vast chemical space, supervised GNNs often generalize poorly, especially on out-of-distribution samples. Self-supervised learning (SSL) on large-scale unlabeled molecules has emerged as a promising solution, but existing methods face two critical bottlenecks. First, pre-training tasks are ill-defined: generative methods that randomly mask nodes/edges fail to recognize that small structural changes in molecules can drastically alter properties, capturing only weak valency rules rather than the rich semantics linking structure to molecular properties. Contrastive methods that apply graph augmentations (node dropping, edge perturbation) similarly risk corrupting fundamental molecular semantics. Second, model capacity is limited: most SSL methods rely on GNNs like GIN, which struggle to capture long-range dependencies and the diverse information needed across properties spanning quantum mechanics, physical chemistry, biophysics, and physiology. While transformer-based models have revolutionized NLP and CV, their application to molecular graphs remains underexplored due to the difficulty of encoding graph structural information. KPGT addresses both issues by proposing a high-capacity graph transformer and a knowledge-guided pre-training strategy that injects chemically meaningful semantics into the generative SSL framework.
content.method: KPGT comprises two synergistic components: the Line Graph Transformer (LiGhT) architecture and the knowledge-guided pre-training strategy. **LiGhT**: A molecular graph G = (V, E) is first transformed into a line graph Ĝ where each edge e_{i,j} in G becomes a node v̂_{i,j} in Ĝ, and two nodes in Ĝ are connected if their corresponding edges in G share a common node. Each line-graph node's initial feature embedding is the concatenation of the transformed sum of its two endpoint atom features and the transformed bond features. This design explicitly elevates chemical bonds—which encode rich information about how atoms are held together and strongly influence molecular properties—to first-class entities, unlike prior graph transformers that treat edge features as mere attention biases or ignore them entirely. LiGhT employs a standard transformer encoder with multi-head self-attention and feed-forward networks, but crucially augments the attention mechanism with two structural encodings: Path Encoding (PE), which encodes the complete shortest path between two nodes—importantly including node features along the path, not just edge features as in prior work—into a scalar added to the attention matrix; and Distance Encoding (DE), which encodes the shortest-path distance between nodes via a learned MLP into an attention scalar. These encodings inject graph connectivity into the otherwise structure-agnostic transformer. **Knowledge-Guided Pre-training**: The core insight is that directly masking and predicting nodes in molecular graphs provides only weak supervision because many different atoms can satisfy local valency rules. To supply the missing semantics, KPGT introduces a virtual Knowledge Node (K node) connected to all nodes, initialized with readily available molecular descriptors (200 quantitative descriptors from RDKit, e.g., LogP) and fingerprints (512-bit RDKit fingerprints encoding substructure presence). These serve as the semantic context lost during masking. During pre-training, a proportion (optimally 50%) of line-graph nodes are masked (80% replaced with a [MASK] token, 10% random, 10% unchanged), and simultaneously a proportion of the K node's features are masked. The model predicts the original node types via cross-entropy loss, masked descriptors via RMSE regression loss, and masked fingerprint bits via binary cross-entropy loss. The K node's knowledge can be attended to by all other nodes through self-attention, thus guiding the model to learn meaningful structure-property relationships rather than merely memorizing valency patterns. The entire framework has approximately 100 million parameters.
content.experiment: KPGT was pre-trained on 2 million unlabeled molecules from ChEMBL29. Molecular graphs were constructed and features initialized using RDKit, with atom features (atom type, degree, formal charge, chirality, hybridization, etc.) and bond features (bond type, stereo, ring membership, conjugation). LiGhT used 12 transformer layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads, and ~100M parameters. Pre-training used Adam optimizer (lr=2e-4, weight decay=1e-6), batch size 1024, 100K steps, on four Nvidia A100 GPUs (~2 days). Masking rate was set to 0.5. After pre-training, KPGT was evaluated on 11 downstream datasets: 8 classification (BACE, BBBP, ClinTox, SIDER, Estrogen, MetStab, Tox21, ToxCast) measured by AUROC, and 3 regression (FreeSolv, ESOL, Lipophilicity) measured by RMSE. Scaffold splitting (8:1:1 train/val/test) was used with 3 random seeds. Two evaluation protocols were employed: feature extraction (frozen pre-trained encoder, only predictor trained) and transfer learning (full fine-tuning). For fine-tuning, a 2-layer MLP predictor with ReLU was added; Adam optimizer with batch size 32, 50 epochs, early stopping (patience=20); 48 hyperparameter combinations (learning rates [1e-6,3e-6,1e-5,3e-5], dropout [0,0.05,0.1,0.2], weight decay [0,1e-6,1e-4]) were grid-searched per dataset. Baselines included 12 state-of-the-art SSL methods: generative (Edgepred, Masking, Contextpred, Masking+Sup, Contextpred+Sup, GROVER) and contrastive (Infomax, GraphLoG, GraphCL, JOAO, 3DInfomax, GraphMVP). Ablation studies compared LiGhT against GIN, vanilla Transformer, and Graphormer (all at ~3.5M parameters for fairness); evaluated the contribution of pre-training; compared against directly using descriptors+fingerprints (MD+FP) and GROVER+FP; and tested masking rates of 15%, 30%, 50%, and 60%.
content.result: KPGT consistently outperformed all baseline methods across both evaluation settings. Under feature extraction, KPGT achieved an average AUROC of 0.825 (vs. second-best GROVER at 0.790) on classification and RMSE of 1.273 (vs. GROVER 1.557) on regression, representing overall relative improvements of 5% (3.5% classification, 8.9% regression). Under transfer learning, KPGT achieved 0.843 AUROC and 1.175 RMSE, with 3.9% overall improvement (2.2% classification, 8.3% regression). Several key findings emerged: (1) Methods incorporating additional molecular knowledge (Contextpred+Sup, Masking+Sup, GROVER) generally outperformed those without, validating the importance of semantic guidance. (2) High-capacity models (GROVER's transformer) outperformed GNN-based methods, confirming the need for large model capacity. (3) Transfer learning generally improved over feature extraction, though on some datasets (BACE, SIDER, MetStab) performance was comparable or worse, suggesting catastrophic forgetting as a future challenge. Ablation studies confirmed: LiGhT backbone outperformed GIN, vanilla Transformer, and Graphormer; pre-training provided 5.1% (classification) and 18.8% (regression) relative improvements over training from scratch; KPGT outperformed simply concatenating descriptors and fingerprints (MD+FP and GROVER+FP), showing it learned semantics beyond the injected knowledge; and a 50% masking rate was optimal, much higher than the typical 15% in prior work, indicating the knowledge node effectively guided prediction. Limitations include: potential catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning; reliance on 2D molecular graphs without 3D geometry; and the additional knowledge was not carefully curated (only RDKit defaults). Future directions include exploring better fine-tuning strategies and incorporating 3D structural information.
content.dataset: Pre-training: ChEMBL29 (2M molecules). Downstream: BACE, BBBP, ClinTox, SIDER, ToxCast, Tox21, Estrogen, MetStab (classification, AUROC); FreeSolv, ESOL, Lipophilicity (regression, RMSE). All from MoleculeNet benchmark.
content.topic_relation: This paper directly relates to the hypothesis that self-supervised pre-training with domain-specific knowledge integration can improve molecular representation learning. It provides evidence that (1) graph transformers with structural encodings outperform GNNs for molecular graphs, (2) knowledge-guided masking outperforms standard generative SSL, and (3) the line graph representation is an effective way to emphasize chemical bond information. It also demonstrates that high masking rates (50%) are viable when semantic guidance is provided, contrasting with the typical 15% in BERT-style molecular pre-training.
content.topic_contribution: KPGT provides actionable evidence that: (1) A line graph representation combined with path/distance structural encodings is a strong backbone design choice for molecular graph transformers. (2) Incorporating readily available cheminformatics knowledge (descriptors, fingerprints) as a virtual node during pre-training significantly improves downstream performance. (3) The optimal masking rate for knowledge-guided pre-training is around 50%, enabling the design of more efficient pre-training regimes. These findings enable experimental decisions about architecture selection (LiGhT vs. GIN vs. Graphormer), pre-training strategy (knowledge-guided vs. standard masking vs. contrastive), and hyperparameter configuration (masking rate, knowledge sources) for molecular property prediction tasks.

memory.abstract: Day 3 Exp#1: GraphMAE-style masked node feature pretraining on PI1M yields marginal +0.34-0.58K improvement over non-pretrained baseline — hypothesis NOT supported. Key lessons: (1) node-level masked reconstruction may be too local a pretraining task for graph-level Tg prediction, (2) pretrained models overfit more severely (4.5K val-test gap vs 1.8K baseline), (3) pretraining loss reduction (69%) confirms the task is learnable but doesn't transfer.

memory.abstract: PSPE: Polymer-Specific Positional Encodings (distance-to-chain-end, monomer-index-along-backbone) as additive node features to improve upon static RWPE for polymer Tg prediction — testing whether explicit 1D chain-geometry signals capture what RWPE's spectral encoding only implicitly represents

memory.content: {"H": ["PSPE Hypothesis: RWPE k=32 encodes chain position implicitly through random walk landing probabilities — a spectral, global encoding. But polymer graphs are fundamentally 1D chains with well-defined backbone geometry. Explicit chain-geometry features — distance to nearest chain terminus (dce) and monomer index along backbone (mi) — should provide a cleaner, more direct positional signal that complements or surpasses RWPE. Since these features directly encode the physical reality of polymer chains (end effects, monomer position), they should improve Tg prediction by 1-3K over the RWPE-only baseline.", "Chain-End Effect Hypothesis: Polymer chain ends have higher free volume and mobility than interior segments, affecting Tg. Distance-to-chain-end encodes this physical effect explicitly. If dce alone provides ≥0.5K improvement, chain-end physics is a learnable signal for Tg.", "Monomer-Sequence Hypothesis: In 3-RU multimers, different monomer positions (first, middle, last repeat unit) experience different local environments due to end-group proximity. Monomer-index encodes this. If mi alone provides ≥0.5K, monomer position matters beyond what RWPE captures.", "Additivity Hypothesis: PSPE-combined (dce + mi concatenated) should outperform either alone, as the two encodings capture complementary aspects of chain geometry (radial position from ends vs. sequential position along backbone)."], "X": {"dataset": "Tg (7170 polymers, 3-RU multimer graphs, 72/8/20 split seed=71)", "architecture": "4-layer GAT (GATv2Conv), 256 hidden dim, 4 attention heads, mean readout, predictor MLP (256→128→64→1) with ReLU, Dropout=0.1. AdamW (lr=1e-3, wd=1e-5).", "features": "Rich chemical features (atomic number, hybridization, aromaticity, degree, formal charge, ring membership, chirality, hydrogen count) + static RWPE k=32 (proven 35.94K baseline)", "pspe_variants": ["a) PSPE-dce: distance-to-chain-end (scalar, normalized [0,1])", "b) PSPE-mi: monomer-index-along-backbone (scalar, normalized [0,1])", "c) PSPE-combined: dce + mi concatenated (2 scalars)", "d) BASELINE: RWPE k=32 only (35.94K target)"], "backbone_identification": "Find longest simple path in heavy-atom graph via double-BFS: BFS from arbitrary node to find farthest node A, BFS from A to find farthest node B, path A→B is backbone approximation. memory.abstract: Integration: PSPE pushes non-pretraining ceiling to 35.44K (-0.50K from Day 2). Improvement trajectory shows exponential decay (+4.75K→+0.91K→+0.50K), confirming we are asymptotically approaching the GAT+RWPE non-pretraining ceiling. Remaining 4.64K gap to SOTA likely requires pretraining. Round 1 pitfall demonstrates critical importance of reproducing known baselines before measuring experimental effects.
