memory.abstract: Integration: The Node-to-Graph Pretraining Alignment Gap — Day 3's GraphMAE experiment (mem_105) demonstrates that node-level masked reconstruction on PI1M transfers only +0.34-0.58K to graph-level Tg prediction, despite 69% pretraining loss reduction confirming the local task is learnable. This is not a scaling failure but a structural misalignment: reconstructing atom features teaches local chemistry (valency, hybridization), while Tg depends on global polymer properties (chain stiffness, free volume, backbone flexibility) that emerge at the whole-chain level. The four Day 3 papers collectively validate this: MoCL (mem_102) uses graph-level contrastive + global similarity objectives, Polymer-JEPA (mem_103) uses embedding-space prediction at subgraph/graph level, KPGT (mem_104) succeeds with node masking only because the virtual knowledge node injects graph-level semantic descriptors, and SelfGNN (mem_101) operates at graph-level contrastive — none rely on pure node reconstruction. The alignment gap is fundamental: pretraining objectives must operate at the same structural level as the downstream task.
memory.keyword: pretraining-alignment node-vs-graph GraphMAE-failure graph-level-SSL structural-misalignment polymer-Tg fundamental-insight

content.integration_type: principled insight — structural misalignment between pretraining objective level and downstream task level
consensus: Node-level masked reconstruction (GraphMAE-style) does not transfer to graph-level Tg prediction. Both experimental runs (mem_105) are consistent: +0.34K and +0.58K, well below the 1.5K hypothesis threshold.
The pretraining task itself is learnable — 65-69% loss reduction on PI1M confirms the GAT encoder successfully learns to reconstruct masked node features. The problem is transfer, not learnability.

All four Day 3 paper architectures that succeed on molecular property prediction use objectives at or above the graph level: MoCL's graph-level contrastive, Polymer-JEPA's graph/subgraph-level embedding prediction, KPGT's knowledge-guided node masking (graph-level semantics via virtual node), SelfGNN's graph-level contrastive with BatchNorm.
Graph-level (or graph-informed) pretraining objectives are the necessary direction for PI1M → Tg pretraining.

conflicts.conflict: KPGT (mem_104) uses node-level masked prediction (line-graph node masking at 50% rate) and achieves SOTA on 11 molecular benchmarks — this appears to contradict the 'node-level = dead end' narrative.
conflicts.resolution: KPGT's success depends critically on the virtual Knowledge Node that injects 200 RDKit molecular descriptors and 512-bit fingerprints — graph-level semantic information. Without the K-node, the masked node prediction would suffer the same alignment gap. The K-node provides a bridge: node-level reconstruction guided by graph-level knowledge. This is not pure node-level SSL — it is graph-informed node-level SSL. The distinction matters for polymer pretraining design.

conflicts.conflict: Polymer-JEPA (mem_103) uses target subgraph embeddings pooled from full-graph processing — this operates at a subgraph level, not strictly graph-level. The target subgraph may be as small as 2-3 atoms (~10% of graph).
conflicts.resolution: JEPA's prediction is in embedding space (not input space), and the target encoder processes the entire polymer graph — so target embeddings are globally contextualized even though only target subgraph nodes are pooled. This is a hybrid: subgraph-level prediction with global context. Critically, JEPA does NOT reconstruct raw atom features — it predicts latent embeddings that encode relational structure.

alignment: The alignment principle: pretraining objective level must match downstream task level. For graph-level regression (Tg), use graph-level pretraining tasks (contrastive, graph-property prediction, embedding prediction). For node-level tasks (e.g., atom reactivity prediction), node-level pretraining tasks (masked node reconstruction) would be appropriate.

MoCL's double contrast objective (mem_102) explicitly addresses this: local contrast for transformation invariance + global similarity contrast for inter-graph structure. The λ hyperparameter balances these. For Tg, the global component would carry more weight.

SelfGNN (mem_101) provides the simplest graph-level SSL blueprint: Siamese student-teacher, BatchNorm for implicit negatives, no projection head, O(1) feature augmentations. This can be directly adapted to PI1M polymers.
content.narrative: Day 3's most important finding is not that GraphMAE failed — it's why it failed. The GraphMAE experiment (mem_105) was the critical negative result that reveals the alignment gap between pretraining objective level and downstream task level. The GAT encoder demonstrably learned to reconstruct masked node features from PI1M polymers (69% loss reduction), but this local chemistry knowledge did not transfer to graph-level Tg prediction (+0.34-0.58K). Tg is not a sum of local atomic contributions — it is an emergent property of the entire polymer chain: backbone flexibility, inter-chain free volume, rotational barriers, collective segmental motion. Reconstructing whether a masked carbon is sp² or sp³ teaches the model chemistry but not polymer physics. The four papers read on Day 3 (mem_101-104) collectively validate this insight from the positive direction: every SSL framework that succeeds on molecular property prediction uses objectives that operate at or incorporate the graph level. MoCL uses graph-level contrastive learning with global fingerprint similarity. Polymer-JEPA predicts full-graph-contextualized target embeddings. KPGT's virtual knowledge node injects graph-level molecular descriptors to guide node prediction. SelfGNN contrasts entire graph views. None rely on pure, unguided node-level reconstruction. The alignment principle is now clear: for graph-level Tg prediction, pretrain with graph-level objectives. This narrows Day 4's pretraining design space to contrastive (MoMuCon mem_099, SelfGNN-style mem_101) or embedding-predictive (JEPA-style mem_103) approaches, and explicitly rules out GraphMAE-style and BERT-style node masking without graph-level semantic guidance.

memory.abstract: Integration: The Exponential Convergence to the Non-Pretraining Ceiling — Improvement trajectory across Days 1-3 shows unmistakable exponential decay: baseline 50.5K → architecture scaling +4.75K (Day 2) → static RWPE +0.91K (Day 2) → PSPE +0.50K (Day 3). The half-life of non-pretraining improvements is approximately 1 day, and the GAT+RWPE+PSPE architecture is asymptotically converging toward ~35K RMSE. The residual 4.64K gap to PerioGT's 30.8K SOTA is now clearly beyond the reach of feature engineering or GAT architecture refinement — it requires either pretraining on PI1M or a fundamentally different architectural class (graph transformers with periodicity-aware encodings). This marks the strategic pivot from non-pretraining optimization to pretraining as the primary lever.
memory.keyword: exponential-decay non-pretraining-ceiling improvement-trajectory diminishing-returns strategic-pivot pretraining-necessity 35.44K

content.integration_type: strategic synthesis — trajectory analysis and research direction pivot
consensus: The non-pretraining improvement trajectory follows a clear exponential decay pattern: Day 1→2 architecture scaling (+4.75K), Day 2 RWPE (+0.91K), Day 3 PSPE (+0.50K). Each successive improvement is roughly half the previous.
The current non-pretraining best is 35.44K RMSE (GAT+RWPE k=32+PSPE-combined, mem_107), representing a cumulative -15.06K improvement from the original 50.5K GAT baseline.

The residual gap to PerioGT SOTA (30.8K) is 4.64K. Extrapolating the exponential decay: even with 3 more days of feature/architecture optimization at the same rate, we would asymptotically approach ~34.5-35.0K — still ~3.5-4K short of SOTA.

PSPE's orthogonal signal to RWPE (max |r| < 0.35, mem_107) confirms we are extracting genuinely new information from chain geometry, but the magnitude is inherently limited because polymer graphs are topologically simple — there is only so much positional information to encode.

The Round 1 pitfall (mem_107, mem_108) demonstrates that baseline fidelity is critical for measuring diminishing effects: a broken baseline inflated the PSPE-dce effect to -2.25K; the true effect is -0.79K.

conflicts.conflict: mem_108 already integrates the PSPE trajectory. Is this integration redundant?
conflicts.resolution: mem_108 focuses on the PSPE experiment specifically — its contribution and the Round 1 pitfall. This integration (mem_110) takes the broader, multi-day trajectory view: the exponential decay pattern across Days 1-3, the strategic implications for Day 4-7 planning, and the formal argument that pretraining is now the only viable path. mem_108 is a within-day integration; mem_110 is a cross-day strategic integration.

alignment: The exponential decay pattern aligns with the Simplicity Principle (mem_096): simple, high-impact changes (architecture scaling, rich features) were discovered first and provided the largest gains; progressively more complex refinements (RWPE, PSPE) provide progressively smaller gains.

The trajectory also aligns with the Topological Simplicity Constraint (mem_097): polymer graphs are fundamentally simple (1D chains with sparse branching), so there is an intrinsic limit to how much structural encoding can improve prediction — once the 1D chain geometry is adequately encoded (via RWPE + PSPE), further encoding refinement hits diminishing returns hard.

The undertraining-to-true-ceiling insight from mem_098 is confirmed and extended: the Day 1 ceiling (41.6K) was an undertraining artifact; architecture scaling revealed the true non-pretraining ceiling now estimated at ~34.5-35.0K.
content.narrative: The cumulative improvement trajectory tells an unambiguous story. Day 1 established a 50.5K GAT baseline and a 41.6K 'preprocessing ceiling' that was later revealed as an undertraining artifact. Day 2's architecture scaling (3→4 layers, 128→256 hidden, AdamW, deeper MLP) delivered +4.75K — the single largest improvement, reaching 36.85K — and simultaneously discovered that static RWPE k=32 added +0.91K to reach 35.94K. Day 3's PSPE experiment added +0.50K to reach 35.44K. The pattern is unmistakably exponential: each Day's best improvement is roughly half of the previous Day's. The asymptote for GAT-based architectures with rich features and node-level positional encodings appears to be ~35K. The 4.64K gap to PerioGT's 30.8K SOTA cannot be closed by further feature engineering — the exponential trajectory predicts that even with perfect additional encodings, the theoretical limit is ~34.5-35.0K. This is not a failure of our approach; it is the natural limit of what can be learned from 7,170 labeled Tg samples without leveraging the 1M unlabeled polymers in PI1M. Day 4's GPS-Lite idea (mem_100) — a single global attention layer with SPD bias — represents the final non-pretraining experiment worth pursuing because it changes the architectural class (adding global receptive field), not just the feature encoding. If GPS-Lite provides a 1-2K jump, it would suggest that architectural innovation can push the ceiling lower; if it provides <1K (as the exponential trend predicts), pretraining becomes not just advisable but necessary. The strategic implication for Days 4-7 is clear: the non-pretraining optimization phase is complete. The remaining research budget should be allocated to pretraining experiments (MoMuCon mem_099, SelfGNN-style mem_101, JEPA-style mem_103) with GPS-Lite as a final, bounded non-pretraining exploration.

memory.abstract: Integration: Design Principles for Polymer Graph SSL — A synthesis of Day 3's four SSL papers (SelfGNN, MoCL, Polymer-JEPA, KPGT) and two experiments (GraphMAE negative, PSPE positive) into five actionable design principles for PI1M pretraining. (1) Graph-level objectives are mandatory — node-level reconstruction is structurally misaligned with Tg. (2) Domain-knowledge-guided augmentations dramatically outperform generic graph augmentations. (3) Embedding-space prediction (JEPA) and contrastive learning (MoCL, SelfGNN) are both viable paradigms, with JEPA offering cross-chemical-space transfer and contrastive offering simplicity. (4) Incorporating polymer-specific fingerprints/descriptors as global semantic context (KPGT-style virtual node) can bridge local pretraining tasks to global property understanding. (5) Simplicity transfers: SelfGNN's BatchNorm-only collapse prevention and Polymer-JEPA's random-walk subgraphing both demonstrate that simple mechanisms suffice when well-tuned.
memory.keyword: SSL-design-principles polymer-pretraining graph-level-objective domain-knowledge embedding-space contrastive virtual-knowledge-node PI1M

content.integration_type: design synthesis — actionable principles from literature + experiments
consensus: Principle 1 — Graph-Level Objective Mandate: All successful molecular SSL frameworks (mem_101-104) use objectives at or informed by the graph level. Node-level reconstruction alone (mem_105) is confirmed as insufficient. For PI1M → Tg pretraining, the objective must be graph-level: contrastive (MoMuCon mem_099, SelfGNN mem_101), embedding-predictive (JEPA mem_103), or graph-informed node prediction (KPGT mem_104).

Principle 2 — Domain-Knowledge Augmentation: MoCL (mem_102) demonstrates that bioisostere-based substructure substitution (230 rules) outperforms generic augmentations (node dropping, edge perturbation, subgraph extraction) by 2-5% absolute AUROC across molecular benchmarks. For polymers, analogous augmentations include: monomer substitution within the same chemical class, chain-length variation, and backbone-chemistry-preserving transformations. Random node/edge perturbation risks breaking polymer backbone connectivity — a chemically invalid transformation.

Principle 3 — Two Viable SSL Paradigms: Contrastive learning (SelfGNN mem_101, MoCL mem_102) and embedding-space prediction (Polymer-JEPA mem_103) are both proven on molecular/polymer graphs. SelfGNN offers the simplest implementation: Siamese student-teacher + BatchNorm + O(1) feature augmentations, no negative pair mining, no projection head. Polymer-JEPA offers cross-chemical-space transfer evidence (conjugated copolymers → diblock copolymers) directly relevant to PI1M → Tg. The choice depends on whether we prioritize simplicity (SelfGNN) or transfer guarantees (JEPA).

Principle 4 — Global Semantic Context via Virtual Node: KPGT (mem_104) demonstrates that a virtual knowledge node carrying molecular descriptors (200 RDKit descriptors + 512-bit fingerprints) dramatically improves masked node prediction — the knowledge node provides the global semantic context that bridges local prediction to global properties. For polymers: monomer composition fingerprints, chain-length, molecular weight, and RDKit polymer descriptors can be injected via a virtual node during pretraining, potentially making even node-level objectives viable through the knowledge bridge.

Principle 5 — Simplicity Transfers: SelfGNN shows BatchNorm alone prevents representational collapse without negative samples, projection heads, or momentum encoders beyond EMA. Polymer-JEPA shows random-walk subgraphing matches or outperforms chemically meaningful motif-based subgraphing. Both align with the Simplicity Principle (mem_096): simple mechanisms, well-tuned, beat complex frameworks imported from other domains.

conflicts.conflict: SelfGNN (mem_101) uses contrastive learning without negative samples (BatchNorm as implicit negative) while MoCL (mem_102) uses explicit InfoNCE with negative pairs. Which approach is better for polymer graphs?
conflicts.resolution: This is an empirical question, but structural reasoning favors SelfGNN's implicit approach for PI1M-scale pretraining: (1) SelfGNN's design avoids the need for large batch sizes to provide sufficient negatives — critical when pretraining on 200K+ polymer graphs with limited GPU memory. (2) MoCL's explicit negative sampling requires careful negative pair construction — the global similarity contrast component ensures structurally similar molecules aren't treated as negatives. For polymers, avoiding false negatives (different polymers that happen to share backbone chemistry) is harder without fingerprint guidance, making SelfGNN's implicit approach more robust. (3) SelfGNN's BatchNorm mechanism has been validated only on node classification; its behavior on graph-level regression tasks is untested. This is a risk.

conflicts.conflict: Polymer-JEPA (mem_103) shows that JEPA and input-space SSL (node/edge masking) perform comparably — JEPA slightly better in very low data, input-space slightly better with more data. This seems to contradict the node-level-is-dead-end finding (mem_105).
conflicts.resolution: Gao et al.'s input-space SSL on polymer graphs is NOT pure node-level reconstruction — it combines node-level AND graph-level SSL tasks (pseudolabel prediction of molecular weight). The graph-level component provides the global signal. Our GraphMAE experiment (mem_105) used only node-level reconstruction. This distinction reinforces Principle 1: graph-level signals, whether explicit (contrastive) or implicit (pseudolabel), are necessary.

conflicts.conflict: KPGT (mem_104) uses a 100M-parameter Line Graph Transformer — far larger than our ~1.2M GAT. Can these principles transfer to smaller architectures?
conflicts.resolution: KPGT's ablation shows that its architecture (LiGhT) outperforms GIN, vanilla Transformer, and Graphormer at equal ~3.5M scale, so the knowledge-guided pretraining principle is architecture-agnostic. The virtual knowledge node concept can be added to any GNN architecture (including GAT) with minimal parameter cost (~50K additional). The 100M scale amplifies the benefit but is not required for the principle to work.

alignment: All four papers converge on the importance of domain knowledge in SSL: MoCL uses bioisostere rules for augmentation, Polymer-JEPA uses polymer-specific subgraphing, KPGT uses RDKit descriptors/fingerprints in a virtual node, and SelfGNN uses feature augmentations that preserve chemical semantics. Generic, domain-agnostic SSL is consistently weaker.

The papers also converge on the insufficiency of pure node-level objectives: even KPGT (which masks nodes) adds graph-level knowledge; Polymer-JEPA's subgraph prediction is inherently graph-contextualized; MoCL's contrastive operates at graph level; SelfGNN contrasts graph views.

Both experiments (mem_105, mem_107) independently support the 'graph-level matters' principle: GraphMAE's node-level pretraining fails to transfer; PSPE's success comes from encoding chain-level (graph-level) geometry — distance-to-chain-end and monomer-index encode polymer-scale positional information, not atom-scale.
content.narrative: Day 3 inaugurated the SSL exploration phase with four carefully selected papers spanning the pretraining design space: contrastive without negatives (SelfGNN), knowledge-aware contrastive (MoCL), embedding-space predictive (Polymer-JEPA), and knowledge-guided generative (KPGT). Read together with our two experimental results, a coherent set of design principles emerges. First, the GraphMAE experiment (mem_105) provides the critical negative evidence: node-level masked reconstruction does not transfer to graph-level Tg prediction — this is not a scaling issue but a structural misalignment. All four papers validate this from the positive side: every SSL framework that succeeds uses graph-level or graph-informed objectives. Second, domain knowledge is the key differentiator between mediocre and strong SSL. MoCL's bioisostere substitution rules provide a template for polymer-specific augmentation (monomer substitution within chemical classes, chain-length variation). Polymer-JEPA's cross-chemical-space transfer result directly supports PI1M → Tg pretraining viability. KPGT's virtual knowledge node shows how to inject polymer descriptors (composition fingerprints, chain statistics) into any pretraining objective. SelfGNN provides the simplest implementation blueprint. Third, the Simplicity Principle (mem_096) extends to SSL: BatchNorm-only collapse prevention, random-walk subgraphing, and O(1) feature augmentations all match or outperform more complex alternatives. For Day 4 pretraining execution, these principles recommend: start with graph-level contrastive pretraining (MoMuCon mem_099 using SelfGNN's BatchNorm architecture), incorporate polymer domain augmentations (not random node dropping), add a virtual knowledge node with RDKit polymer descriptors, and use the GAT+RWPE+PSPE encoder as backbone. If contrastive pretraining fails, pivot to JEPA-style embedding prediction — which has the strongest polymer-specific evidence (mem_103).

memory.abstract: SelfGNN-Polymer: Simplex Graph-Level SSL on PI1M — adapting SelfGNN's BatchNorm-only Siamese architecture with polymer-adapted Split/Standardize feature augmentations, establishing the simplest possible graph-level pretraining baseline before advancing to domain-specific SSL frameworks.
memory.keyword: SelfGNN graph-level-SSL BatchNorm-contrastive feature-augmentation PI1M Simplicity-Principle polymer-pretraining

H: H1 — Graph-Level SSL Transfer Hypothesis: A graph-level contrastive pretraining objective on PI1M transfers to graph-level Tg prediction substantially better than node-level objectives (GraphMAE: +0.34-0.58K). SelfGNN's graph-level objective — enforcing embedding consistency between two augmented views of the same polymer — operates at the same structural level as Tg (an emergent whole-chain property). This alignment is the key differentiator. If SelfGNN-Polymer closes ≥1.5K of the 4.64K gap (reaching ≤33.94K, from 35.44K baseline), the Pretraining-Task Alignment Principle is validated: graph-level SSL > node-level SSL for graph-level downstream tasks.

H2 — Simplicity-First SSL Hypothesis: SelfGNN's O(1) feature augmentations (Split, Standardize), developed for citation/co-purchase graphs, transfer to polymer graphs without requiring domain-specific augmentation engineering. Split augmentation forces the encoder to reconstruct the full graph embedding from half the feature space; Standardize removes scale information, forcing reliance on relational patterns. These generic augmentations provide a viable pretraining signal for polymers, and domain-specific augmentations (multimer contrast, monomer substitution) should only be introduced if this simplest baseline proves insufficient. This is the Simplicity Principle (mem_096) applied to SSL.

H3 — BatchNorm-as-Implicit-Negative Hypothesis for Graph Regression: SelfGNN's BatchNorm mechanism, which prevents representational collapse in node classification by introducing implicit negative terms through batch statistics, extends to graph-level regression on polymer graphs. Unlike MoMuCon's NT-Xent (which requires explicit negative pair construction and large batch sizes), BatchNorm-only collapse prevention works with modest batch sizes (32-64) — critical for 11GB VRAM with ~104-node polymer graphs. If the model trains stably with BatchNorm and no explicit negatives, SelfGNN's minimalist design is validated for polymer graphs. If training collapses (constant embeddings), explicit negatives (NT-Xent) may be necessary for graph regression tasks.

pretraining_phase.dataset: 200K polymers randomly sampled from PI1M (seed=42). 1-RU graphs (simplest construction, ~35 nodes avg), rich node features (atomic number, hybridization, aromaticity, degree, formal charge, ring membership, chirality, hydrogen count) + PSPE-combined (distance-to-chain-end + monomer-index, concatenated to node features at input). No RWPE during pretraining to reduce computation; PSPE provides chain-geometry signal at lower cost. The 1-RU choice is deliberate: 1-RU graphs are simpler (fewer nodes → larger batch sizes, faster pretraining) and the SSL task is to make the encoder robust to feature perturbations regardless of graph size.
pretraining_phase.architecture: Siamese Student-Teacher with GAT backbone (4 layers, 256 hidden, 4 attention heads, mean aggregation, BatchNorm after each GAT layer). Student has an additional prediction MLP g: 2-layer MLP (256→128→256), BatchNorm+ReLU. Teacher is EMA of student (τ=0.999). NO projection head (SelfGNN ablation shows it adds no gain for graphs). The graph-level embedding is obtained via mean readout of all node embeddings from the final GAT layer. Both student and teacher produce 256-dim graph embeddings. Loss: MSE cosine similarity L = 2 − 2·⟨z_student, z_teacher⟩ / (||z_student||₂ · ||z_teacher||₂). Gradients flow only through student; teacher updated via EMA.
pretraining_phase.augmentations: Two views per polymer graph, using SelfGNN's best O(1) augmentations adapted for polymer node features: (1) Split: randomly partition the node feature dimension into two halves [F/2 dims each]; student sees one half, teacher sees the other. For polymers with F=15+2(PSPE)=17 features, this yields two 8/9-dim views. Zero-pad to original dimension for GAT input. (2) Standardize: z-score normalize all node features across the graph (per-feature-dimension mean=0, std=1) — applied to teacher view only, student sees raw features. This forces the encoder to be scale-invariant and rely on relational patterns. (3) Monomer-Drop (polymer-specific, used in ablation): randomly zero out 20% of side-chain atom features (identified as atoms not in the backbone path between polymerization sites), testing whether domain-specific augmentation helps beyond generic ones. The primary experiment uses Split+Standardize combined (SelfGNN's strongest FA combination).
pretraining_phase.training: AdamW optimizer (lr=3e-4 pretraining, weight_decay=1e-5). Batch size 64 (128 graphs: 64 pairs of student/teacher views). Cosine annealing to 1e-6, 200 epochs. GPU memory estimate: ~8-9GB for batch size 64 with 35-node 1-RU graphs and dual-encoder. Early stopping on pretraining loss plateau (patience=30).

finetuning_phase.encoder_init: Pretrained GAT student encoder weights (prediction MLP g discarded). The pretrained encoder weights replace random initialization.
finetuning_phase.predictor: 2-layer MLP (256→128→1) with ReLU, BatchNorm, Dropout=0.1 — same as Day 3 best (mem_107)
finetuning_phase.full_architecture: GAT (4 layers, 256 hidden, 4 heads, mean agg, BatchNorm) + RWPE k=32 + PSPE-combined at input + Set2Set readout (processing steps=3, to complement pretrained encoder with attention-based readout). Note: RWPE is added at finetuning even though not used in pretraining — this tests whether pretrained encoder can incorporate new positional features.
finetuning_phase.training: AdamW (lr=1e-4, lower than from-scratch 3e-4 to avoid catastrophic forgetting, weight_decay=1e-4). Linear warmup 5 epochs, cosine decay to 1e-6. Early stopping patience=50 on validation RMSE. Batch size 64, max 200 epochs.
finetuning_phase.data: Full Tg dataset (7170 polymers, 3-RU graphs, rich features, RWPE k=32, PSPE-combined), 72/8/20 split (seed=71). Note: finetuning uses 3-RU graphs (best supervised format) even though pretraining used 1-RU — the pretrained encoder should generalize across RU scales.

ablation_plan: A: No pretraining baseline = 35.44K (Day 3 best, GAT+RWPE+PSPE-combined)
B: SelfGNN-Polymer with Split only — tests whether single augmentation suffices
C: SelfGNN-Polymer with Standardize only
D: SelfGNN-Polymer with Split+Standardize (primary)
E: +Monomer-Drop augmentation — tests polymer-specific augmentation value
F: Pretrain on 100K vs 200K vs 500K PI1M — data scale sensitivity
G: Frozen encoder finetuning (only predictor trained) vs full finetuning
H: Remove BatchNorm from GAT during pretraining — tests collapse prevention necessity
I: SelfGNN-Polymer vs GraphMAE (mem_105) — direct graph-level vs node-level SSL comparison
J: 1-RU vs 3-RU graphs for pretraining — tests whether larger graphs provide better SSL signal
X.hardware_feasibility: 11GB VRAM is sufficient. With batch size 64, 1-RU graphs (~35 nodes, dual encoder): ~6-7GB for GAT weights (2× ~2.5M params ≈ 20MB) + activations + graph batch. Peak memory ~8-9GB. For larger 3-RU graphs (~104 nodes), reduce batch size to 32 for pretraining (~9-10GB). If OOM: use gradient accumulation (effective batch 64 via 2×32 micro-batches).

Y: H1 confirmation (≥1.5K improvement, reaching ≤33.94K): SelfGNN-Polymer closes 32-48% of the remaining 4.64K gap. This is a strong result: a simple, generic graph-level SSL framework with no domain-specific augmentations transfers effectively to polymer Tg. The Pretraining-Task Alignment Principle is validated, and the path forward is to add domain-specific augmentations (Idea 2: MoMuCon-Lite) to close more of the gap.

H1 partial (0.5-1.5K improvement, reaching 33.94-34.94K): Graph-level SSL provides a genuine but modest signal. The alignment principle is weakly supported — graph-level > node-level (GraphMAE: +0.34-0.58K) but the margin is small. Either: (a) generic feature augmentations are too weak to force learning of rich polymer representations; (b) 1-RU graphs lack sufficient structural detail for effective pretraining. Proceed to domain-specific augmentations (Idea 2).

H1 disconfirmation (<0.5K improvement, ≥34.94K): Graph-level SSL with generic feature augmentations does not meaningfully transfer. Possible reasons: (a) Split and Standardize are too trivial — the encoder can solve the contrastive task using superficial statistics without learning polymer structure; (b) SelfGNN's BatchNorm mechanism, validated for node classification, fails for graph-level regression because graph embeddings lack the within-batch diversity that makes BN-based implicit negatives work; (c) 200K PI1M polymers may not overlap Tg chemical space. If all ablations (B-E) also fail, pivot to MoMuCon-Lite (Idea 2) with multimer contrast as a stronger domain-specific signal, or to JEPA-style (mem_103).

H2 confirmation (Split+Standardize ≥ Monomer-Drop): If ablation D performs similarly to or better than E, generic augmentations suffice and polymer-specific augmentation engineering is unnecessary at this stage. This aligns with SelfGNN's finding that simple FA matches complex TA. If Monomer-Drop (E) significantly outperforms, domain knowledge matters for polymer SSL augmentation.

H3 confirmation (stable training, no collapse): If the pretraining loss decreases smoothly and t-SNE of pretrained embeddings shows diverse, well-separated graph representations (not a single collapsed cluster), SelfGNN's BatchNorm mechanism works for polymer graph regression. If training collapses (loss plateaus at 2.0 = random, all embeddings identical), ablation H (remove BatchNorm) diagnoses whether BN is the cause. Collapse → explicit negatives are needed → MoMuCon with NT-Xent.

H2 disconfirmation — if Standardize augmentation causes training instability: Z-scoring molecular features (especially one-hot encodings) may produce degenerate distributions. In this case, use only Split augmentation (ablation B) which is purely structural and cannot cause numerical issues.

Critical diagnostic — Embedding quality check: After every 50 pretraining epochs, compute: (a) pairwise cosine similarity of 500 random graph embeddings — healthy pretraining should show median similarity ~0.3-0.7, not 1.0 (collapse) or 0.0 (random). (b) Nearest-neighbor consistency: for a held-out set of 100 polymers with both Split views, check whether the nearest neighbor of the student embedding is the teacher embedding of the same polymer — should exceed 80% for effective pretraining.

Overall expected range: Best variant (Split+Standardize, 200K PI1M) expected to achieve 33.0-34.5K (0.9-2.4K improvement). If improvement <0.5K, SelfGNN-style SSL is insufficient and MoMuCon-Lite (Idea 2) should be run immediately.

memory.abstract: MoMuCon-Lite: SelfGNN-Style Multimer Contrastive Pretraining — replacing SelfGNN's feature augmentations with 1-RU→3-RU multimer views as the two contrastive branches, using BatchNorm-only architecture (no NT-Xent, no projection head) to test whether the multimer effect provides a stronger pretraining signal than generic feature augmentations.
memory.keyword: MoMuCon-Lite multimer-contrast SelfGNN-architecture BatchNorm polymer-scale-invariance PI1M graph-level-SSL

H: H1 — Multimer-as-Augmentation Hypothesis: Using 1-RU and 3-RU graphs of the same polymer as the two 'views' in SelfGNN's Siamese architecture provides a stronger graph-level pretraining signal than generic feature augmentations (Idea 1). The 1-RU→3-RU mapping is polymer-specific: it teaches the encoder that backbone chemistry is invariant to repeat-unit resolution. This exploits the Day 1 finding that 3-RU > 1-RU for Tg — the encoder must learn to extract the scale-invariant polymer identity that 3-RU graphs make explicit. If MoMuCon-Lite outperforms SelfGNN-Polymer (Idea 1) by ≥1K, the multimer signal is genuinely valuable for pretraining and should be the basis for all further SSL work.

H2 — Architecture Simplification Hypothesis: SelfGNN's BatchNorm-only architecture (no NT-Xent, no projection head, no explicit negative pair mining) is sufficient for multimer contrast on PI1M polymer graphs. The original MoMuCon design (mem_099) uses NT-Xent with explicit negatives, requiring careful temperature tuning, large batch sizes, and a projection head — all adding complexity. SelfGNN's BatchNorm mechanism, which uses batch statistics as implicit negatives, removes these requirements. If MoMuCon-Lite matches or exceeds the theoretical performance of NT-Xent MoMuCon (as estimated in mem_099), the simpler architecture is preferred — aligning with the Simplicity Principle.

H3 — Chain-Length Curriculum Hypothesis: Pretraining on 1-RU→3-RU multimer contrast creates a natural curriculum: 1-RU graphs are simpler (fewer nodes, pure monomer chemistry), forcing the encoder to extract core chemical identity from minimal structure; 3-RU graphs are richer (repeat-unit connectivity, emerging chain properties), providing the target representation. This curriculum may be more effective than pretraining on 3-RU→3-RU with feature augmentations because the structural gap between 1-RU and 3-RU forces learning of non-trivial polymer features rather than surface-level statistics. If MoMuCon-Lite outperforms SelfGNN-Polymer with 3-RU graphs (ablation), the curriculum effect is supported.

H4 — Pretraining-Task Alignment Refinement: The 1-RU→3-RU contrast task is more closely aligned with Tg prediction than generic feature augmentations because: (a) it teaches the model that the same polymer at different scales has the same Tg — a physical truth; (b) it forces the encoder to learn backbone-identity features that are invariant to chain length, which are precisely the features that determine Tg (backbone stiffness, inter-chain interactions); (c) the 3-RU teacher provides a richer, more informative target than a feature-perturbed 1-RU student, creating a stronger gradient signal.

pretraining_phase.dataset: 200K polymers randomly sampled from PI1M (same seed=42 as Idea 1 for comparability). For each polymer, construct BOTH 1-RU and 3-RU graphs. 1-RU: ~35 nodes, 3-RU: ~104 nodes. Rich node features for both: atomic number, hybridization, aromaticity, degree, formal charge, ring membership, chirality, hydrogen count. PSPE-combined (distance-to-chain-end + monomer-index) concatenated at input for both 1-RU and 3-RU — critical because monomer-index is proportional to chain position in both scales, providing a consistent positional reference across RU scales. No RWPE during pretraining (PSPE provides sufficient positional signal at lower cost).
pretraining_phase.architecture: Same Siamese Student-Teacher SelfGNN architecture as Idea 1, but with a key modification: the two branches process DIFFERENTLY-SIZED graphs. Student branch: GAT processes 1-RU graphs. Teacher branch: GAT processes 3-RU graphs. Both GATs share identical architecture (4 layers, 256 hidden, 4 heads, mean agg, BatchNorm) but the teacher's weights are EMA of student (τ=0.999). The student has a prediction MLP g: 2-layer (256→128→256) with BatchNorm+ReLU. Graph embeddings via mean readout → 256-dim. Loss: MSE cosine similarity L = 2 − 2·⟨z_student(1-RU), z_teacher(3-RU)⟩ / (||z_student||₂ · ||z_teacher||₂). No projection head, no NT-Xent, no explicit negatives — BatchNorm in GAT layers provides implicit contrastive terms.
pretraining_phase.training: AdamW (lr=5e-4, slightly higher than Idea 1 because multimer contrast is more challenging; weight_decay=1e-5). Batch size 32 (32 polymer pairs: 32×1-RU + 32×3-RU = 64 graphs). Cosine annealing to 1e-6, 300 epochs (longer than Idea 1 because multimer contrast is a harder task). GPU memory: ~9-11GB. 3-RU graphs are ~3× larger than 1-RU, so batch size must be smaller. With batch 32: 32×104-node 3-RU graphs + 32×35-node 1-RU graphs + dual GATs ≈ 9-10GB. If OOM: reduce to batch 24 (~8-9GB) or use gradient accumulation.
pretraining_phase.critical_implementation_detail: The 1-RU and 3-RU graphs of the same polymer may have different numbers of nodes but share the same feature dimension. The student GAT processes only 1-RU graphs (batch of 32), the teacher GAT processes only 3-RU graphs (batch of 32). After mean readout, both produce 256-dim embeddings. The loss pairs the i-th 1-RU embedding with the i-th 3-RU embedding (positive pair). There are NO cross-polymer negatives — BatchNorm provides implicit contrast.

finetuning_phase.encoder_init: Pretrained GAT student encoder weights (the one that processed 1-RU graphs during pretraining). The prediction MLP g is discarded.
finetuning_phase.full_architecture: GAT (4 layers, 256 hidden, 4 heads, mean agg, BatchNorm) + RWPE k=32 + PSPE-combined at input + Set2Set readout (processing steps=3). Note: the pretrained encoder saw only 1-RU graphs; at finetuning it processes 3-RU graphs. The PSPE positional features (distance-to-chain-end, monomer-index) provide a consistent coordinate system across RU scales, helping the encoder adapt.
finetuning_phase.training: AdamW (lr=1e-4, weight_decay=1e-4). Linear warmup 5 epochs, cosine decay to 1e-6. Early stopping patience=50 on validation RMSE. Batch size 64, max 200 epochs.
finetuning_phase.data: Full Tg dataset (7170 polymers, 3-RU graphs, rich features, RWPE k=32, PSPE-combined), 72/8/20 split (seed=71).

ablation_plan: A: No pretraining baseline = 35.44K (Day 3 best)
B: SelfGNN-Polymer (Idea 1, Split+Standardize on 1-RU graphs) — direct comparison: multimer contrast vs feature augmentations
C: MoMuCon-Lite with 1-RU→3-RU contrast (primary)
D: MoMuCon-Lite with 1-RU→2-RU contrast — tests whether 2-RU provides sufficient scale difference
E: MoMuCon-Lite with 2-RU→3-RU contrast — tests whether larger RU difference helps
F: SelfGNN-Polymer with Split+Standardize on 3-RU graphs (not 1-RU) — controls for graph size effect
G: Original MoMuCon with NT-Xent (mem_099) — direct comparison: BatchNorm vs explicit negatives
H: Frozen encoder finetuning vs full finetuning
I: Pretrain on 100K vs 200K vs 500K PI1M
J: PSPE-only vs RWPE-only vs PSPE+RWPE at finetuning — tests positional encoding interaction with pretrained encoder
K: Teacher as 1-RU, Student as 3-RU (reversed) — tests asymmetry of the curriculum; hypothesis: Student=1-RU, Teacher=3-RU is better because the student learns from a richer target
X.hardware_feasibility: 11GB VRAM is sufficient with careful batching. Dual GAT encoders: each ~2.5M params (~20MB). Peak memory is dominated by 3-RU graphs in teacher branch. Batch size 32: 32×104×17(features)×4(bytes) ≈ 226KB for node features; adjacency and message-passing intermediates add ~1-2GB per branch. Total ~9-11GB. If OOM at batch 32: reduce to 24 (peak ~8-9GB). Gradient accumulation can simulate batch 48-64 with 2-3 micro-batches. Pretraining 200K polymers × 300 epochs ≈ 1.9M iterations at batch 32, estimated ~8-12 hours on single GPU.

Y: H1 confirmation (MoMuCon-Lite outperforms SelfGNN-Polymer by ≥1K, reaching ≤32.9K): The multimer contrast signal is genuinely more informative than feature augmentations. This would be a major result: the multimer effect, discovered as a supervised phenomenon on Day 1, generalizes as a self-supervised pretraining signal using the simplest possible architecture. The remaining gap to PerioGT SOTA (30.8K) would be 1.1-2.1K, likely requiring periodicity-aware contrast (PerioGT-style) or JEPA-style embedding prediction.

H1 partial (MoMuCon-Lite outperforms by 0.5-1K, reaching 33.4-33.9K): The multimer signal adds value over generic augmentations but the margin is modest. Either: (a) 1-RU and 3-RU graphs are already quite similar for many polymers (especially rigid-rod polymers where adding repeat units just extends a linear chain), making the contrastive task too easy; (b) the BatchNorm mechanism, while functional, provides weaker contrastive pressure than NT-Xent's explicit negatives, limiting the benefit of the stronger multimer signal.

H1 disconfirmation (MoMuCon-Lite ≤ SelfGNN-Polymer, or <0.5K improvement over baseline): The multimer contrast signal is surprisingly weak as an SSL objective. Possible explanations: (a) The 1-RU→3-RU mapping may be too easy — for many polymers, the 3-RU graph is just a concatenated 1-RU graph with minimal new chemistry, so the contrastive task collapses to trivial structural matching; (b) The PSPE features (monomer-index) already encode chain-scale information, so the 3-RU view adds little new information beyond what the 1-RU view with PSPE already contains; (c) The BatchNorm mechanism, validated on node classification with 2708-34493 node graphs, may not produce sufficient implicit contrast for graph-level embeddings over 200K diverse polymer graphs. In this case, pivot to original MoMuCon with NT-Xent (ablation G) to test whether explicit negatives rescue the multimer signal, or pivot to JEPA-style (mem_103).

H2 confirmation (MoMuCon-Lite ≈ or > estimated MoMuCon-NT-Xent): If the BatchNorm-only architecture achieves comparable or better performance than NT-Xent MoMuCon (ablation G), the Simplicity Principle is strongly validated: the complex machinery of NT-Xent (projection head, temperature tuning, large batch size for negatives) provides no benefit over SelfGNN's minimalist design. This would be a significant methodological finding for polymer graph SSL.

H3 confirmation (Student=1-RU, Teacher=3-RU > reversed): If ablation K shows that the 1-RU→3-RU direction outperforms 3-RU→1-RU, the curriculum hypothesis is supported: the student benefits from a simpler input and a richer target, learning to extract scale-invariant features from minimal structure.

Critical diagnostic — Cross-scale embedding consistency: After every 50 pretraining epochs, measure: (a) For 500 held-out polymers, cosine similarity between 1-RU student embedding and 3-RU teacher embedding — should increase from ~0.3 to ~0.7-0.9 during training, indicating the encoder learns scale invariance; (b) For the same polymer, compute similarity between its 3-RU embedding and a random different polymer's 3-RU embedding — should remain low (~0.1-0.3), confirming the model distinguishes polymers, not just matching RU scales; (c) Ablation: also compute 1-RU→1-RU similarity and 3-RU→3-RU similarity for the same polymer (using feature augmentations) as baselines.

Negative result contingency — if both Idea 1 and Idea 2 fail (<1K combined improvement): The graph-level SSL paradigm with contrastive objectives may be fundamentally limited for polymer Tg. Possible root causes: (a) PI1M polymers (synthetically generated, focused on bifunctional monomers with '*' sites) may have insufficient chemical overlap with the Tg dataset polymers; (b) Graph-level contrastive SSL with mean-readout graph embeddings may lose the fine-grained structural information that Tg depends on; (c) The 4.64K residual gap may require PerioGT's specific periodicity-aware contrast (contrasting polymers with different backbone periodicity), which neither Idea 1 nor Idea 2 provides. In this case, Day 5 should pivot to Polymer-JEPA (mem_103) — embedding-space prediction with subgraph-level objectives — or directly implement PerioGT's periodicity-aware pretraining on PI1M.

Overall expected range: If multimer contrast provides a stronger signal than feature augmentations, MoMuCon-Lite should reach 32.0-33.5K (1.9-3.4K improvement). If it matches Idea 1, both provide ~1-2K improvement. If both fail, the contrastive SSL paradigm may need revision for polymer graphs.

memory.abstract: Differentiable Free Volume Head (DFVH): Physics-structured neural readout that computes Tg from GNN-predicted occupied volume and chain flexibility parameters via the Simha-Boyer free volume equation — replacing the black-box MLP predictor with a polymer-physics bottleneck, and enabling self-supervised V_occ pretraining on PI1M.
memory.keyword: DFVH physics-enforced free-volume Simha-Boyer occupied-volume Tg-readout group-contribution pretraining PI1M

H: H1 — Physics-Bottleneck Hypothesis: Replacing the standard MLP readout (2-layer, 256→128→1) with a physics-structured Differentiable Free Volume Head forces the GNN encoder to learn chemically meaningful intermediate representations (occupied volume V_occ, backbone flexibility φ, and critical free volume f_g) that are causally upstream of Tg. This physics bottleneck acts as a regularizer, reducing the effective degrees of freedom and preventing overfitting to spurious correlations. Expected effect: 1.5-3.0K RMSE improvement from the physics structure alone (without pretraining), by constraining the prediction manifold to physically plausible (V_occ, φ, f_g) → Tg mappings.

H2 — V_occ Pretraining Transfer Hypothesis: Pretraining the GNN encoder to predict the van der Waals occupied volume V_vdw (computable from tabulated atomic volumes for all 1M PI1M polymers) creates a physics-informed latent space that accelerates downstream Tg learning. V_vdw is causally upstream of Tg through the Simha-Boyer equation (Tg ∝ V_occ / free volume expansion), making it an aligned pretraining target at graph level. This is fundamentally different from node-level masked reconstruction (failed, +0.34K) and generic contrastive SSL (untested): V_occ prediction teaches the model about molecular bulk, packing, and the volumetric consequences of chemical structure — concepts directly relevant to Tg. Expected: V_occ pretraining on 200K PI1M transfers +1.0-2.0K, and combining DFVH + V_occ pretraining yields +2.0-4.0K cumulative, sufficient to close most or all of the 4.64K gap.

H3 — Conformer-Free 3D Awareness Hypothesis: The model can learn to estimate 3D-derived properties (V_occ, chain cross-sectional area, effective chain diameter) from 2D graph topology alone, without explicit 3D conformer generation. The GNN's message-passing over the 2D molecular graph captures sufficient steric and topological information to approximate 3D volumetric properties. This is testable by comparing V_occ prediction accuracy against ground-truth RDKit-computed volumes — correlation r > 0.95 would validate the hypothesis. If successful, this enables '3D-aware 2D GNNs' without the computational burden of conformer generation.

H4 — Group-Contribution-Guided Attention Hypothesis: Adding an auxiliary attention head that soft-assigns atoms to known functional groups (using RDKit substructure matching as weak labels during pretraining) improves V_occ prediction and downstream Tg by encouraging chemically meaningful atom pooling. This bridges neural attention with the century-old group contribution paradigm (van Krevelen). If the attention weights align with known functional group boundaries without hard supervision, the model has independently rediscovered group contribution logic.

architecture.encoder: GAT (4 layers, 256 hidden dim, 4 attention heads, mean aggregation, BatchNorm after each layer). Input: rich node features + PSPE-combined (distance-to-chain-end + monomer-index) concatenated. No RWPE during DFVH pretraining; RWPE k=32 added during finetuning.
architecture.intermediate_heads: Three parallel prediction heads branching from the graph-level embedding h_G (obtained via mean readout of final GAT node embeddings, 256-dim): (1) V_occ head: 2-layer MLP (256→128→1) with Softplus output activation (V_occ > 0). Predicts total van der Waals occupied volume in Å³. (2) φ head: 2-layer MLP (256→64→1) with sigmoid output. Predicts 'backbone flexibility index' φ ∈ (0,1), where 0 = fully rigid (all backbone bonds locked in rings), 1 = freely jointed chain. (3) f_g head: 2-layer MLP (256→32→1) with sigmoid output (offset by 0.02). Predicts critical fractional free volume at Tg, expected ≈0.025.
architecture.physics_head: Differentiable Simha-Boyer module computing: Tg_pred = T_0 + (V_occ / (α_l·V_occ + φ·β)) · (f_g - f_0) / Δα, simplified for training stability to: Tg_pred = a·(V_occ^p)·(1 + b·(1-φ)^q) + c, where {a, b, c, p, q} are learnable scalar parameters (initialized: a=200, b=0.5, c=150, p=0.3, q=0.5, covering the 200-500K Tg range in Kelvin). This parametric form encodes the physics that Tg increases with occupied volume (larger monomers pack less efficiently → higher Tg) and decreases with backbone flexibility φ. The learnable parameters allow the model to fit the exact scaling from data while the functional form provides the physics prior.
architecture.loss: L_total = L_Tg + λ_v·L_Vocc + λ_φ·L_flexibility + λ_f·L_fg. L_Tg = Huber loss (δ=5.0) on Tg prediction (robust to outliers). L_Vocc = MSE on V_occ prediction. L_flexibility: if using weak supervision from RDKit rotatable bond counts → MSE. λ hyperparameters: λ_v=0.1, λ_φ=0.05, λ_f=0.01 during supervised training; λ_v=1.0, others=0 during pretraining.

pretraining_phase.dataset: 200K polymers from PI1M (seed=42), 1-RU graphs with rich features (no PSPE during pretraining — keep encoder input-agnostic). For each polymer, compute ground-truth V_vdw using tabulated atomic van der Waals volumes (Bondi radii: C=16.6, H=5.5, O=14.7, N=13.4, F=9.2, Cl=21.5, S=22.6, Br=26.5, I=32.5, P=22.8 Å³). Also compute: (a) number of rotatable backbone bonds (RDKit RotatableBondSmarts filtered to backbone), (b) number of ring-locked bonds, (c) side-group bulkiness = V_vdw(side groups) / V_vdw(backbone). These serve as auxiliary pretraining targets.
pretraining_phase.task: Predict V_vdw + rotatable bond count + ring-locked count + side-group ratio from graph embedding. This is multi-target regression at graph level. Loss: MSE on all targets, normalized by target standard deviation.
pretraining_phase.training: AdamW, lr=1e-4, batch_size=128 (1-RU graphs ~35 nodes, ~7GB VRAM), 300 epochs, cosine annealing to 1e-6, early stopping patience=50. No data augmentation — the task is purely predictive, not contrastive.
pretraining_phase.validation: Hold out 10K PI1M polymers for V_occ prediction R². Target: R² > 0.90 on V_occ (atom counting alone can achieve ~0.85; the model must learn volume additivity patterns beyond simple counting).

finetuning_phase.initialization: GAT encoder weights from V_occ pretraining. DFVH heads (V_occ, φ, f_g) initialized from pretraining where applicable; physics head parameters {a,b,c,p,q} randomly initialized.
finetuning_phase.data: Full Tg dataset, 3-RU graphs, rich features + PSPE-combined + RWPE k=32. 72/8/20 split (seed=71).
finetuning_phase.training: AdamW (lr=3e-4 for scratch parameters, 1e-4 for pretrained encoder — differential learning rates). Linear warmup 5 epochs, cosine decay. Early stopping patience=50 on val RMSE. Batch size 64, max 300 epochs.
finetuning_phase.ablation: A: Standard MLP readout (no DFVH) + random init = 35.44K baseline. B: DFVH + random init (no pretraining) — tests physics bottleneck alone. C: DFVH + V_occ pretraining (full pipeline). D: DFVH + pretraining but V_occ head frozen during finetuning. E: Standard MLP + V_occ pretraining (tests whether pretraining benefit is readout-dependent). F: DFVH without φ head — tests whether flexibility index matters. G: DFVH with φ supervised by RDKit rotatable bonds during finetuning.

X.hardware_feasibility: Pretraining: 1-RU graphs (~35 nodes), batch 128, single GAT encoder (no Siamese), ~5-6GB VRAM. Finetuning: 3-RU graphs (~104 nodes), batch 64, single encoder, ~6-8GB VRAM. Well within 11GB limit. RDKit V_vdw computation for 200K polymers: ~5-10 min CPU.

Y: H1 strong confirmation (≥2.0K improvement from DFVH alone, reaching ≤33.44K): The physics bottleneck is highly effective. The functional form constraint prevents overfitting and the intermediate heads (V_occ, φ, f_g) provide a chemically meaningful latent structure that dramatically improves sample efficiency. This is a paradigm-level result: physics-structured readouts should replace black-box MLPs for all polymer property prediction tasks.

H1 moderate (1.0-2.0K, reaching 33.44-34.44K): The physics bottleneck provides genuine regularization benefit. The intermediate representations are partially learned but the model struggles with the flexibility index φ (no direct supervision during finetuning). Ablation G (RDKit-supervised φ) may unlock further gains.

H1 disconfirmation (<1.0K, ≥34.44K): The physics bottleneck does not meaningfully constrain the model — either (a) the parametric form is too rigid and cannot capture real Tg variation, (b) the intermediate heads (V_occ, φ, f_g) are not identifiable from graph embeddings without explicit supervision, or (c) the learnable parameters {a,b,c,p,q} absorb all physics structure, reducing DFVH to an overparameterized MLP. If (c), replace the parametric form with a hard-coded Simha-Boyer equation using literature values for expansion coefficients.

H2 strong confirmation (combined DFVH + pretraining ≥3.0K total, reaching ≤32.44K): V_occ pretraining on PI1M transfers powerfully. The pretrained encoder has learned to map 2D graph topology to 3D volumetric properties, and this skill generalizes to Tg. The gap to SOTA (30.8K) is mostly closed. This validates the H2 hypothesis and establishes V_occ as a privileged pretraining target for polymer property prediction.

H2 moderate (1.0-3.0K, reaching 32.44-34.44K combined): Pretraining helps but the transfer is noisy. Polymers where V_occ correlates strongly with Tg (rigid, bulky monomers) benefit most; flexible-chain polymers see less benefit because other factors (intermolecular forces, hydrogen bonding) dominate their Tg.

H2 disconfirmation (<1.0K combined, ≥34.44K): V_occ is too trivial a learning target — the GNN can predict it from atom-type counting without learning deep structural features. The V_occ pretraining R² > 0.95 but this skill does not transfer to Tg. This would suggest that pretraining targets must require non-trivial structural reasoning. Ablation E (standard MLP + pretraining) would show the same pattern.

H3 diagnostic: V_occ prediction accuracy on PI1M holdout set. If R² > 0.95, the 2D GNN captures 3D volumetric information effectively. If R² < 0.85, the encoder cannot bridge the 2D→3D gap from graph topology alone, and explicit 3D conformer features may be necessary.

H4 diagnostic: Visualize the group-contribution attention weights (if auxiliary head is added). If attention maps align with chemically meaningful functional groups (e.g., all -CH2- atoms attend similarly, distinct from aromatic carbons), the model learns group-contribution logic. Quantify via adjusted mutual information between attention clusters and RDKit functional group labels.

Expected overall range: DFVH alone: 33.0-34.5K (0.9-2.4K). DFVH + V_occ pretraining: 31.5-33.5K (1.9-3.9K cumulative). Best case (H1+H2 both strong): ≤31.5K, within 0.7K of PerioGT's 30.8K SOTA — at which point the remaining gap can be closed by ensemble methods or GPS-Lite global attention. Worst case (both disconfirmed): ≥34.4K, and the physics-structured approach does not outperform standard SSL — pivot to contrastive methods (SelfGNN mem_112, MoMuCon-Lite mem_113).

Critical diagnostic — Embedding shift after pretraining: Compare t-SNE of graph embeddings before vs after V_occ pretraining on the Tg dataset. If pretraining separates polymers by molecular volume and backbone rigidity (not just atom count), the pretrained space is physics-informed. If separation is purely by atom count/molecular weight, the pretraining was trivial.

memory.abstract: MolCHG proposes a Compositional Hierarchical Graph that elevates bonds from auxiliary edge attributes to independent node representations operating in parallel with atom nodes, and designs three level-specific self-supervised pretraining objectives (atom-bond cross-view contrastive, fragment functional group prediction, graph-level structure prediction), achieving best performance on 7/9 MoleculeNet benchmarks.
memory.keyword: molecular representation learning, hierarchical graph, bond graph, multi-level pretraining, self-supervised learning

content.background: Molecular property prediction is central to drug discovery, computational biology, and toxicity assessment, yet large-scale annotated datasets remain scarce due to expensive wet-lab experiments, motivating self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled molecular data. Existing molecular pretraining methods fall into two categories: contrastive learning (maximizing agreement between augmented views) and predictive learning (masked attribute recovery, context prediction). However, most methods operate at a single structural granularity—typically atom-level or graph-level—failing to reflect the hierarchical nature of molecular structures spanning atoms, bonds, functional substructures, and global topology. Recent fragment-aware methods like MGSSL and GraphFP introduced chemically meaningful substructures as intermediate semantic units, but they still derive fragment-level semantics primarily from atom-centered message passing, treating bond information as auxiliary edge attributes rather than independent semantic entities. In these methods, edge features only modulate messages between nodes without maintaining independently evolving representations, leaving bond-level semantics inherently less prominent than atom-level semantics—despite bonds being equally important compositional elements of fragments from a chemical standpoint. Prior supervised methods (DMPNN, CMPNN, DeMol) confirmed that explicit atom-bond interaction modeling yields more expressive representations, but their bond-level modeling relies on downstream labels and has not been extended to label-free pretraining. Hierarchical approaches like HiMol construct node-motif-graph hierarchies but still encode bonds only as edge attributes. MolCHG addresses these limitations by decoupling bond information from edge attributes and organizing it as an independent structural layer within a hierarchical pretraining framework, enabling fragment nodes to aggregate atom-level and bond-level semantics on an equal footing.
content.method: MolCHG is built on a novel Compositional Hierarchical Graph (CHG) that organizes molecular structure into four node types across three semantic levels. At the bottom level, an atom graph G_a = (V_a, E_a) and a bond graph G_b = (V_b, E_b) operate in parallel. The atom graph is the standard molecular graph where nodes are atoms and edges are chemical bonds. The bond graph is constructed by treating each bond as a node, connecting two bond nodes if their corresponding bonds share a common atom; this is effectively the line graph of the atom graph. At the intermediate level, fragment nodes V_f are introduced by decomposing the molecule into chemically meaningful substructures using Principal Subgraph Mining (chosen over rule-based methods like BRICS because it identifies a compact vocabulary of recurring substructures from the pretraining corpus, concentrating training signal on frequently occurring patterns). Each fragment node is explicitly connected to ALL of its constituent atom nodes and ALL of its constituent bond nodes, serving as a compositional hub that aggregates both atomic and bond-level semantics. Fragment nodes are also interconnected according to adjacency relationships among their corresponding substructures, forming a fragment-level graph G_f. At the top level, a single virtual graph node g is connected to all fragment nodes, serving as the graph-level representation hub. All edges in the entire CHG serve solely as topological connectors with no additional feature information. Initial node features (all 15-dimensional) are carefully designed to capture relevant chemical/structural descriptors while deliberately excluding information targeted by pretraining objectives to prevent leakage: atom nodes encode atomic number, degree, formal charge, radical electrons, hybridization, mass, hydrogens, chirality; bond nodes encode bond type, connectivity, conjugation, stereochemistry; fragment nodes encode atom/bond counts, heteroatom counts, bond type distributions, average properties; graph node encodes counts of atoms/bonds/fragments, fragment size statistics. Three level-specific self-supervised pretraining objectives are designed. (1) Atom-Bond Cross-View Contrastive (L_ab): For each fragment f_k, mean pooling is applied over its constituent atom node representations and bond node representations separately, yielding two summary vectors which pass through learnable projection heads to produce z_a^(k) and z_b^(k). The atom and bond summaries of the same fragment form a positive pair; all cross-fragment pairings are negatives. Uses symmetric NT-Xent loss with temperature τ=0.1. This aligns atom-view and bond-view representations in a shared semantic space, reinforcing that atoms and bonds jointly constitute the same fragment. Importantly, fragments of the same substructure type in different molecules are treated as negatives, since the same substructure may serve different functional roles in distinct molecular contexts. (2) Fragment-Level Functional Group Prediction (L_frag): A multi-label classification task where each fragment node predicts which functional groups are present within the corresponding substructure. The C most frequent functional groups from the pretraining corpus are used as targets; RDKit substructure matching produces binary label vectors. Binary cross-entropy loss is used. This injects domain-relevant chemical knowledge into the intermediate layer. (3) Graph-Level Structure Prediction: Two complementary tasks. Topological fingerprint prediction (L_topo): the graph node predicts a D-bit topological fingerprint (computed via RDKit) using binary cross-entropy. Scaffold property prediction (L_scaf): predicts five scaffold-related properties—total ring count, aromatic ring count, and three binary indicators (fused rings, heterocyclic rings, bridged rings). The total loss is L = λ_ab·L_ab + λ_frag·L_frag + λ_topo·L_topo + λ_scaf·L_scaf, with default weights 0.2, 0.4, 0.4, 0.4 (contrastive loss weight is smaller because its magnitude is typically larger). The theoretical foundation rests on three synergistic mechanisms: (a) the bond graph as an independent layer enables bond representations to evolve through message passing independently rather than being consumed as static edge attributes, allowing bond-level semantics to be explicitly captured; (b) fragment nodes as compositional hubs connected to both atom and bond nodes create an architectural pathway for atom-bond semantic interaction that is absent in conventional atom-centric hierarchies; (c) the three-level objectives provide complementary supervision—local compositional patterns (atom-bond contrastive), domain-relevant substructure semantics (fragment prediction), and global topology (graph prediction)—ensuring that representations across all granularities are meaningfully trained.
content.experiment: The GNN encoder is a 5-layer GIN with hidden dimension 300, dropout 0.5, and sum-based jumping knowledge aggregation. Fragment vocabulary is constructed via Principal Subgraph Mining with vocabulary size 800. Pretraining uses 250K unlabeled molecules from ZINC15 (same subset as HiMol for fair comparison), trained for 100 epochs with Adam (lr=1e-3, weight decay=1e-5), batch size 256 (provides sufficient negatives for contrastive objective), temperature τ=0.1. Downstream evaluation uses nine MoleculeNet benchmarks: six classification tasks (BACE, BBBP, ClinTox, SIDER, Tox21, HIV) evaluated by ROC-AUC (%), and three regression tasks (ESOL, FreeSolv, Lipophilicity) evaluated by RMSE. All datasets are randomly split 6:2:2 (train/val/test) following S-CGIB protocol, with mean and standard deviation over 10 independent runs. For finetuning, pretrained GNN encoder weights are transferred; mean pooling is applied over atom nodes, bond nodes, and fragment nodes separately, and the three pooled vectors are concatenated with the graph node representation to form the final molecular representation; a single linear prediction head maps to the target property. Finetuning runs 100 epochs with Adam (lr=1e-3, batch size 32). Baselines span three categories: node-level pretraining (ContextPred, AttrMasking, EdgePred), contrastive learning (Infomax, JOAO, JOAOv2, GraphCL, GraphLoG), and subgraph/fragment-level pretraining (GraphFP, MICRO-Graph, MGSSL, GROVER, SimSGT, MoAMa, HiMol, S-CGIB). HiMol results were reproduced using public code with identical pretraining corpus and splitting protocol. Ablation studies include: (1) Graph structure ablation: comparing standard atom graph vs. hierarchical graph (atoms+fragments+graph, no bond graph) vs. full Compositional Hierarchical Graph, all trained from scratch without pretraining on 5-layer GIN; (2) Pretraining objective ablation: systematically removing individual loss terms (L_ab, L_frag, L_topo, L_scaf) and groups (entire graph-level, entire atom-bond+fragment-level); (3) Sensitivity analysis of loss weights: varying each λ while keeping others at default. Representation visualizations: t-SNE of graph-level representations colored by Murcko scaffolds (10 most frequent, 500 molecules each), fragment-level representations colored by functional group types (8 common groups, 500 fragments each), bond-level representations colored by bond types (single/double/triple/aromatic, 1500 bonds each from 2000 molecules). Clustering quality quantified by Davies-Bouldin Index (DBI) and Silhouette Score computed on the original 300-dimensional representation space.
content.result: MolCHG achieves best performance on 7/9 MoleculeNet benchmarks. Classification: on BACE (87.20% vs S-CGIB 86.46%), BBBP (89.46% vs 88.75%), ClinTox (80.83% vs 78.58%), Tox21 (82.51% vs 80.94%). ClinTox improvement is particularly substantial (+2.25 points). On SIDER and HIV, MolCHG is competitive with best baselines (differences within one std). Regression: ESOL (0.797 vs 0.816), FreeSolv (1.523 vs 1.648, 7.6% relative reduction), Lipophilicity (0.745 vs 0.762). Compared to HiMol (closest related work), MolCHG outperforms on all 9 datasets, notably BBBP (89.46% vs 82.24%) and Tox21 (82.51% vs 80.16%). Ablation on graph structures confirms that the CHG (76.33 BACE) outperforms both the standard atom graph (71.61) and the hierarchical graph without bond layer (74.34), validating that elevating bonds to independent node representations provides richer structural semantics. Ablation on pretraining objectives: removing L_frag causes the largest average drop among classification tasks (BACE: 87.20→84.14, Tox21: 82.51→78.55), highlighting the importance of domain-relevant functional group knowledge. Removing L_topo causes pronounced decline on HIV (77.83→75.34). Removing entire levels produces substantially larger drops than any single loss, confirming that multi-level supervision signals are complementary. The w/o Graph-level variant drops BBBP from 89.46% to 84.30%; w/o Atom-bond & Fragment-level yields the lowest performance overall. Visualization: graph-level t-SNE shows pretraining organizes molecules by scaffold (DBI: 7.95→6.06, Silhouette: -0.050→0.074); fragment-level shows improved functional group separability (DBI: 7.54→4.36); bond-level shows clearer bond-type clustering (DBI: 3.49→2.97, Silhouette: -0.093→0.053). Limitations: the method adds computational overhead from maintaining parallel atom and bond graphs; fragment vocabulary construction via Principal Subgraph Mining requires pretraining corpus preprocessing; the approach has only been validated on small-molecule benchmarks, not macromolecules or polymers. Future directions could explore extending the hierarchical graph to other molecular domains and further investigating the interaction between atom-level and bond-level representations.
content.dataset: Pretraining: ZINC15 (250K unlabeled subset). Downstream: MoleculeNet (BACE, BBBP, ClinTox, SIDER, Tox21, HIV for classification; ESOL, FreeSolv, Lipophilicity for regression).
content.topic_relation: This paper directly supports and extends the Pretraining-Task Alignment Principle established on Day 3: MolCHG demonstrates that multi-level pretraining objectives spanning atom-bond, fragment, and graph levels provide complementary supervision signals that jointly improve downstream performance—consistent with the finding that pretraining level must align with downstream task demands. The paper also provides architectural evidence that elevating bond information from edge attributes to independent node representations (bond graph) enriches molecular representations, which could be adapted for polymer backbones where bond-level semantics (bond type, conjugation along the chain) are critical for Tg prediction. The fragment-level functional group prediction task validates that injecting domain-relevant chemical knowledge into intermediate layers improves representation quality, analogous to how polymer-specific descriptors (monomer type, chain flexibility indicators) could be injected into polymer pretraining. The finding that removing entire pretraining levels causes larger degradation than any single loss reinforces that graph-level-only pretraining, while necessary, may benefit from complementary lower-level objectives—counterbalancing the strong Day 3 conclusion that node-level SSL alone is insufficient.
content.topic_contribution: MolCHG provides three actionable insights for polymer Tg pretraining: (1) The bond graph as an independent structural layer is a novel architectural pattern that could be adapted to polymer graphs—polymer backbone bonds (C-C, C-O, etc.) carry rich semantic information about chain flexibility that is currently encoded only as edge attributes; a polymer bond graph could explicitly model backbone bond semantics. (2) The multi-level pretraining paradigm suggests that for polymer Tg, a three-level hierarchy (monomer-atoms → monomer-bonds → chain-graph) with corresponding level-specific objectives may outperform single-level graph contrastive approaches; this is a concrete hypothesis to test against the current plan of pure graph-level contrastive pretraining. (3) The fragment functional group prediction task demonstrates that auxiliary domain-knowledge injection during pretraining improves transfer—for polymers, predicting monomer identity, chain flexibility indicators, or repeat-unit properties during pretraining could similarly enrich representations. This paper should be referenced when designing the polymer-specific hierarchical pretraining architecture (Day 4-7), specifically as evidence that multi-level supervision is complementary and that bond-level semantics deserve explicit architectural treatment.
