memory.abstract: Introduces k-Maximum Inner Product (k-MIP) self-attention for graph transformers — a sparse attention mechanism that selects the top-k most relevant keys per query, achieving linear memory complexity and up to 10× speedup over full attention. Proves k-MIP transformers can universally approximate any full-attention transformer to arbitrary precision, and establishes an upper bound on GraphGPS expressive power via the S-SEG-WL test. Empirically validated on LRGB, City-Networks (569k-node graphs), and point cloud segmentation benchmarks, consistently ranking among top scalable graph transformers.

content.background: Graph transformers have emerged as a promising alternative to message-passing neural networks (MPNNs), enabling global information exchange between any pair of nodes and overcoming limitations such as oversmoothing, oversquashing, and restricted expressive power bounded by the 1-WL test. However, the standard multi-head self-attention mechanism inherits quadratic O(N²) memory and computational complexity from the Transformer architecture, rendering it infeasible for graphs with more than a few thousand nodes. This scalability bottleneck severely limits the applicability of graph transformers to real-world problems where graphs often contain millions of nodes. Existing approaches to address this limitation fall into four categories: (1) graph subsampling methods that process only sampled portions of large graphs but fail to capture long-range dependencies; (2) engineered attention patterns that restrict attention along predefined patterns (e.g., BigBird, Exphormer), potentially missing important node relationships; (3) linearized attention methods that approximate standard attention via kernel tricks or matrix factorization (e.g., Performer, Nodeformer), achieving linear complexity but often degrading predictive performance; and (4) learnable attention patterns that dynamically determine relevant node pairs, promising both efficiency and strong performance but remaining relatively underexplored. This paper positions k-MIP attention within the learnable patterns category. The core motivation is to address both the computational inefficiency and the noise introduced by irrelevant attention computations simultaneously — most attention scores in full attention are small, as each node typically has only a few truly relevant connections. By dynamically selecting only the k most relevant keys per query, k-MIP attention focuses computational resources on the most important connections while maintaining the flexibility of full attention to propagate information between any two nodes. The work is integrated into the GraphGPS framework (Rampášek et al., 2022), a modular architecture combining MPNN layers with global attention layers and MLPs. The authors provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of expressive power, proving both an upper bound (GraphGPS is bounded by S-SEG-WL test) and a lower bound (k-MIP can universally approximate full-attention transformers), establishing that the sparsification does not compromise model expressivity.
content.method: The k-MIP self-attention mechanism extends multi-head self-attention by restricting each query to attend only to the k keys with the highest inner product scores. Formally, given input matrix X ∈ ℝ^{N×d}, attention heads H, and learnable weight matrices W_Q^h, W_K^h ∈ ℝ^{d×d_K} and W_V^h ∈ ℝ^{d×d_V}, the attention scores are computed as: A^h = softmax((1/√d_K) · T_k(X W_Q^h (X W_K^h)ᵀ)), where T_k is the top-k operator that retains only the k largest elements in each row and sets all other elements to -∞. The output is then computed as kMIP(X) = Σ_{h=1}^H A^h X W_V^h W_O^h. The key innovation enabling scalability is the use of symbolic matrices via Kernel Operations (KeOps, Charlier et al., 2021). Rather than materializing the N×N intermediate matrix in GPU global memory, symbolic matrices represent the matrix as a formula M_{i,j} = F(x_i, y_j) and evaluate reductions lazily in CUDA registers with high parallelism. Specifically, the algorithm first defines a symbolic matrix S = X W_Q^h (X W_K^h)ᵀ, then applies a row-wise top-k reduction that computes the indices I_argtopk ∈ ℕ^{N×k} and values E_topk ∈ ℝ^{N×k} of the k largest elements per row. Value vectors are gathered at these indices, attention scores are computed via row-wise softmax on E_topk/√d_K, and outputs are aggregated via weighted summation. While the computational complexity remains O(N²) due to the hardness of exact maximum inner product search in high dimensions, the symbolic matrix approach achieves linear memory complexity because the N² intermediate inner products are never stored in global memory. Furthermore, the top-k indices are reused during backpropagation without recomputation, making the backward pass nearly instantaneous for large N. The authors note that they experimented with approximate maximum inner product search techniques (IVF, PQ, LSH via FAISS) but these failed to deliver speedups justifying the associated recall loss. k-MIP attention is integrated into the GraphGPS framework, where each layer consists of: (1) an MPNN layer (GatedGCN by default), (2) a global attention layer (k-MIP replacing full attention), and (3) a 2-layer MLP, with residual connections throughout. The theoretical analysis proceeds in two parts. Theorem 1 establishes that any GraphGPS instance is upper-bounded in graph distinguishing power by the S-SEG-WL test with a structural encoding scheme S = (f_A, f_R) determined by the node/edge feature enhancements used. This embeds GraphGPS into the expressiveness hierarchy of Zhu et al. (2023), enabling direct comparison to other graph transformers. Theorem 2 (k-MIP Approximation Theorem) proves that for any full-attention transformer T_full, any ε > 0, any compact set U ⊆ ℝ^{N×d}, there exists a k-MIP transformer T_kMIP ∈ T_{kMIP}^{2,1,4} (2 heads, dimension 1, MLP dimension 4) such that the Lp approximation error over U is less than ε. The proof builds on Yun et al. (2019)'s universal approximation result for full-attention transformers, noting that the only property of softmax used in that proof — that softmax(λZ) → hardmax(λZ) as λ → ∞ — is also satisfied by softmax ∘ T_k.
content.experiment: The experimental evaluation comprises three objectives: (1) computational efficiency benchmarking, (2) prediction quality on the Long Range Graph Benchmark (LRGB), and (3) scalability to large-scale graph datasets. For efficiency benchmarking, runtime and memory usage were compared across full attention and k-MIP attention (with and without symbolic matrices) while varying N ∈ {10^{i/2} | i=4,...,12} with d_K=10 and k=10. Both inference (forward pass only) and training (forward+backward) settings were evaluated on a single 40GB A100 GPU, with 5 runs per data point. For LRGB evaluation, five attention mechanisms (Transformer/full attention, BigBird, Performer, Exphormer, and k-MIP) were integrated into the GraphGPS architecture and compared against MPNN baselines (GCN, GINE, GAT, GatedGCN). The evaluation followed the methodology of Tönshoff et al. (2023) with a 500k parameter budget across four datasets: PascalVOC-SP (F1 score), COCO-SP (F1 score), Peptides-Func (AP), and Peptides-Struct (MAE). Results are reported as mean ± std over four runs. For scalability evaluation, two benchmarks were used: (1) City-Networks (Liang et al., 2025) for transductive learning on road network graphs from four cities (LA, NYC, Chicago, London, with London having 569k nodes), comparing GPS+k-MIP against GPS+Performer, GPS+BigBird, Exphormer, and GAT; and (2) two custom large-scale inductive point cloud segmentation datasets based on ShapeNet-Part (Yi et al., 2016) and S3DIS (Armeni et al., 2016), where point clouds were converted to k-NN graphs. These compared GPS+k-MIP against GCN, GINE, GAT, GatedGCN, GPS+BigBird, GPS+Performer, and Exphormer, with results reported as mean ± std over three runs. Additional profiling included a per-stage runtime breakdown comparing full attention and k-MIP attention in the training setting at N=10^{4.5}. The paper also provides complementary performance measurements and a direct comparison with FlashAttention in the appendices.
content.result: Computational efficiency results demonstrate that k-MIP attention achieves a 12.43× speedup over full attention during inference at N=10^6 and 8.46× speedup during training at N=10^{4.5}. Crucially, while full attention encounters out-of-memory errors for N ≥ 10^5, k-MIP scales to N=10^7 nodes on a single 40GB A100 GPU. Per-stage profiling reveals that the top-k search dominates the forward pass, while the backward pass is nearly instantaneous due to index reuse. On LRGB, MPNNs outperform graph transformers on both Peptides datasets, consistent with prior work. On PascalVOC-SP and COCO-SP, graph transformers excel, with GPS+k-MIP achieving 39.69 ± 0.92 F1 and 35.56 ± 0.45 F1 respectively, matching or outperforming other scalable attention mechanisms but remaining below full attention (44.40 and 38.84). On City-Networks, GAT outperforms all graph transformer variants. Among graph transformers, GPS+k-MIP achieves comparable accuracy to GPS+Performer and significantly outperforms Exphormer and GPS+BigBird. Most notably, GPS+k-MIP scales to the London dataset with 569k nodes, while GPS+Transformer, Exphormer, and GPS+BigBird returned OOM errors. The absence of positional encodings (Laplacian eigenvectors become computationally prohibitive at this scale) may explain the underperformance of graph transformers relative to GAT on this benchmark. On ShapeNet-Part, GPS+k-MIP achieves the best F1 score of 82.68 ± 0.64, roughly on par with Exphormer (82.62 ± 0.31) and significantly outperforming GPS+BigBird and GPS+Performer. On S3DIS, GPS+k-MIP achieves 67.99 ± 1.51 mIoU, second only to Exphormer. Key limitations include: (1) computational complexity remains O(N²) which may be prohibitive for extremely large graphs; (2) potential supervision starvation if the most relevant keys consistently fall outside the top-k selection during training; (3) the need for low-level GPU optimizations similar to FlashAttention for widespread adoption. Future directions include investigating curriculum learning for k (starting large, decreasing), and developing mitigation strategies for supervision starvation.
content.dataset: Long Range Graph Benchmark (LRGB: PascalVOC-SP, COCO-SP, Peptides-Func, Peptides-Struct); City-Networks benchmark (LA, NYC, Chicago, London road networks); ShapeNet-Part; S3DIS (converted to k-NN graphs)
content.topic_relation: This paper directly addresses the architectural class hypothesized in TopicState as necessary to close the residual 4.64K RMSE gap to PerioGT SOTA (30.8K): 'graph transformers with global attention' as a fundamentally different architectural class beyond GAT-based non-pretraining approaches. The k-MIP attention mechanism provides a practical, scalable path to apply graph transformers to polymer datasets where the ~35-104 node polymer graphs are well within k-MIP's demonstrated scale (up to 569k nodes). The theoretical guarantee that k-MIP transformers universally approximate full-attention transformers addresses concerns about expressiveness loss from sparsification — critical for regression tasks like Tg prediction where precision matters. The S-SEG-WL upper bound analysis highlights the importance of positional/structural encodings for expressiveness, directly connecting to TopicState's ongoing exploration of RWPE and PSPE positional encodings. The GraphGPS framework (MPNN + Global Attention + MLP) provides a modular architecture that could incorporate existing polymer-specific components (PSPE, GatedGCN backbone) while adding global attention capability. The City-Networks finding that GAT outperforms graph transformers without positional encodings reinforces TopicState's emphasis on positional encoding design.
content.topic_contribution: Enables a concrete, actionable experiment: GPS+k-MIP applied to polymer Tg prediction as the 'fundamentally different architectural class' hypothesized in TopicState. The architecture would combine: (1) GatedGCN MPNN layer (already validated as strong on polymer graphs via GatedGCN baseline), (2) k-MIP global attention layer for capturing long-range chain flexibility relationships, (3) existing PSPE + RWPE positional encodings as node feature enhancements, and (4) 2-layer MLP. The linear memory complexity means the architecture can scale to PI1M-scale pretraining data (~1M polymers) on modest GPU hardware. The universal approximation theorem provides theoretical justification that the sparsification will not compromise regression accuracy. Recommended experiment design: (a) supervised GPS+k-MIP on 7,170 Tg samples with PSPE+RWPE as baseline, (b) compare k values (5, 10, 20, 50) to find optimal sparsity for ~35-104 node polymer graphs, (c) if successful, extend to PI1M pretraining using the complementary hierarchy principle (graph-level SSL objectives). The S-SEG-WL analysis also suggests a diagnostic: if GPS+k-MIP underperforms, verify whether positional encodings are sufficiently expressive for 1D chain geometry — PSPE should theoretically provide the needed expressiveness boost per Theorem 1's implications about more expressive encodings raising the distinguishability upper bound.

memory.abstract: CardinalGraphFormer introduces query-conditioned cardinality-preserving attention (CPA) into graph transformers, theoretically proving softmax attention is "cardinality-blind" and CPA restores 1-WL expressivity via a gated unnormalized sum channel. Combined with K-hop structured sparse attention, Graphormer biases (SPD, centrality, direct-bond), and dual-objective pretraining (masked + contrastive) on ~28M molecules, CPA yields statistically significant gains across 11 public benchmarks (MoleculeNet, OGB, TDC ADMET) under rigorously matched protocols with extensive ablation controls.

content.background: Molecular property prediction is a cornerstone proxy task in drug discovery, where labeled experimental data are scarce but candidate chemical space is vast (~10^60 molecules). Graph neural networks and graph transformers have emerged as leading architectures for learning molecular representations from 2D topological graphs. Among these, Graphormer demonstrated that injecting structural biases—shortest-path distance (SPD) encodings, centrality embeddings, and edge features—into global transformer attention achieves strong performance. However, standard softmax attention suffers from a fundamental limitation: it is 'cardinality-blind.' Softmax computes a convex combination (weighted average) over value vectors, which discards information about how many nodes exist in the support set, i.e., the cardinality/multiplicity of value occurrences. Two nodes with different numbers of neighbors but identical empirical value distributions and attention profiles produce identical softmax outputs despite representing different local topologies. This expressivity gap is formalized through the Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) framework: injective multiset aggregation is necessary for 1-WL expressivity, but softmax normalization destroys injectivity over multiplicities. Prior work by Zhang & Xie (2020) addressed cardinality preservation for message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) by adding unnormalized sum channels. However, adapting this principle to transformer attention—with its distinct query-key-value mechanics, multi-head design, and support-set dynamics under augmentation—remains underexplored. Meanwhile, self-supervised pretraining on large molecular corpora (contrastive learning, masked modeling) has proven effective, but the interaction between pretraining objectives and attention mechanisms that preserve structural signals like cardinality has not been systematically studied. This work addresses these gaps by (1) providing a theoretical framework connecting CPA to multiset discrimination and 1-WL expressivity, (2) designing a query-conditioned CPA mechanism integrated into transformer attention with shared support sets, and (3) demonstrating that CPA synergizes with dual-objective pretraining to yield consistent, statistically significant improvements across diverse molecular benchmarks under rigorously controlled experimental protocols.
content.method: CardinalGraphFormer's core innovation is the cardinality-preserving attention (CPA) channel, which augments standard multi-head softmax attention with a query-conditioned gated unnormalized sum. For each attention head at layer ℓ, the per-node output is: o_i = Σ_{j∈S(i)} α_{ij} v_j + g_i ⊙ Σ_{j∈S(i)} v_j, where α_{ij} are softmax-normalized attention weights, v_j are head-specific value projections, and g_i = σ(W_g q_i) is a query-conditioned gate (σ = sigmoid, W_g ∈ R^{d_h×d_h}). Both sums share the same support set S(i) and include self (j=i). The CPA channel adds only ~1% parameters (the gate projection matrix per head) and is parameter-matched to baselines via FFN width adjustment. The theoretical motivation is grounded in multiset discrimination: softmax attention computes a weighted mean over distinct values, which is invariant to value multiplicity (Proposition 1, formally proved). CPA resolves this by including the raw unnormalized sum Σ v_j, whose magnitude scales with |S(i)|, creating injectivity over the neighbor multiset. Theorem 1 proves that with strictly positive gates (sigmoid ensures this), CPA-augmented aggregation is at least as expressive as one 1-WL color refinement iteration—the sum over embedded features is injective over multisets by Xu et al.'s Lemma 5, the gating bijection preserves injectivity, and composing with self-features via (1+ε) scaling prevents cancellation. Corollary 1 proves that degree-normalized CPA (dividing the unnormalized sum by |S(i)|) loses 1-WL expressivity because mean aggregation maps distinct multisets to identical values. The structured sparse attention uses K-hop SPD masking: S(i) = {j | SPD(i,j) ≤ K}, with K=3 in main experiments. Logits include three Graphormer-inspired biases: (1) b_{φ(SPD(i,j))} — learnable SPD bin embeddings (K+1 bins), (2) b_{e_ij} — direct-bond feature embeddings (active only when SPD=1), (3) b_c(j) — key-side centrality bias as degree-bin embedding lookup. After attention, per-layer static centrality injection adds c_i (node degree bin embedding) to the output. The support mask is implemented via precomputed neighbor index lists with batch bucketing and padding to a fixed length L (batch max of |S(i)|), achieving <10% average padding on the corpus. For contrastive pretraining, two augmented views per graph are generated via random subgraph sampling (50-75% nodes), node dropout (rate 0.1-0.3), and edge dropout (rate 0.1-0.3). Crucially, SPD distances and degree bins are recomputed per view (multi-source BFS) to maintain semantic consistency between masks and actual topology—this adds ~15% pretraining cost but improves performance (+0.005 AUC). Masked modeling masks 15% of nodes and 15% of edges independently, with a single-layer shared MLP decoder predicting original features. Total loss: L = L_mask + 0.5·L_contrast. The architecture uses 12 layers, hidden dim 512, 8 heads, FFN 2048, LayerNorm, dropout 0.1, pretrained on ~28M molecules (ZINC20 + ChEMBL35, Lipinski-filtered, scaffold-decontaminated) with AdamW optimizer, cosine decay from 2e-4 to 1e-6, global batch 4096, 500k optimizer steps, bf16 precision.
content.experiment: The evaluation spans 11 public benchmarks across three suites: (1) MoleculeNet (ESOL, Lipophilicity, BBBP, Tox21, ClinTox) with 80/10/10 Bemis-Murcko scaffold splits; (2) OGB (ogbg-molhiv, ogbg-molpcba) with official splits; (3) TDC ADMET (Caco2_Wang, hERG, Clearance_Hepatocyte_AZ, Clearance_Microsome_AZ) with scaffold splits. Metrics follow dataset conventions: RMSE (regression), ROC-AUC (binary classification), average precision (multilabel), MAE, and Spearman correlation. All benchmark molecules are scaffold-decontaminated from the pretraining corpus (~20k removed). The primary comparison is between CardinalGraphFormer and SparseGraphormer-K3—both share the same backbone (12 layers, 512 dim, 8 heads), pretraining corpus, dual objectives, optimization budget, and K=3 sparse attention, differing only in the CPA channel. This isolates CPA's contribution. Additional baselines include GraphMAE-K3 (mask-only pretraining), GraphCL (contrast-only), Graphormer (faithful implementation with global attention, full SPD binning, shortest-path edge encodings), D-MPNN, and GIN. All transformer-family baselines share the same encoder, pretraining data, and fine-tuning protocol. Statistical significance uses paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples per task/seed, identical resample indices across models), with Holm correction across 11 tasks. Ablation studies systematically evaluate: (1) CPA variants—degree-normalized CPA, mismatched-support CPA (global sum), sum+mean aggregation; (2) cardinality-control baselines—explicit size injection (N and |S(i)| appended to input embeddings or as additive bias), learned |S(i)| scaling, learned temperature modulation; (3) structural bias ablations—removing per-layer centrality injection c_i, removing key-side b_c(j), varying K (2, 5, ∞); (4) pretraining ablations—mask-only, contrast-only, no pretraining, reduced pretraining budgets (10%, 25% steps); (5) augmentation ablations—chemistry-aware variants (attribute masking, valency-constrained edge dropout), per-view vs. stable SPD recomputation; (6) gate function variants—sigmoid, linear, tanh. Size-stratified evaluations partition test sets by graph size N (small: N<30, mid: 30≤N<50, large: N≥50) and include size-shift splits (train on small, test on large). A size-only baseline (ridge logistic regression) and explicit size injection baselines confirm CPA benefits are not simple size shortcuts. Pretraining used ~2784 GPU-hours on 4×A100 80GB (29 days wall-clock). Fine-tuning per task/seed averaged 2-4 GPU-hours.
content.result: CardinalGraphFormer achieves statistically significant improvements over SparseGraphormer-K3 across all 11 benchmarks after Holm correction (all adjusted p<0.05). ESOL: 0.542 vs 0.598 RMSE (-0.056, 9.4% reduction); Lipophilicity: 0.629 vs 0.658 (-0.029); BBBP: 0.938 vs 0.918 AUC (+0.020); Tox21: 0.921 vs 0.908 (+0.013); ClinTox: 0.954 vs 0.939 (+0.015); ogbg-molhiv: 0.819 vs 0.802 (+0.017); ogbg-molpcba: 0.304 vs 0.294 (+0.010); Caco2_Wang: 0.241 vs 0.265 MAE (-0.024); hERG: 0.898 vs 0.870 (+0.028, the largest gain); Clearance_Hepatocyte_AZ: 0.538 vs 0.525 (+0.013); Clearance_Microsome_AZ: 0.621 vs 0.614 (+0.007, the smallest gain). hERG's disproportionate benefit is attributed to the task's sensitivity to local structural discrimination, where cardinality signals help disambiguate subtle neighborhood differences. Ablations confirm CPA's unique contribution: explicit size injection recovers only 20-30% of the CPA gain; degree-normalized CPA underperforms (consistent with Corollary 1); mismatched-support CPA (global sum) underperforms aligned CPA by 0.008 AUC; learned temperature and scaling baselines approach but do not match CPA. Removing individual structural biases causes smaller degradations than removing CPA. Size-stratified results show CPA gains persist across all size strata (small, mid, large, size-shift), ruling out simple size shortcut learning. The L2 norm of the gated unnormalized sum correlates positively with |S(i)| even after controlling for node degree (partial r=0.52±0.03), confirming CPA captures dynamic cardinality signals beyond static degree bins. Under augmentations, |S(i)| shifts by ~15%, and the CPA norm correlation adapts (r=0.48±0.04 post-augmentation), demonstrating dynamic adaptation to support-size changes. Sigmod gating proved most stable; unbounded linear gates diverged in 2/5 seeds. Chemistry-aware augmentations (attribute masking, valency-constrained edge dropout) preserve CPA gains, confirming robustness beyond random augmentation artifacts. For typical drug-like molecules (median N≈22), K=3 is near-global (median coverage >95%), so gains arise primarily from CPA and structural biases rather than strict sparsity. Genuine efficiency benefits (2.5×-4.4× speedup) emerge on larger molecules (N≥35, ~15% of pretraining corpus). The dual-objective pretraining is confirmed beneficial: mask-only or contrast-only pretraining underperforms the combined objective.

content.topic_relation: This paper advances graph transformer architectures for molecular property prediction with a theoretically-grounded cardinality-preserving mechanism. For the TopicState's polymer Tg prediction goal, CPA is directly relevant because (a) polymer graphs are tree-like 1D chains where support-set cardinality correlates with chain length—a physically meaningful quantity for Tg (longer chains → higher Tg via entanglements and reduced free volume); (b) the theoretical framework connecting CPA to 1-WL expressivity via injective multiset aggregation provides formal justification for preserving multiplicity signals that softmax attention discards; (c) the rigorous ablation methodology (matched protocols, cardinality-control baselines, size-stratified evaluation, partial correlation analyses) sets an exemplar for isolating mechanism contributions—directly applicable to polymer experiments; (d) the dual-objective pretraining (masked + contrastive) with ~28M molecules confirms that combined objectives outperform single objectives, relevant to TopicState's exploration of graph-level SSL for PI1M; (e) the finding that per-view SPD recomputation improves contrastive learning (+0.005 AUC) suggests that topological consistency under augmentation matters—analogous reasoning could apply to polymer backbone augmentations. However, the TopicState's 'Topological Simplicity Constraint' and 'Collapse Prevention Constraint' must be considered: polymer graphs (~35-104 nodes, 1D tree-like) differ fundamentally from drug-like molecular graphs, so CPA's behavior on polymers requires empirical validation. The per-task effect size variation (hERG +0.028 vs Clearance_Microsome +0.007) also suggests CPA benefits are task-dependent—Tg prediction's sensitivity to chain-length cardinality signals is an open empirical question.
content.topic_contribution: Provides an actionable architectural component (CPA channel) that can be integrated into graph transformer backbones for polymer Tg prediction. Specific decisions enabled: (1) CPA can be added to any multi-head attention layer with minimal parameter overhead (~1%), making it a low-risk experiment for the polymer transformer architecture being considered; (2) The theoretical analysis (Proposition 1, Theorem 1, Corollary 1) provides clear design guidance—use sigmoid-gated unnormalized sum (NOT degree-normalized, NOT global sum) aligned to the same support set as softmax attention; (3) The ablation template (explicit size injection baselines, degree-normalized CPA, learned temperature/scaling controls) provides a ready-made protocol for isolating whether CPA benefits in polymers come from cardinality signals vs. parameter count vs. shortcut learning; (4) The finding that per-view SPD recomputation aids contrastive learning suggests that for polymer contrastive pretraining, recomputing chain-geometry features (PSPE distances, monomer positions) after augmentation may improve semantic consistency; (5) The dual-objective pretraining success (mask + contrast > either alone) directly informs TopicState's pretraining strategy selection, supporting the Complementary Hierarchy Hypothesis that multiple objective types are synergistic; (6) The size-stratified evaluation methodology provides a template for verifying that polymer model improvements are not merely exploiting graph-size artifacts (critical since polymer Tg correlates with molecular weight). However, three caveats from TopicState apply: (a) the 'Collapse Prevention Constraint' means CPA alone cannot solve pretraining collapse on small polymer graphs—explicit NT-Xent or EMA+predictor asymmetry is still needed; (b) the 'Topological Simplicity Constraint' means CPA's cardinality signals may be partially redundant with explicit PSPE chain-length features (distance-to-chain-end already encodes position along the backbone); (c) the K=3 sparsity is near-global for drug-like molecules but polymer graphs (1-RU ~35 nodes, 3-RU ~104 nodes) are larger, so K-hop hyperparameter tuning would be needed.

memory.abstract: The paper unifies over-smoothing, over-squashing, and vanishing gradients in GNNs through linear control theory, showing they share a common cause: the contractive spectrum of layer-wise Jacobians. It reinterprets GNNs as recurrent state-space models (GNN-SSM) with a fixed state transition matrix Λ whose spectrum can be directly controlled, enabling edge-of-chaos dynamics that prevent feature collapse and improve long-range modeling without extra trainable parameters.
memory.keyword: vanishing gradients, over-smoothing, over-squashing, state-space models, graph neural networks, Jacobian spectrum, edge of chaos

content.background: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), particularly Message-Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) such as GCN, GAT, GIN, and GraphSAGE, have become the dominant paradigm for learning on graph-structured data. Despite widespread success, they suffer from three well-documented but poorly unified failure modes: (1) over-smoothing — node feature representations become exponentially similar as depth increases, causing representational collapse; (2) over-squashing — information from distant nodes is compressed into fixed-size vectors, preventing effective long-range modeling; and (3) vanishing/exploding gradients — the product of layer-wise Jacobians approaches zero or infinity during backpropagation, making training of deep GNNs impossible. While each issue has been studied independently, no unified theoretical framework has established whether they share a common underlying cause or explained why certain mitigation strategies succeed. The GNN community has largely overlooked vanishing gradients, which have been extensively studied in the Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) literature. Recent advances in linear state-space models (e.g., Mamba, S4) and dynamical isometry theory for feedforward networks have demonstrated that controlling the eigenvalue spectrum of layer-wise Jacobians is crucial for stable training and long-range memory. This paper bridges these two surprisingly disjoint bodies of literature — recurrent/state-space models and graph learning — by showing that GNNs are recurrent models in disguise, and that the same mechanism causing extreme gradient vanishing also drives over-smoothing and contributes to over-squashing. The motivation is to provide a principled framework for designing deep GNN architectures that can propagate information over many layers without collapse, and to establish that techniques from the RNN and state-space model literature can be effectively adapted to graph learning.
content.method:
The paper's methodology operates at three interconnected levels: (1) spectral analysis of GNN Jacobians revealing extreme gradient vanishing, (2) a state-space model reformulation (GNN-SSM) enabling direct Jacobian control, and (3) theoretical connections linking vanishing gradients to over-smoothing and over-squashing.

**Level 1: Jacobian Analysis of Classical GNNs.** Using the vectorization operation vec(·) and Kronecker product properties, the authors derive the layer-wise Jacobian for a linear GCN layer H^(k) = Ã H^(k-1) W as J = W^T ⊗ Ã. Lemma 3.1 shows that the squared singular values of J are {λ_i² μ_j | i=1,...,n; j=1,...,d_k}, where λ_i are eigenvalues of the normalized adjacency Ã (satisfying |λ_i| ≤ 1) and μ_j are eigenvalues of WW^T. Theorem 3.2 then shows that with Gaussian i.i.d. weight initialization, the mean and variance of each squared singular value γ_{i,j} are E[γ] = λ_i²σ² and Var[γ] = λ_i⁴σ⁴(d_k/d_{k-1}). Since |λ_i| ≤ 1, the spectrum is systematically contracted by the adjacency, yielding a phenomenon they term "extreme gradient vanishing" — even a single layer exhibits a long tail of near-zero singular values, far more severe than in standard MLPs or RNNs. The same analysis extends to GATs because the learned attention-based adjacency also retains contractive spectral structure.

**Level 2: GNN-SSM Architecture.** To overcome this contraction, the authors rewrite any GNN's layer-to-layer update in state-space form: H^{(k+1)⊤} = Λ H^{(k)⊤} + B F_θ(H^{(k)}, k)^⊤, where Λ ∈ ℝ^{d×d} is the state transition matrix, B ∈ ℝ^{d×d} is the input matrix, and F_θ is a time-varying coupling function representing any MPNN layer. The key insight is that Λ and B are fixed (untrained) matrices designed to control the Jacobian spectrum, while only F_θ is optimized. Λ is constructed by generating a random unitary matrix (with all eigenvalues on the unit circle) and scaling it to control the spectral radius. Proposition 3.3 bounds the Jacobian norm: ‖J‖₂ ≤ ‖Λ‖₂ + ‖B‖₂‖Γ‖₂, where Γ is the Jacobian of F_θ. Setting eig(Λ) ≈ 1 and eig(B) ≈ 0.1 places the full Jacobian at the edge of chaos — neither contracting nor expanding — without requiring careful weight initialization or activation function selection. This is a general framework: any MPNN can serve as F_θ, and more complex gating mechanisms (LSTM-style) or orthogonality constraints can be incorporated.

**Level 3: Theoretical Connections to Over-smoothing and Over-squashing.** For over-smoothing: The authors view each GNN layer as a map f_k with Lipschitz constant ‖f_k‖_Lip (the supremum of the Jacobian norm over its domain). When ‖f_k‖_Lip < 1 for all layers (contractive case), the Banach Fixed Point Theorem guarantees convergence to a unique fixed point. Lemma 4.2 shows that for activations with σ(0)=0 (ReLU, tanh), zero is a fixed point. Proposition 4.3 proves that ‖f(H)‖ < (1-ε)^K ‖H‖, so features monotonically collapse to zero as depth K → ∞. Proposition 4.4 bounds the Dirichlet energy: E(f(H)) ≤ 2|E| ∏‖f_k‖_Lip² ‖H‖², proving that contractive layers artificially minimize smoothness measures. This reframes over-smoothing not as convergence to a rank-one subspace (the conventional view) but as zero feature collapse driven by the same Jacobian contraction that causes vanishing gradients.

For over-squashing: The sensitivity bound from Di Giovanni et al. (2023) decomposes into a model term (controlled by weight norms and activation Lipschitz constants) and a topology term (controlled by the message-passing matrix). The paper argues that most prior work addressed only the topology term via graph rewiring, while the model term — directly linked to vanishing gradients — is equally critical. The GNN-SSM framework with eig(Λ) ≈ 1 ensures the model term does not further attenuate signals. The kGNN-SSM variant combines k-hop aggregation (for connectivity) with edge-of-chaos dynamics (for non-dissipativity), addressing both terms simultaneously.
content.experiment:
The empirical evaluation is organized around three research questions corresponding to the three theoretical contributions.

**Over-smoothing Experiments (Section 4.2):** The Cora dataset (2,708 nodes, 10,556 edges) is used as the primary testbed, with GNN layers ranging from 1 to 80. Three metrics are tracked: Dirichlet energy (Equation 12), latent vector norms, and node classification accuracy. The GNN-SSM model is tested with varying ‖Λ‖₂ (0.5, 0.75, 1.0) to demonstrate exact control over the energy decay rate. Baselines include standard GCN, GCN with residual connections, and GCN-SSM without edge-of-chaos tuning. Additional experiments on Texas (183 nodes) and a 10×10 grid graph confirm topology-independence. The Jacobian eigenvalue histograms for GIN and Gated-GCN are also analyzed to show that these architectures exhibit unstable dynamics (eigenvalues > 1) rather than contraction, explaining their observed Dirichlet energy divergence in prior work. ADGN, SWAN, and PHDGN — architectures with near-unit Jacobian norms — are shown to maintain stable energy across layers.

**Over-squashing and Long-Range Experiments (Section 5.2):** Three benchmark suites are employed: (i) RingTransfer task from Di Giovanni et al. (2023), a synthetic task with certifiable long-range dependencies where a label must be propagated around a ring; (ii) Graph Property Prediction (GPP) tasks — Diameter, Single-Source Shortest Path (SSSP), and Eccentricity — on synthetic graphs (5,120 train / 640 val / 1,280 test) from Erdős-Rényi, Barabási-Albert, grid, caveman, tree, ladder, line, star, caterpillar, and lobster distributions (25-35 nodes each); (iii) Long-Range Graph Benchmark (LRGB) — peptides-func (multi-label graph classification, 15,535 graphs) and peptides-struct (multi-label graph regression, 15,535 graphs). The kGNN-SSM model combines GNN-SSM with k-hop aggregation (Equation 20). Ablation studies systematically remove: (a) the SSM layer, (b) eig(Λ) ≈ 1 (reverting to dissipative dynamics), (c) k-hop rewiring, (d) increased hidden dimensions. DRew-GCN with and without delay is included as a strong baseline. For GPP, models use 10 layers, hidden dims 20-30, tanh activation, with eig(Λ) ∈ {0.5, 0.75, 1.0}. For LRGB, peptides-func uses 40 layers (requiring substantial long-range capacity), peptides-struct uses 17 layers, hidden dim 105, ReLU activation, eig(Λ)=1.0, with AdamW optimizer. All GPP results are averaged over 4 random weight initializations; LRGB results follow the standard protocol from Dwivedi et al. (2022).

**Ablation Design:** Table 1 provides a granular ablation on LRGB datasets, incrementally adding/removing components: +d↑ (increased hidden dimensions), -eig(Λ)≈1 (removing edge-of-chaos tuning), -SSM (removing the state-space layer), -khop (removing k-hop rewiring), and comparing against DRew-GCN ± delay. Table 2 provides analogous ablations on GPP tasks. Figure 5 (left) shows RingTransfer performance for kGNN-SSM with varying eig(Λ), and Figure 5 (right) shows how increasing dissipativity degrades long-range modeling.
content.result:
The experimental results provide strong empirical support for all three theoretical claims. On over-smoothing: GNN-SSM with eig(Λ) ≈ 1 maintains stable Dirichlet energy and node classification accuracy even at 80 layers on Cora, while standard GCN collapses to near-zero energy within 10-15 layers. The control is precise — varying ‖Λ‖₂ from 0.5 to 1.0 produces correspondingly graduated energy decay rates, validating Proposition 4.4. GIN and Gated-GCN exhibit unstable dynamics with Jacobian eigenvalues exceeding 1, explaining their divergent rather than collapsed behavior. ADGN, SWAN, and PHDGN — all with near-unit Jacobian norms — show flat Dirichlet energy across 80 layers, confirming the generality of the Jacobian-based analysis beyond MPNNs.

On over-squashing and long-range modeling: kGNN-SSM achieves state-of-the-art performance on RingTransfer only when both k-hop connectivity and eig(Λ) ≈ 1 are active. Making the model more dissipative (lower eig(Λ)) directly degrades performance, demonstrating the model term's importance in Theorem 5.1. On GPP tasks (Table 2), kGNN-SSM achieves log10(MSE) of -3.075 (Diameter), -3.604 (SSSP), and -4.265 (Eccentricity), significantly outperforming DRew-GCN (-2.369, -1.591, -2.100) and DRew+delay (-2.402, -1.602, -2.029). The full results (Table 4 in Appendix) show kGNN-SSM surpassing all baselines including GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, GIN, GCNII, DGC, GRAND, GraphCON, ADGN, SWAN, and PH-DGN. On LRGB (Table 1), kGNN-SSM achieves 72.12 AP on peptides-func and 25.81×10⁻² MAE on peptides-struct, outperforming DRew-GCN+delay (68.05 and 27.08×10⁻²). Ablation confirms that removing either SSM or edge-of-chaos tuning causes significant performance degradation. Increased hidden dimensions are particularly important for the 40-layer peptides-func task, consistent with sequence modeling findings.

Key principles emerging from the results: (1) The layer-wise Jacobian spectrum is a sufficient diagnostic for both over-smoothing and trainability — architectures with eigenvalues near the unit circle avoid collapse; (2) Mitigating over-squashing requires combining increased graph connectivity (rewiring, k-hop) with non-dissipative model dynamics — neither alone suffices; (3) The state-space formulation incurs no extra trainable parameter cost since Λ and B are fixed. Limitations: the analysis assumes specific activation functions (σ(0)=0) for the zero-fixed-point argument; GNN-SSM requires manual tuning of the Λ spectrum; and the framework has not been tested on very large graphs (million-node scale). Future directions include integrating learned gating mechanisms (LSTM-style) into the SSM layer, exploring structured state-space matrices beyond random unitary constructions, and applying the Jacobian diagnostic to guide architecture search for specific graph topologies.

content.topic_relation: This paper relates to the TopicState through several active hypotheses and constraints. (1) The Topological Simplicity Constraint — polymer graphs are 1D tree-like chains with sparse branching — means that the extreme gradient vanishing diagnosed in this paper is likely even more severe for polymer GNNs, since long linear chains maximize the number of message-passing steps needed for end-to-end communication. (2) The finding that contractive Jacobians cause zero feature collapse provides a mechanistic explanation for why naive deep GNN architectures consistently underperform on polymer Tg prediction: features collapse before global chain properties (backbone flexibility, free volume) can be encoded. (3) The GNN-SSM framework offers a concrete architectural solution for building deeper polymer GNNs without collapse, which could benefit 3-RU and longer multimer representations where chain-level properties emerge. (4) The paper's demonstration that long-range tasks require both graph rewiring AND non-dissipative dynamics directly parallels the Pretraining-Task Alignment Principle: effective graph-level pretraining on polymer chains likely requires both architectural support for deep propagation and domain-relevant inductive biases.
content.topic_contribution: Provides actionable architectural guidance for polymer deep learning: (1) The layer-wise Jacobian eigenanalysis should become a diagnostic test for any deep polymer GNN architecture — architectures with contracting Jacobians will collapse before encoding global chain properties, especially for long 3-RU polymers (~104 nodes). (2) GNN-SSM with eig(Λ) ≈ 1 is a lightweight (zero extra trainable parameters) modification that can be applied to any existing polymer GNN backbone (GAT, GIN, etc.) to enable deeper architectures. (3) For polymer-specific adaptations: the k-hop rewiring could be replaced with chain-aware connectivity (connecting nodes by backbone distance rather than graph distance), and Λ could potentially encode polymer physics priors (e.g., persistence length, bond rotation energetics). (4) The finding that increasing hidden dimension helps long-range tasks (peptides-func at 40 layers) suggests that wider latent spaces may be necessary for encoding polymer chain-level properties. Decision support: if attempting deep (>4 layer) polymer architectures, Jacobian analysis should be performed first; if contraction is detected, GNN-SSM is the recommended mitigation before considering more complex solutions.

memory.abstract: The Global Attention Paradox: Why Transformers Succeed on Molecules but Fail on Polymers — GPS-Lite's catastrophic +8K degradation (mem_132) appears to contradict the transformer-without-graph-priors success on molecular force fields (mem_128, 1B-param Transformer matches equivariant GNNs). This integration resolves the paradox: global attention is harmful for polymer Tg not because attention is inherently bad, but because (a) 4-hop GAT already saturates the polymer backbone receptive field, making global O(N²) attention pure noise injection; (b) GNN-SSM's Jacobian analysis (mem_131) reveals contractive dynamics that are well-matched to 1D chain topology — adding dense attention disrupts this spectral alignment; (c) Transformers succeed on molecules (mem_128) because molecular graphs have diverse, unpredictable topologies where adaptive receptive fields (inverse distance decay, rank-based attention) provide genuine value — polymers lack this topological diversity (mem_097). k-MIP (mem_129) provides the path to reconciliation: sparse learnable attention that selects only top-k relevant keys could provide the benefits of global attention (long-range chain periodicity) without the noise of full O(N²) attention. But the 4.64K SOTA gap cannot be closed by architecture alone — the non-pretraining asymptote at ~35K is now ironclad.

content.integration_type: paradox resolution — reconciling GPS-Lite failure with transformer success literature
content.central_paradox: Day 5's GPS-Lite experiment (mem_132) shows that a single global multi-head self-attention layer atop a proven GAT encoder degrades polymer Tg prediction by ~8K RMSE (35.19K → 43.14-43.43K). Yet mem_128 demonstrates that unmodified Transformers trained directly on Cartesian coordinates without any graph priors achieve competitive energy and force errors against state-of-the-art equivariant GNNs (eSAEN: energy 117.99 vs 129.77 meV, forces 18.35 vs 13.01 meV/Å) on the OMol25 molecular dataset, discovering physically consistent attention patterns (inverse distance decay, adaptive receptive fields) purely from data. How can global attention be simultaneously powerful enough to rival equivariant GNNs on molecular forces and destructive enough to add +8K error on polymer Tg? The resolution is not 'attention is bad' or 'polymers are special' — it lies in the interaction between receptive field requirements, graph topology, and data scale.
consensus: GPS-Lite failure is conclusive: both variants (no-bias 43.43K, SPD-bias 43.14K) substantially underperform the GAT-only baseline (35.19K). Adding global attention is actively harmful for polymer Tg under current data conditions (7,170 labeled samples).

The root cause is NOT that attention cannot learn useful patterns — mem_128 proves it can. The root cause is that 4-layer GAT already provides complete receptive field coverage for polymer graphs (~54-atom backbone, 4 hops covers the full chain). Adding global O(N²) attention introduces noise from irrelevant distant atom pairs that drowns out the already-sufficient local chemical signals.

GNN-SSM's unified framework (mem_131) provides a mechanistic explanation: the layer-wise Jacobian spectrum of stacked GAT on 1D chain topology has eigenvalues well-matched to the graph Laplacian — the contractive dynamics naturally filter high-frequency noise while preserving chain-level signal. Adding global attention perturbs this spectrum with a dense matrix whose eigenvalues are near-uniform, introducing gradient conflict (mem_132 notes 'attention gradients conflict with GAT gradients') that destabilizes the carefully balanced local-to-global information flow.

Transformers succeed on OMol25 (mem_128) because molecular graphs in that dataset (biomolecules, metal complexes, electrolytes) have diverse, unpredictable topologies — cycles, branches, 3D conformational complexity — where fixed-radius cutoff graphs (the GNN baseline) may miss critical long-range interactions (charge transfer, polarization). The Transformer's adaptive receptive fields (attention expands to ~15Å for isolated atoms, contracts to ~2Å in dense regions) provide genuine value that GNN cutoffs cannot match. Polymer graphs (mem_097), by contrast, are 1D tree-like chains where the local chemical environment IS the full relevant context — there are no non-local surprises that local message passing cannot capture.

The over-squashing hypothesis for polymers is DISCONFIRMED. GPS-Lite was motivated by the idea that long-range chain interactions (end-to-end effects on Tg) require global attention to alleviate over-squashing (mem_100). The experimental result (+8K) and GNN-SSM's analysis (mem_131) converge: over-squashing is not the bottleneck. The polymer chain's 1D topology means 4-hop message passing already propagates end-to-end signals. What DOES matter is representation quality — local chemistry, chain geometry (PSPE), monomer identity — not information propagation distance.

conflicts.conflict: mem_128 shows Transformers without graph priors OUTPERFORM GNNs on molecular forces. GPS-Lite shows Transformers with graph priors (GAT encoder + attention) UNDERPERFORM pure GNNs on polymer Tg. Is the Transformer success in mem_128 real, or is it an artifact of the specific task (force prediction vs. property regression), dataset scale (4M vs. 7K), or training regime (two-stage pretrain+finetune vs. supervised from scratch)?
conflicts.resolution: Both results are real, but they operate in different regimes. mem_128's Transformer benefits from: (1) 4M training structures vs. 7K — global attention needs data scale to learn meaningful patterns; (2) two-stage training (autoregressive pretraining + force/energy finetuning) — the pretraining phase learns the joint distribution of atomic positions, providing a strong initialization that prevents the noise-injection problem; (3) continuous coordinate inputs — the positions themselves carry geometric information that guides attention patterns. GPS-Lite had none of these advantages: trained from scratch on 7K samples, no pretraining, discrete graph topology rather than continuous coordinates. The failure mode is not 'attention can't work for polymers' — it's 'attention needs pretraining and data scale that our supervised Tg setting cannot provide.' This is consistent with mem_128's key finding that Transformer scaling laws are predictable: at 7K samples, we are far below the data threshold where attention becomes beneficial. The implication is that global attention might become viable AFTER pretraining on PI1M, but as a standalone supervised component it is harmful.

conflicts.conflict: k-MIP (mem_129) demonstrates that sparse attention (top-k relevant keys) can universally approximate full attention and scales to 569k-node graphs — shouldn't we try GPS+k-MIP for polymers before declaring global attention dead?
conflicts.resolution: k-MIP addresses the computational efficiency problem of global attention, but GPS-Lite's failure is not computational — it's about signal quality. The issue is not that O(N²) attention is too expensive for polymer graphs (~104 nodes for 3-RU — well within full attention's capacity). The issue is that attending to ALL node pairs introduces noise. k-MIP could theoretically help by selecting only the most relevant keys — but the question is: what are the 'most relevant keys' for polymer Tg? If the answer is 'nearby atoms along the backbone' (as the GAT success suggests), then k-MIP would converge to a local attention pattern that replicates GAT's message passing — adding complexity without benefit. If k-MIP discovers genuinely useful non-local patterns (e.g., attending to atoms with similar backbone positions across different monomers — a periodicity signal), it could provide value. But the GPS-Lite result strongly suggests that such patterns, if they exist, are too weak to overcome the noise from the remaining attention connections. k-MIP is worth exploring ONLY after pretraining, not as a non-pretraining architectural addition.

alignment: The Simplicity Principle (mem_096) is strongly confirmed and extended: for polymer Tg with 7,170 labeled samples, the optimal architecture is stacked GATConv+ELU WITHOUT residual connections, LayerNorm, or global attention. Complexity (global attention, residual connections, LayerNorm) systematically degrades performance. GPS-Lite is the most expensive confirmation of this principle to date.

The Topological Simplicity Constraint (mem_097) is also confirmed from a new angle: polymer graphs are not just topologically simple — they are RECEPTIVE-FIELD-SATURATED. A 4-layer GAT covers the entire polymer backbone. There is literally no structural information beyond 4 hops that the model cannot access through message passing. This makes global attention structurally redundant — not just potentially noisy, but definitionally unnecessary.

The Exponential Convergence to Non-Pretraining Ceiling (mem_110) is now IRONCLAD. With GPS-Lite's failure, the asymptote at ~35K for GAT-based non-pretraining architectures is confirmed from both the improvement side (exponential decay: +4.75K → +0.91K → +0.50K → now 0K for attention) and the degradation side (adding complexity doesn't plateau — it actively hurts). The 4.64K gap to PerioGT SOTA (30.8K) requires either pretraining or a fundamentally different supervised approach.

GNN-SSM (mem_131) provides theoretical backing for the Simplicity Principle: the contractive Jacobian spectrum of simple stacked GNNs is well-matched to 1D chain topology. The edge-of-chaos dynamics (eig(Λ)≈1) that GNN-SSM prescribes for complex graphs are UNNECESSARY for polymers — the natural GAT dynamics are already optimally tuned for the chain topology. This explains why residual connections and LayerNorm were detrimental (mem_132): they perturb the naturally well-conditioned Jacobian spectrum.
content.key_insight: The global attention paradox resolves into a data-scale × topology interaction: Transformers succeed on molecules because molecular graphs have diverse topologies where adaptive receptive fields add genuine value AND the training sets are large enough (4M+) to learn meaningful attention patterns. Polymers fail with global attention because (1) 1D chain topology is already saturated by local message passing — there is no structural information beyond 4 hops, (2) 7K labeled samples are insufficient for attention to learn useful non-local patterns rather than noise, and (3) adding dense attention disrupts the well-conditioned Jacobian spectrum of stacked GAT. This does not mean attention is permanently useless for polymers — it means attention requires pretraining to become beneficial, consistent with mem_128's two-stage pretrain-then-finetune approach. The non-pretraining asymptote at ~35K is now confirmed from both the improvement ceiling and the complexity-failure floor. The strategic implication: abandon non-pretraining architectural exploration. All remaining paths — whether graph transformers, bond graphs, or supervised multi-task — must involve pretraining or external data.

memory.abstract: The Identity-Property Antagonism: Why Contrastive SSL Destroys Property-Relevant Representations — MoMuCon's -3.31K degradation (mem_134) completes the triple-negative PI1M SSL trajectory (GraphMAE +0.34K, SelfGNN -0.55K, MoMuCon -3.31K). The escalating degradation pattern is the key signal: more sophisticated, domain-relevant pretraining produces WORSE transfer. This integration formalizes the Identity-Property Antagonism: contrastive objectives that maximize inter-sample discrimination (NT-Xent) teach the encoder to separate polymers by identity, actively destroying the shared property-relevant feature correlations (e.g., 'aryl groups → high Tg') that Tg regression depends on. This is NOT a collapse problem — MoMuCon training was stable (cos ~0.39) — but a transfer problem that the Collapse Prevention Taxonomy (mem_121) did not anticipate. The Pretraining-Task Alignment Principle v3 adds a Property-Preservation criterion: pretraining must not only be graph-level, challenging, domain-relevant, and collapse-resistant, but must also PRESERVE the feature manifold structure needed for the downstream property. Masked reconstruction preserves this manifold (GraphMAE: near-zero effect); contrastive discrimination destroys it (MoMuCon: -3.31K).
memory.keyword: identity-property-antagonism PI1M-SSL-dead-end contrastive-destruction property-preservation escalating-degradation Pretraining-Task-Alignment-v3

content.integration_type: mechanistic explanation — why contrastive SSL destroys property-relevant representations for polymer Tg
content.central_discovery: Day 5's MoMuCon-NT-Xent experiment (mem_134) produced the third consecutive PI1M SSL failure — and the worst one. Monomer-vs-multimer contrastive pretraining with explicit NT-Xent loss degraded Tg prediction by 3.31K (35.44K → 38.75K). Together with GraphMAE (+0.34K, mem_105) and SelfGNN BYOL (-0.55K, mem_119), this establishes PI1M self-supervised pretraining as a triple-confirmed dead end. But the most informative signal is not the failure itself — it is the ESCALATING DEGRADATION PATTERN: +0.34K (masked reconstruction, no discrimination) → -0.55K (BYOL, weak discrimination via BatchNorm) → -3.31K (NT-Xent, strong explicit discrimination). The stronger the inter-sample discrimination pressure, the worse the transfer. This pattern reveals the Identity-Property Antagonism: contrastive objectives that push polymer representations apart by identity destroy the shared property-relevant feature correlations that regression depends on.
consensus: PI1M SSL is a triple-confirmed dead end for polymer Tg prediction. Three fundamentally different SSL approaches — node-level masked reconstruction (GraphMAE), graph-level BYOL (SelfGNN), and graph-level domain-relevant contrastive (MoMuCon) — all fail. The convergence across diverse methods rules out methodological flaws and points to a structural mismatch between PI1M pretraining and Tg finetuning.

The escalating degradation pattern (+0.34 → -0.55 → -3.31) is the opposite of theoretical predictions: more sophisticated, domain-relevant pretraining produces WORSE transfer. GraphMAE (weakest pretraining signal, no inter-sample discrimination) produces near-zero effect. SelfGNN BYOL (moderate discrimination via BatchNorm implicit negatives) produces slight degradation. MoMuCon NT-Xent (strongest discrimination via explicit negatives) produces substantial degradation. The correlation between discrimination strength and transfer degradation is the key signal.

The Identity-Property Antagonism: NT-Xent teaches the encoder that 'polymer A ≠ polymer B' — maximizing embedding distance between all polymers in the batch. But Tg prediction requires 'polymer A and polymer B share property-relevant features because both contain aryl backbones / both are semi-crystalline / both have similar free volume.' The contrastive objective systematically destroys the feature correlations that constitute the property manifold. After MoMuCon pretraining, two polymers with similar Tg may have maximally separated embeddings because they are different polymers — the encoder has learned to be a polymer identity function, not a polymer property function.

The Collapse Prevention Taxonomy (mem_121) correctly predicted that NT-Xent would prevent collapse — and it did (cos ~0.39, healthy). But collapse prevention ≠ transfer. The taxonomy addressed the STABILITY problem (will training converge?) but not the TRANSFER problem (will learned representations help Tg?). MoMuCon is the critical negative result that separates these two problems: stable, non-collapsed pretraining can still produce negative transfer if the objective teaches the wrong thing.

Masked reconstruction (GraphMAE, mem_105) preserves the property manifold better than contrastive learning because it operates WITHIN each polymer graph — reconstructing masked atom features teaches local chemistry without comparing polymers against each other. This is why GraphMAE produced near-zero transfer rather than negative transfer: it learned something (local chemistry rules) that was irrelevant to Tg rather than actively destructive to Tg-relevant features. Contrastive learning, by teaching inter-polymer separation, actively destroys the shared feature space that property prediction needs.

conflicts.conflict: MolCHG (mem_115), MoCL (mem_102), and CardinalGraphFormer (mem_130) all use contrastive pretraining (NT-Xent or InfoNCE) and achieve SOTA on molecular property prediction. How can contrastive learning be simultaneously SOTA on MoleculeNet and destructive for polymer Tg?
conflicts.resolution: There are two key differences. First, SCALE: MolCHG pretrains on ~2M molecules (or CardinalGraphFormer on ~28M), with diverse chemical structures spanning many property classes. The contrastive signal is diluted across chemical space — the model cannot simply learn 'molecule A ≠ molecule B' because there are millions of molecules. It must learn structured representations that capture chemical similarity (which correlates with property similarity). With only 200K polymers in MoMuCon's pretraining set, the contrastive signal may be strong enough to drive identity separation without forcing property-relevant structure. Second, DUAL OBJECTIVES: MolCHG and CardinalGraphFormer combine contrastive loss WITH masked reconstruction — the masked objective preserves local feature structure while contrastive provides global structure. The dual objective may prevent identity-only representations. MoMuCon used only contrastive loss — pure inter-sample discrimination without any feature-preserving objective.

conflicts.conflict: mem_135 already integrates the PI1M SSL dead end and proposes the Property-Preservation criterion. Why is this integration needed?
conflicts.resolution: mem_135 establishes THAT PI1M SSL is a dead end and WHAT the revised principle should be. This integration (mem_137) provides the mechanistic WHY: the Identity-Property Antagonism as the specific causal mechanism through which contrastive objectives destroy transfer, and the escalating degradation pattern as the empirical signature that identifies this mechanism. mem_135 is the summary; mem_137 is the explanation. The distinction matters for future research: if we understand WHY contrastive SSL fails, we can design pretraining objectives that avoid the antagonism — for example, masked objectives that operate within-graph rather than between-graph, or supervised multi-task pretraining where the 'discrimination' is between property values, not polymer identities.

alignment: The Pretraining-Task Alignment Principle v3 (mem_135) gains mechanistic depth: the Property-Preservation criterion is operationalized as 'avoid inter-sample discrimination that destroys the feature manifold needed for property regression.' This explains why masked reconstruction (property-preserving, near-zero transfer) outperforms contrastive learning (property-destroying, negative transfer).

The Complementary Hierarchy Principle (mem_122) is refined: dual-objective pretraining (masked + contrastive) may succeed where pure contrastive fails because the masked objective preserves local feature structure while contrastive provides global structure. This is consistent with MolCHG and CardinalGraphFormer's success with dual objectives. MoMuCon's failure with pure contrastive supports the hierarchy principle: single-signal pretraining is fragile; complementary signals provide robustness.

The escalating degradation pattern also validates the Topological Simplicity Constraint (mem_097) from a data perspective: PI1M polymers, being 1D chains with limited topological diversity, may provide insufficient structural variation for contrastive learning to discover meaningful feature dimensions. In a diverse molecular dataset, contrastive learning can organize embeddings by scaffold, functional groups, molecular weight etc. — features that correlate with properties. In a polymer dataset where most variation is chain length and monomer identity, contrastive learning may organize embeddings by these trivial features, which are then discarded at finetuning (Tg models already have explicit chain-length features via PSPE).

The non-pretraining asymptote at ~35K (mem_110, mem_133) now has a mirror image: the pretraining floor at ~38.75K. Not only does PI1M pretraining fail to improve — it actively degrades below the no-pretraining baseline. The gap between the pretraining floor (38.75K) and the non-pretraining ceiling (35.19K) is 3.56K — this is the 'damage zone' that contrastive pretraining inflicts. The implication: PI1M pretraining is not just unhelpful; it is COUNTERPRODUCTIVE, at least with contrastive objectives.
content.key_insight: The Identity-Property Antagonism is the causal mechanism behind the PI1M SSL dead end: contrastive objectives that maximize inter-sample discrimination teach the encoder to separate polymers by identity, destroying the shared property-relevant feature correlations needed for Tg regression. The escalating degradation pattern (+0.34 → -0.55 → -3.31) is the empirical signature — stronger discrimination produces worse transfer. This reframes the Pretraining-Task Alignment Principle: the pretraining task must not only be at the right level, challenging, domain-relevant, and collapse-resistant, but must also PRESERVE the feature manifold structure that the downstream property depends on. Masked reconstruction (within-graph) preserves this manifold; contrastive discrimination (between-graph) destroys it. The strategic implication: if pretraining is revisited, it must use either (a) supervised multi-task learning where 'discrimination' is between property values (not sample identities), (b) masked/JEPA-style objectives without inter-sample contrast, or (c) dual objectives where a masked component preserves local feature structure against the destructive pressure of contrastive discrimination.

memory.abstract: Post-PI1M Architecture Design: What GNN-SSM, CPA, and Transformer Scaling Laws Teach About Closing the 4.64K SOTA Gap — With PI1M SSL confirmed dead (mem_135) and GPS-Lite confirmed harmful (mem_132), the only viable path to PerioGT's 30.8K SOTA is architectural innovation on supervised data (7,170 Tg samples) or pretraining on alternative data sources. Today's readings (mem_128-131) collectively illuminate three actionable directions: (1) GNN-SSM's Jacobian diagnosis (mem_131) confirms that 4-layer GAT without residuals/LayerNorm is near-optimal for 1D chain topology — the contractive spectrum is naturally aligned with polymer graphs, explaining why 'edge-of-chaos' fixes are unnecessary and residual connections are detrimental (mem_132). (2) CardinalGraphFormer's CPA mechanism (mem_130) reveals that softmax attention is 'cardinality-blind' — it discards multiplicity signals. For polymers, cardinality encodes chain length (correlates with Tg), branching count, and monomer count — all physically meaningful quantities that CPA's gated unnormalized sum channel preserves. CPA added to GAT could capture these signals without the noise of global attention. (3) mem_128's key finding is not 'Transformers work' but 'data scale enables attention' — the 1B-parameter Transformer needed 4M structures to learn meaningful attention patterns. The polymer analog: bond-graph architectures (PolyBG mem_125), hierarchical message passing, or supervised multi-task pretraining on related polymer properties — anything that increases effective data scale beyond 7K labeled samples.
memory.keyword: post-PI1M-architecture GNN-SSM-Jacobian CPA-cardinality data-scale bond-graph supervised-multi-task polymer-design-directions

content.integration_type: forward-looking synthesis — architectural and data strategies after PI1M dead end and GPS-Lite failure
content.context: Day 5 establishes two definitive negatives: (1) GPS-Lite global attention degrades Tg by ~8K (mem_132), confirming the non-pretraining asymptote at ~35K and ruling out global-attention-based architectures as standalone solutions. (2) MoMuCon-NT-Xent degrades Tg by 3.31K (mem_134), completing the triple-negative PI1M SSL trajectory and ruling out PI1M self-supervised pretraining. The remaining 4.64K gap to PerioGT's 30.8K SOTA must be closed through either architectural innovation on the 7,170 supervised samples, supervised pretraining on alternative data sources, or both. Today's four paper readings (mem_128-131) provide converging guidance on what architectures and strategies are most promising.
consensus: GNN-SSM (mem_131) provides a UNIFIED DIAGNOSTIC for polymer GNN architectures: the layer-wise Jacobian spectrum determines whether the architecture will suffer from feature collapse, gradient vanishing, or training instability. For polymer graphs (1D chains with sparse branching), the spectrum of stacked GATConv+ELU is naturally well-conditioned — eigenvalues are bounded by the graph Laplacian, which for 1D paths has spectral radius < 1 but not ≪ 1. This explains the empirical finding (mem_132) that adding residual connections and LayerNorm to GAT DEGRADES performance: they perturb a naturally well-conditioned Jacobian spectrum by introducing identity shortcuts that dilute the graph-structure signal. GNN-SSM's prescription — control the Jacobian spectrum directly — is essentially what 4-layer GAT already achieves for polymer chains. The implication: further architectural modifications to GAT are likely to degrade rather than improve performance. The Jacobian is already optimally tuned.

CardinalGraphFormer's CPA (mem_130) identifies a specific expressivity gap in softmax attention that is directly relevant to polymer Tg: softmax is 'cardinality-blind' — it computes a weighted mean over value vectors, discarding information about HOW MANY nodes exist in the support set. For polymers, cardinality signals encode physically meaningful quantities: chain length (more repeat units → higher Tg via entanglement and reduced free volume), branching count (more branches → lower Tg via increased free volume), and the number of specific functional groups (more aryl groups → higher Tg). Standard GAT with mean aggregation is also cardinality-blind — the mean over neighbor features discards neighbor count. CPA's gated unnormalized sum channel (~1% parameter increase) preserves these signals. While CPA is designed for transformer attention, the same principle — adding an unnormalized sum channel to complement mean aggregation — could be applied to GAT message passing. Polymer Tg, which depends on chain-level statistics (average molecular weight, crosslink density, free volume), may be particularly sensitive to cardinality signals that mean aggregation discards.

Transformers-without-graph-priors (mem_128) succeeds NOT because attention is inherently superior to message passing, but because of DATA SCALE and TRAINING REGIME: 4M structures, two-stage training (autoregressive pretraining + force/energy finetuning), and predictable scaling laws. The key insight for polymers: the success of any architecture — GNN, Transformer, or hybrid — depends more on data scale and training strategy than on architectural details. PerioGT (30.8K SOTA) uses periodic-vs-nonperiodic contrastive pretraining — it increases effective data scale by leveraging the periodicity structure of polymers. The lesson is not 'use Transformers' but 'use architectures and training strategies that effectively increase data scale beyond 7K labeled samples.'

k-MIP (mem_129) provides the most viable path to incorporate attention into polymer architectures without the GPS-Lite noise problem: sparse, learnable attention that selects only top-k relevant keys. For polymers, k-MIP with small k (5-20) would automatically learn to attend to nearby backbone atoms (like GAT) while optionally discovering non-local patterns (periodicity, chain-end effects) when they exist. k-MIP also provides theoretical guarantees (universal approximation of full attention) and demonstrated scalability (569k-node graphs). The key advantage over GPS-Lite: k-MIP's sparsity is data-driven, not hard-coded — it could learn that for polymers, local attention dominates, while for molecules, longer-range attention matters. This adaptivity is exactly what GPS-Lite lacked.

conflicts.conflict: GNN-SSM prescribes edge-of-chaos dynamics (eig(Λ)≈1) for deep GNNs, but our 4-layer GAT performs best WITHOUT such tuning (no residuals, no LayerNorm, no spectral control). Is GNN-SSM's prescription wrong, or is 4-layer GAT already at the edge of chaos for polymer topology?
conflicts.resolution: GNN-SSM's analysis reveals that the Jacobian spectrum depends on BOTH the weight initialization AND the graph topology (via the adjacency matrix). For 1D chain graphs, the normalized adjacency eigenvalues are cos(πk/(N+1)) for k=1,...,N — the largest eigenvalue is cos(π/(N+1)) ≈ 1 for large N, but subsequent eigenvalues decay. This means the graph Laplacian already provides a near-unit spectral radius for the dominant mode — the 'edge of chaos' is naturally achieved for the primary chain-direction signal, while higher modes (noise, local fluctuations) are naturally damped. Standard GAT on polymer chains is effectively self-tuning to the edge of chaos because the graph topology does the tuning. Adding residual connections or spectral control mechanisms would perturb this natural alignment. GNN-SSM's prescription is correct for complex, non-chain graphs; for polymer chains, the topology itself provides the optimal spectral conditioning. This is a domain-specific insight, not a contradiction.

conflicts.conflict: CardinalGraphFormer (mem_130) achieves SOTA via dual-objective pretraining on 28M molecules + CPA. With PI1M pretraining confirmed dead, how can CPA be useful for polymer Tg?
conflicts.resolution: CPA is an architectural mechanism, not a pretraining mechanism. It can be added to a supervised GAT backbone without any pretraining. The CPA channel (gated unnormalized sum) adds ~1% parameters and can be integrated into GAT's message-passing aggregation: instead of mean aggregation over neighbor features, use mean + g·sum, where the gate is query-conditioned. This preserves cardinality signals (how many neighbors of each type) that may correlate with Tg-relevant properties like chain length and functional group density. The CPA experiment would be: GAT+CPA (supervised, no pretraining) vs. GAT (supervised, no pretraining) — testing whether cardinality preservation alone closes any portion of the SOTA gap. Because CPA is parameter-matched (~1% overhead), this is a clean ablation.

alignment: The data-scale insight from mem_128 aligns with the Exponential Convergence trajectory (mem_110): the non-pretraining asymptote at ~35K is the limit of what can be learned from 7K samples with GAT-based architectures. Breaking through requires increasing effective data scale — whether through architectural inductive biases that extract more signal per sample (bond graphs, CPA), supervised multi-task pretraining on related polymer properties, or alternative pretraining data sources.

GNN-SSM's Jacobian diagnostic aligns with the Simplicity Principle (mem_096): the reason simple architectures work best is that they are naturally well-conditioned for polymer topology. Complexity (residuals, LayerNorm, global attention) degrades performance because it perturbs this natural alignment. The principle now has a mechanistic foundation: the Jacobian spectrum explains WHY simplicity works, not just THAT it works.

CPA's cardinality-preservation aligns with the Topological Simplicity Constraint (mem_097): since polymer graphs are 1D chains, cardinality signals (chain length, branch count) are among the FEW sources of structural variation. In topologically diverse molecular graphs, cardinality is one signal among many; in topologically simple polymer graphs, it may be disproportionately important.

The bond-graph direction (PolyBG mem_125, MolCHG mem_115) aligns with the Complementary Hierarchy Principle (mem_122): adding bond-as-node representations complements atom-as-node representations because backbone bond types (C-C single, C=C double, C-O, amide) directly encode chain flexibility — the primary determinant of Tg. The bond graph is a form of architectural data augmentation: it provides a second, complementary view of the same polymer graph without requiring additional labeled samples.
content.key_insight: The post-PI1M landscape is defined by a clear constraint and three actionable directions. The constraint: 7K labeled Tg samples set a hard ceiling of ~35K for GAT-based architectures. The three directions: (1) CPA-augmented GAT — adding a cardinality-preserving sum channel to GAT's mean aggregation, with ~1% parameter overhead, to capture chain-length and branching-count signals that softmax/mean aggregation discards. This is the lowest-risk, highest-ROI supervised architectural experiment remaining. (2) Bond-graph architectures (PolyBG, mem_125) — representing backbone bonds as independent nodes with bond-type features (bond order, conjugation, ring membership, rotation barrier proxy) to explicitly model chain flexibility. This provides a complementary view of the polymer graph without additional data. (3) Supervised multi-task pretraining or alternative data — the PI1M dead end rules out SSL on PI1M but not supervised pretraining on related polymer properties (density, solubility, thermal decomposition from other polymer databases) or contrastive pretraining on alternative datasets where the contrastive signal is between PROPERTY VALUES rather than sample identities. The unifying theme across all three directions: increase effective data scale — through better inductive biases (CPA, bond graphs) that extract more signal per labeled sample, or through external data sources that provide genuinely transferable signal.

memory.abstract: CPA-GAT: Cardinality-Preserving Message Aggregation for supervised polymer Tg — adapting CardinalGraphFormer's sigmoid-gated unnormalized sum channel to GAT message-passing at ~1% parameter overhead, capturing chain-length and branching-density signals that softmax-normalized attention discards.
memory.keyword: CPA cardinality-preserving GAT-aggregation supervised chain-length branching-density sigmoid-gate

H: H1 — Cardinality-Blindness in GAT: GAT's per-node aggregation h_i' = Σ_j α_{ij} W_v h_j with softmax-normalized α_{ij} computes a weighted mean over neighbor value vectors. This is cardinality-blind — it discards HOW MANY neighbors of each type exist around node i, encoding only the average neighbor profile. For polymer graphs, cardinality signals encode physically meaningful quantities: chain length (more backbone neighbors → longer chain → higher Tg via reduced free volume), branching density (more branch-point neighbors → lower Tg via increased free volume), and functional group multiplicity (more aromatic neighbors → higher Tg). Mean aggregation collapses all of these to 'average neighbor type,' losing multiplicity information.

H2 — CPA as Minimal Architectural Increment: Adding a query-conditioned sigmoid-gated unnormalized sum channel to GAT — h_i' = Σ_j α_{ij} W_v h_j + σ(W_g h_i) ⊙ Σ_j W_v h_j — preserves cardinality signals with ~1% parameter overhead (only W_g per attention head). The sigmoid gate is learned per node: nodes where cardinality matters (chain ends, branch points) can open the gate; nodes where it doesn't (interior backbone atoms with uniform neighborhood) can close it. This is the lowest-risk architectural modification remaining under the Simplicity Principle — it adds no attention, no residuals, no LayerNorm, no global operations.

H3 — Interaction with PSPE: PSPE (distance-to-chain-end + monomer-index) already encodes chain-position signals that partially correlate with cardinality (chain ends have fewer neighbors). However, PSPE encodes position explicitly while CPA encodes multiplicity — they are complementary. PSPE says 'this atom is near the chain end'; CPA says 'this atom has only 2 neighbors, both backbone carbons.' The combination should provide richer chain-geometry signal than either alone.
