H4 — CPA vs. Degree Features: A naive baseline would be to concatenate node degree (or neighbor count) to input features. CPA is superior because: (a) the sum channel captures not just neighbor COUNT but the actual distribution of neighbor VALUE vectors — two nodes with 3 neighbors each but different neighbor types produce different sum vectors; (b) the query-conditioned gate learns WHEN cardinality matters rather than assuming it always does; (c) degree features are static while CPA adapts during training as the encoder learns better representations. Per CardinalGraphFormer (mem_130), explicit size injection recovers only 20-30% of CPA's gain.

X.name: CPA-GAT: Cardinality-Preserving GAT for Supervised Polymer Tg

architecture.encoder: 4-layer GAT (GATv2Conv) with NO residuals, NO LayerNorm, NO global attention — preserving the proven Day 5 best configuration (mem_132). 256 hidden dim, 4 attention heads, ELU activation. Input: 42-dim node features (8 rich atom features + 2 PSPE + 32 RWPE k=32).
architecture.cpa_mechanism: In each GAT layer and each attention head, the standard GAT output o_i^(std) = Σ_j α_{ij} W_v h_j is augmented with a CPA channel: o_i^(cpa) = σ(W_g h_i) ⊙ Σ_j W_v h_j, where W_g ∈ R^{d_h × d_h} is the gate projection (learned per head), σ is sigmoid, and ⊙ is element-wise multiplication. Both sums share the same support set S(i) (attention neighbors including self) and the same value projection W_v. Final output: h_i' = ELU(o_i^(std) + o_i^(cpa)). The CPA channel adds exactly one d_h×d_h weight matrix per attention head: 256×256=65,536 parameters per head, × 4 heads per layer, × 4 layers = 1,048,576 parameters (~1.05M). Total model: ~4.35M vs baseline 3.32M (+31%). Note: per CardinalGraphFormer (mem_130), the gate MUST be sigmoid for stability — linear gates diverged in 2/5 seeds. The sum must be UNNORMALIZED — degree-normalized CPA loses 1-WL expressivity (Corollary 1 in mem_130). The support set must be ALIGNED — both mean and sum operate on the same neighbor set.
architecture.readout: Mean pooling over all node embeddings → 256-dim graph representation.

X.training: AdamW (lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4), CosineAnnealingLR (T_max=300, eta_min=1e-6), batch_size=64, max 300 epochs, early stopping patience=50 on val RMSE. Gradient clipping at 1.0. 5 independent runs with different random seeds.
X.data: Tg dataset (7170 polymers, 3-RU multimer graphs), 72/8/20 split seed=71. Rich node features (8 descriptors) + PSPE (distance-to-chain-end, monomer-index) + static RWPE k=32.

ablations.name: A: Standard GAT baseline
ablations.desc: GAT + RWPE + PSPE, no CPA. Target: 35.19K (Day 5 best).

ablations.name: B: CPA-GAT (primary)
ablations.desc: Standard GAT + CPA channel in all layers, all heads.

ablations.name: C: CPA in last layer only
ablations.desc: CPA only in the final (4th) GAT layer. Tests whether cardinality matters most at readout.

ablations.name: D: Degree-baseline
ablations.desc: Instead of CPA, concatenate node degree (scalar, normalized) to input features. Tests explicit size injection vs. CPA's learned cardinality channel. Per mem_130, expected to recover 20-30% of CPA gain.

ablations.name: E: Linear-gate CPA
ablations.desc: Replace sigmoid with linear gate. Per mem_130, expected to be unstable.

ablations.name: F: Degree-normalized CPA
ablations.desc: Divide sum by |S(i)|. Per Corollary 1 in mem_130, expected to lose 1-WL expressivity.

ablations.name: G: Mismatched-support CPA
ablations.desc: Sum over ALL nodes (global sum) rather than attention neighbors. Tests whether global cardinality matters. Expected to be noisy (mem_130).

ablations.name: H: GAT+CPA without PSPE
ablations.desc: Tests interaction between CPA cardinality and PSPE position signals.

X.compute: ~2 GPU-hours per run (300 epochs × 7170 graphs × batch 64 × 4.35M params). 5 seeds + ablations ≈ 40 GPU-hours on 11GB VRAM.

positive_signals: H1-H2 confirmed: CPA-GAT (B) achieves 34.2-34.7K RMSE, representing 0.5-1.0K improvement over the 35.19K baseline. This would be significant given the exponential decay trajectory (+4.75K → +0.91K → +0.50K → now +0.5-1.0K from a ~1% parameter addition), suggesting CPA taps a genuinely new source of signal that exponential convergence had exhausted. Cardinality preservation would join PSPE as a confirmed beneficial architectural mechanism.

H3 supported: CPA-GAT without PSPE (H) degrades more than CPA-GAT with PSPE, suggesting complementary interaction between cardinality channels and positional channels. If CPA-GAT without PSPE still beats baseline (suggesting CPA captures chain-length signal that partially substitutes for PSPE's chain-end encoding), the cardinality signal is independently validated.

H4 supported: CPA significantly outperforms degree-baseline (D). If CPA > degree by ≥0.3K, the learned sum channel captures richer cardinality signals than simple degree counting — validating CardinalGraphFormer's theoretical framework for polymer graphs specifically.

Ablation C (CPA last-layer only): If last-layer CPA achieves most of the full CPA gain, cardinality matters primarily at readout aggregation (graph-level pooling), consistent with the intuition that chain-level statistics (total atom count, branching density) determine Tg rather than per-atom neighborhood size.

Ablation E/F/G confirming mem_130 predictions: Linear gate unstable, degree-normalized underperforms, mismatched-support degrades — validating the theoretical framework for polymer-specific CPA design. This would constitute independent replication of CardinalGraphFormer's architectural insights on a different domain (polymers vs. small molecules).
negative_signals: CPA-GAT (B) ≈ baseline (A) within ±0.2K: Cardinality signals are already fully captured by PSPE (chain position implicitly encodes chain length) and RWPE (random walk statistics encode neighbor multiplicity). CPA adds redundancy, not complementary signal. This would be a NULL result but would narrow the hypothesis space: cardinality preservation is not beneficial for topologically simple 1D chains where neighbor count is highly correlated with chain position.

CPA-GAT significantly WORSE than baseline (>0.3K degradation): The unnormalized sum channel introduces training instability or gradient conflict. The sigmoid gate may not adapt fast enough, causing the sum channel to inject noise early in training. This would suggest CPA requires careful warmup or curriculum scheduling that the simple supervised setting does not provide.

Degree-baseline (D) matches CPA: Simple degree injection captures all cardinality signal. This would refute CardinalGraphFormer's claim that CPA's learned sum channel is superior to explicit size features — at least for polymer graphs where degree and neighbor distribution are highly correlated.
CPA gain disappears in multi-seed average: If the improvement is within seed noise (std ≈ 0.3K), CPA's benefit is not robust. This would be assessed via paired bootstrap across the 5 seeds.
Y.gap_closure_estimate: Best case: 1.0K improvement → reduces SOTA gap from 4.64K to 3.64K (21% closure). Realistic: 0.5K → 4.14K gap (11% closure). This is partial but meaningful progress — and critically, CPA is orthogonal to other Day 6 ideas (bond graph, periodicity features) and could be combined multiplicatively.

content.risk_assessment: LOW. CPA adds ~1% parameters with no architectural complexity (no attention, no residuals, no LN). The mechanism is theoretically grounded (Theorem 1 in mem_130). The primary risk is redundancy with PSPE — but this is testable via ablation H. If null, the experiment is still informative because it demonstrates that for 1D chains, mean aggregation is already sufficient and cardinality signals are captured through correlated positional features. The experiment is computationally cheap (~2 GPU-hours per run), enabling rapid turnaround.
day5_justification: mem_130 (CardinalGraphFormer): Provides the CPA mechanism, theoretical framework (Proposition 1: softmax cardinality-blindness, Theorem 1: CPA restores 1-WL expressivity, Corollary 1: degree-normalized CPA fails), sigmoid gate design, and ablation template. CPA is the single most actionable architectural mechanism from Day 5 readings — it requires NO pretraining, NO global attention, and ~1% parameter overhead.

mem_138 (Post-PI1M Architecture): Explicitly identifies CPA-augmented GAT as the 'lowest-risk, highest-ROI supervised architectural experiment remaining.' The consensus states: 'CPA added to GAT could capture cardinality signals without the noise of global attention.'

mem_131 (GNN-SSM): The Jacobian spectrum of 4-layer GAT on 1D chains is naturally well-conditioned. CPA does not perturb this spectrum because it modifies the aggregation function (which is inside the nonlinearity), not the layer-to-layer transition matrix. CPA preserves the GAT Jacobian structure while adding expressivity to the message aggregation. This is consistent with GNN-SSM's prescription: control the Jacobian spectrum AND enrich message-passing expressivity.

mem_132 (GPS-Lite): Global attention degrades by +8K. CPA avoids this failure mode because it operates locally within the existing GAT message-passing framework — no global operations, no new attention mechanisms, no O(N²) complexity. CPA is an aggregation-level modification, not a connectivity modification.

mem_137 (Identity-Property Antagonism): CPA is supervised, not contrastive. It does not compare polymers against each other, so it cannot trigger the Identity-Property Antagonism. CPA preserves the property manifold by operating within each polymer's local message-passing — it enriches representations rather than discriminating between samples.

memory.abstract: PolyBG-Supervised: Parallel Bond-Graph GAT without cross-attention or pretraining — representing backbone bonds as independent nodes with bond-type and flexibility features, processing through a parallel GAT, and concatenating atom+bond readouts for supervised Tg prediction.
memory.keyword: bond-graph parallel-GAT backbone-flexibility bond-as-node supervised no-cross-attention BPSPE MolCHG-adaptation

H: H1 — Bond-Flexibility Complementarity: Backbone bond types (C-C single, C=C double, C-O ether, C-N amide, aromatic C:C) directly encode chain flexibility — the primary determinant of Tg through segmental motion and free volume. Atom-centric GAT encodes bond information only as scalar edge attributes (bond type, conjugation flag), collapsing rich bond semantics into a single attention-modulating scalar. Elevating bonds to independent node representations in a parallel bond graph (line graph of the atom graph) allows the bond encoder to learn bond-type-specific flexibility representations through its own message-passing. These bond representations complement atom representations: atoms encode local chemistry (electronegativity, hybridization, steric bulk); bonds encode chain connectivity semantics (rotational freedom, conjugation length, backbone rigidity).

H2 — Topology Is Not the Differentiator (and that's OK): For 1D polymer chains, the bond graph is topologically identical to the atom graph (both are linear chains — the line graph of a path is also a path). MolCHG's bond graph benefits arise from molecular graph complexity (rings, branches, diverse bond environments). For polymers, the bond graph must provide value through DIFFERENT FEATURES rather than different topology. Specifically: bond-type sequences compactly encode monomer-identity signatures (polystyrene: alternating C-C(aromatic) and C-C(aliphatic); polyether: alternating C-C and C-O; polyamide: alternating C-C and C-N(amide)). These signatures are more compactly represented as bond-node sequences (2-4 nodes per monomer) than as atom-node sequences with edge attributes (6-15 nodes per monomer). If this hypothesis is correct, the gain comes from feature compression and explicit bond-type semantics, not topological enrichment.

H3 — No Cross-Attention (Simplicity Constraint): GPS-Lite (mem_132) demonstrated that adding even a single global attention layer atop GAT degrades performance by +8K. Cross-attention between atom and bond graphs — while not global in the GPS-Lite sense — adds a second inter-bipartite attention mechanism that may similarly perturb the well-conditioned GAT Jacobian spectrum (mem_131). The safest first test of bond-graph value is parallel independent encoders with concatenation at readout: no cross-attention, no message exchange between graphs during encoding. If parallel encoders provide value, cross-attention can be added as a subsequent increment. If parallel encoders are null, cross-attention is unlikely to rescue them.

H4 — BPSPE Incremental Value: Bond-level positional encodings — bond-distance-along-backbone (normalized) and monomer-index — complement atom-level PSPE. A rotatable C-C bond near the chain end has different flexibility implications than the same bond in the chain interior due to end-group free volume effects. BPSPE encodes this location explicitly. However, per the PSPE incremental pattern (mem_107: +0.50K over RWPE), BPSPE gain is expected to be modest (0.2-0.5K) — useful but not transformative.

H5 — The Bond Graph vs. Edge Features Question: If parallel bond-GAT provides value over atom-GAT alone, is it because (a) bonds-as-nodes enable richer bond representations through message-passing, or (b) the atom-GAT's edge features are simply insufficient? To distinguish: an ablation where atom-GAT receives ENRICHED edge features (bond type one-hot × 4 + conjugation + ring + rotatable + bond order) tests whether the same information, provided as edge attributes rather than node representations, suffices. If enriched-edge GAT matches bond-graph GAT, the bond-graph architecture is unnecessary — better edge features would suffice.

X.name: PolyBG-Supervised: Parallel Bond-Graph GAT without Cross-Attention

architecture.atom_encoder: Standard Day 5 best GAT: 4 layers, 256 hidden dim, 4 attention heads, NO residuals, NO LayerNorm, NO global attention, ELU activation, mean readout. Input: 42-dim node features (8 rich atom features + 2 PSPE + 32 RWPE k=32). Reproduces 35.19K baseline (mem_132).
architecture.bond_graph_construction: Line graph of atom graph. Algorithm: (1) Identify all chemical bonds in the atom graph. (2) Create bond-graph node for each bond. (3) Connect two bond nodes with an edge if their corresponding bonds share a common atom (standard line graph construction). For a linear polymer backbone, the bond graph is also a linear chain of length (N_atoms - 1). Side-chain bonds form short branches off the backbone bond sequence.
architecture.bond_encoder: GAT: 3 layers, 128 hidden dim, 4 attention heads, NO residuals, NO LayerNorm, ELU activation, mean readout. Fewer layers than atom encoder because bond graphs are smaller (N_bonds ≈ N_atoms) and bond-type semantics are more local. 128 hidden dim (not 256) to control parameter budget and prevent overfitting. Input: 14-dim bond node features.
architecture.bond_node_features: 14 dimensions: (1-4) bond_type one-hot [single, double, triple, aromatic]; (5) conjugation_flag (0/1); (6) in_ring_flag (0/1); (7) rotatable_flag (0/1, single bond between heavy atoms not in ring); (8) bond_stereo (0/1); (9) bond_order_float (1.0/1.5/2.0, normalized); (10) is_backbone_bond (0/1, bond is on the longest simple path); (11) avg_endpoint_electronegativity (mean Pauling EN of two endpoint atoms, normalized); (12) bond_distance_along_backbone (normalized [0,1], 0 if not backbone); (13) monomer_index (0/0.5/1 for 3-RU, 0 if not backbone); (14) bond_length_estimate (typical bond length in Å, normalized: C-C=1.54, C=C=1.34, C-O=1.43, C-N=1.47, aromatic C:C=1.40). Features (12-13) constitute BPSPE.
architecture.readout_and_predictor: atom_readout: mean_pool over all atom embeddings → 256-dim. bond_readout: mean_pool over all bond embeddings → 128-dim. Concatenate → 384-dim joint embedding. Predictor: 2-layer MLP (384→192→1) with ReLU, Dropout=0.1.

X.training: AdamW (lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4), CosineAnnealingLR (T_max=300, eta_min=1e-6), batch_size=64, max 300 epochs, early stopping patience=50. 5 independent seeds.
X.data: Tg dataset (7170 polymers, 3-RU multimer graphs), 72/8/20 split seed=71.

ablations.name: A: Atom-only GAT baseline
ablations.desc: Standard GAT + RWPE + PSPE. Target: 35.19K.

ablations.name: B: PolyBG-Supervised (primary)
ablations.desc: Parallel atom-GAT + bond-GAT, concat readout, no cross-attn.

ablations.name: C: Bond-only GAT
ablations.desc: Bond graph only (3-layer, 128-dim). Tests standalone value of bond representations.

ablations.name: D: Enriched-edge GAT
ablations.desc: Atom-GAT with enriched edge features: bond type one-hot (4) + conjugation + ring + rotatable + bond_order_float concatenated to edge_attr. Tests whether bond information is better as enriched edge attributes rather than independent nodes.

ablations.name: E: No BPSPE
ablations.desc: PolyBG without bond features (12-13). Tests incremental value of bond-level positional encoding.

ablations.name: F: Atom-GAT 256 + Bond-GAT 256
ablations.desc: Equal-capacity encoders. Tests whether the 128-dim bond encoder is unnecessarily constrained.

ablations.name: G: Bond-GAT 4 layers
ablations.desc: Equal-depth encoders. Tests whether 3-layer bond encoder is sufficient.

ablations.name: H: Atom-GAT + Bond-GAT + SimpleCrossAttn
ablations.desc: Add ONE cross-attention layer AFTER the final GNN layers (not interleaved). Atom embeddings attend to bond embeddings and vice versa via single-head scaled dot-product attention. Compromise between full cross-attention (risky per GPS-Lite) and no cross-attention.

X.parameter_count: Atom-GAT: ~3.32M. Bond-GAT (3-layer, 128-dim, 4 heads): ~0.68M. Predictor (384→192→1): ~75K. Total: ~4.07M (+23% vs baseline).

positive_signals: H1-H2 confirmed (B > A by ≥0.5K): PolyBG-Supervised achieves 34.2-34.7K. Bond-flexibility semantics are genuinely complementary to atom-level features even for topologically simple polymers. This would be the first successful architectural innovation since PSPE (Day 3) and would validate bond-graph representations as a general design pattern for polymer GNNs — opening the door to more sophisticated bond-graph architectures (cross-attention, hierarchical, pretraining on alternative data).

H3 supported (B > H or H ≈ B): If parallel encoders (B) match or outperform cross-attention (H), the Simplicity Principle holds for bond graphs — complex inter-graph attention is unnecessary. If H > B by ≥0.3K, cross-attention adds value despite GPS-Lite concerns and should be pursued.

H5 critical test (D vs. B): If enriched-edge GAT (D) matches bond-graph GAT (B), bond-as-node is unnecessary — the same information works equally well as edge attributes. This would be a PRACTICAL finding (simpler is better) but would weaken the bond-graph hypothesis. If B > D by ≥0.3K, bonds-as-nodes provide unique representational capacity beyond enriched edge features — supporting MolCHG's (mem_115) architectural thesis for polymers.

C (bond-only) provides 32-35K: Bond information alone captures substantial Tg signal — confirming that backbone bond types are primary Tg determinants. If C underperforms A significantly (35K+), bond information is supplementary rather than primary.

E (no BPSPE): Expected 0.2-0.5K degradation vs. B, similar to PSPE's incremental pattern (mem_107). If BPSPE provides no benefit, bond position is irrelevant beyond bond type — plausible for homopolymers where all backbone bonds of a given type are equivalent.
negative_signals: B ≈ A (within ±0.3K): Bond graph adds no value for polymer Tg. Possible explanations: (a) atom-GAT edge attributes already capture all bond-type information needed for Tg — bonds-as-nodes are redundant; (b) the bond graph of a linear polymer chain is topologically identical to the atom graph (both are paths), so no new structural information is added — the only difference is feature compression, which doesn't help; (c) the 7170-sample supervised setting is too data-limited to support dual encoders — the bond encoder overfits. In this case, enriched-edge GAT (D) becomes the preferred approach.

B significantly WORSE than A (>0.5K degradation): Dual encoders double the effective model complexity and may cause severe overfitting on 7K samples. The bond encoder may learn spurious bond-type patterns from the training set that don't generalize to test polymers — a classic low-data regime failure. This would suggest that bond-graph architectures require pretraining (on PI1M or alternative data) to provide value, consistent with mem_128's finding that architectural complexity needs data scale.

D ≈ A: Even enriched edge features don't help — suggesting that current single edge-attribute encoding (bond type + conjugation) is already sufficient for Tg-relevant bond information. This would be a valuable negative result: it confirms that the GAT architecture already extracts all available bond-level signal.

Cross-attention (H) degrades: If H < B (cross-attention hurts), GPS-Lite's lesson extends to inter-graph attention — adding attention between ANY graph structures is harmful for small-data polymer regression. This would further strengthen the Simplicity Principle.
Y.gap_closure_estimate: Best case: 1.5K improvement → 3.14K gap (32% closure). Realistic: 0.5-1.0K → 3.64-4.14K gap (11-22% closure). Combined with CPA-GAT (Idea 1, estimated 0.5-1.0K), the joint improvement could reach 1.0-2.5K if the mechanisms are orthogonal (CPA captures multiplicity, bond graph captures flexibility — different signal sources).

content.risk_assessment: MODERATE. The primary risk is that bond graphs are redundant for topologically simple 1D polymer chains where bond-type information is already well-captured by atom-GAT edge attributes. MolCHG's bond graph success (mem_115) is on diverse molecular graphs with rings, branches, and complex bond environments — the value may not transfer to polymers. However, the supervised-only design (no PI1M SSL), simplicity constraints (no cross-attention, no residuals/LN), and clean ablation matrix make this a well-controlled experiment. The enriched-edge ablation (D) provides a critical diagnostic: even if bond-as-node fails, it identifies the correct path forward (better edge features).
day5_justification: mem_115 (MolCHG): Provides the bond-graph-as-parallel-layer concept, multi-level hierarchy design, and ablation evidence that bond graphs independently contribute to molecular representations (BACE: 71.61 atom-only → 74.34 hierarchical → 76.33 full CHG with bond graph). MolCHG's fragment-level aggregation over both atom and bond nodes validates that bond-level semantics are non-redundant with atom-level semantics. However, MolCHG's success is on small-molecule benchmarks with diverse topologies — polymer transfer is an open question.

mem_125 (PolyBG-SSL): Provides the bond-graph adaptation for polymers including bond feature design (12-dim), BPSPE (bond-distance-along-backbone, monomer-index), and cross-attention architecture. Our Idea 2 strips PolyBG-SSL of pretraining (PI1M dead end) and cross-attention (GPS-Lite risk), keeping only the core bond-graph supervised architecture with simplified bond features (14-dim, enriched).

mem_138 (Post-PI1M Architecture): Identifies bond-graph architectures as one of three 'actionable directions' for post-PI1M research: 'Bond-graph architectures (PolyBG, mem_125) — representing backbone bonds as independent nodes with bond-type features to explicitly model chain flexibility. This provides a complementary view of the polymer graph without additional data.'

mem_131 (GNN-SSM): The Jacobian spectrum insight justifies keeping atom-GAT and bond-GAT SEPARATE (no cross-attention). Separate GATs each have their own well-conditioned Jacobian spectra tuned to their respective graph topologies (atom graph and its line graph). Cross-attention would couple these spectra, potentially creating the same gradient-conflict problems that made GPS-Lite fail.

mem_132 (GPS-Lite): The +8K degradation from global attention motivates the NO-CROSS-ATTENTION constraint in H3. Ablation H (post-hoc cross-attention) provides a bounded test: if even one layer of cross-attention degrades performance, all inter-graph attention is contraindicated for small-data polymer regression.

mem_137 (Identity-Property Antagonism): Bond-graph architecture is purely supervised — no inter-polymer discrimination, no contrastive objectives, no PI1M. It cannot trigger the Identity-Property Antagonism because it operates entirely within each polymer's internal representation.

memory.abstract: PSE: Periodicity-Structural Encoding — explicit node-level features encoding repeat-unit periodicity (modular position, repeat-unit index, periodic-distance to equivalent atoms, backbone/sidechain flag) as a supervised feature-engineering increment to capture PerioGT's periodicity signal without pretraining.
memory.keyword: periodicity-structural-encoding modular-position repeat-unit PSE feature-engineering PerioGT-inspired supervised no-pretraining

H: H1 — Periodicity as the Missing Signal: PerioGT achieves SOTA 30.8K RMSE through periodicity-aware pretraining — contrasting periodic vs. non-periodic polymer graphs to teach the encoder that polymer properties emerge from repeating backbone structure. The 4.64K gap between our non-pretraining asymptote (~35K) and PerioGT may be partially attributable to the periodicity signal that our current encodings (RWPE, PSPE) do not explicitly capture. PSPE encodes chain position (distance-to-end, monomer-index) but does NOT encode where an atom sits within its repeat unit — the modular periodicity that distinguishes 'first carbon of monomer A' from 'third carbon of monomer A'. Periodicity-Structural Encoding (PSE) captures this modular structure through explicit node-level features, providing a supervised path to partial PerioGT parity without pretraining.

H2 — Modular Position as the Key Innovation: The most novel PSE feature is modular_position = (atom_index_within_monomer) / (monomer_size). For a 3-RU polymer, atoms in the first position of each repeat unit all get modular_position ≈ 0, atoms in the middle get ≈ 0.5, atoms at the end get ≈ 1. This encodes the PERIODIC equivalence of atoms across repeat units — the first carbon of RU-1 is structurally equivalent to the first carbon of RU-2 and RU-3. No existing encoding captures this: RWPE sees different random-walk distances for equivalent atoms in different RUs; PSPE sees different chain positions; only PSE captures their equivalence. This modular periodicity is precisely what PerioGT's pretraining learns to recognize.

H3 — Periodic-Distance: Beyond modular position, atoms in adjacent repeat units that are structurally equivalent (e.g., the first backbone carbon in RU-1 and RU-2) are connected by a specific graph distance (the monomer backbone length). This periodic-distance is a strong signal of chain periodicity — it should be consistent across the polymer. Encoding periodic_distance = graph_distance_to_nearest_equivalent_atom_in_adjacent_RU provides an explicit 'wavelength' of the polymer's repeating structure. Polymers with shorter backbone periods (e.g., polyethylene: 2 backbone atoms/period) vs. longer periods (e.g., polycarbonate: ~6 backbone atoms/period) have fundamentally different flexibility characteristics that affect Tg.

H4 — PSE as a Superset of PSPE: PSE does not replace PSPE; it complements it. PSPE tells the model WHERE an atom is in the chain (absolute position); PSE tells the model WHAT an atom is in the repeat unit (structural role). Together they provide a complete coordinate system: (monomer_index, modular_position) uniquely identifies every atom in the polymer backbone. Sidechain atoms are identified by the is_backbone flag and inherit modular_position from their anchor backbone atom. This complete coordinate system should improve the model's ability to learn structure-property relationships that depend on repeat-unit architecture.

H5 — PSE vs. PerioGT's Pretraining: PSE captures periodicity through EXPLICIT ENCODING; PerioGT captures it through CONTRASTIVE PRETRAINING. PSE's advantages: no pretraining needed, no Identity-Property Antagonism risk, zero additional parameters beyond input feature dimension, immediately testable. PerioGT's advantages: contrastive pretraining may capture emergent periodicity signals (e.g., how period length correlates with Tg across different polymer families) that explicit encoding cannot provide. PSE likely captures 30-50% of PerioGT's periodicity benefit — enough to close 1-2K of the 4.64K gap.

X.name: PSE: Periodicity-Structural Encoding for Supervised Polymer Tg

features.existing: 42-dim: 8 rich atom features + 2 PSPE (distance-to-chain-end, monomer-index) + 32 RWPE k=32.
features.pse_new: 4 new node features, bringing total to 46-dim:

pse_feature_details.modular_position: Computation: (1) Identify backbone atoms via longest simple path (double-BFS, same as PSPE backbone identification). (2) Determine monomer boundaries: in a 3-RU polymer, the backbone is divided into 3 equal segments. Within each segment, atom position is indexed from 0 to (segment_length - 1). modular_position = position_in_segment / max(segment_length - 1, 1), normalized to [0,1]. For non-backbone atoms: modular_position = 0. For atoms in branching side-chains: inherit modular_position from their anchor backbone atom. This captures the structural role within the repeat unit.
pse_feature_details.repeat_unit_index: Computation: For backbone atoms, ru_index = floor(position_along_backbone / (backbone_length / 3)), giving values {0, 1, 2} for 3-RU. Normalized: ru_index / 2 → {0, 0.5, 1}. For non-backbone atoms: inherit from anchor backbone atom. This is technically redundant with PSPE's monomer_index (which also encodes {0, 0.5, 1}) but is computed differently (from backbone segmentation rather than monomer position). The correlation between them (~0.85-0.95) means ru_index may add limited independent signal — included for completeness.
pse_feature_details.periodic_distance: Computation: For each backbone atom: identify its structural role within the monomer (its modular_position value). Find the nearest atom in an adjacent repeat unit with the SAME modular_position (within tolerance 0.05). Compute graph (shortest-path) distance to that atom. Normalize by max_periodic_distance in the polymer. For non-backbone atoms: periodic_distance = 0. For atoms at the first/last RU (no adjacent RU on one side): use distance to the nearest equivalent atom in the only available adjacent RU. This encodes the 'wavelength' of the repeating structure.
pse_feature_details.is_backbone: Computation: Binary (0/1). 1 if atom is on the longest simple path of the heavy-atom graph. This distinguishes backbone atoms (which participate in chain flexibility) from sidechain atoms (which contribute steric bulk but not backbone continuity). Zero-cost feature with potentially high discriminative value: backbone carbons in polystyrene behave differently from pendant phenyl carbons for Tg.

X.architecture: Standard Day 5 best GAT: 4 layers, 256 hidden dim, 4 attention heads, NO residuals, NO LayerNorm, mean readout. Input: 46-dim (42 existing + 4 PSE). Predictor: 2-layer MLP (256→128→1) with ReLU, Dropout=0.1. NO architectural changes — pure feature engineering increment.
X.training: AdamW (lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4), CosineAnnealingLR (T_max=300, eta_min=1e-6), batch_size=64, max 300 epochs, early stopping patience=50. 5 seeds.

ablations.name: A: Baseline (no PSE)
ablations.desc: Standard 42-dim GAT+RWPE+PSPE. Target: 35.19K.

ablations.name: B: Full PSE (primary)
ablations.desc: 42 + 4 PSE features = 46-dim.

ablations.name: C: modular_position only
ablations.desc: Baseline + modular_position (1 feature). Tests H2.

ablations.name: D: periodic_distance only
ablations.desc: Baseline + periodic_distance (1 feature). Tests H3.

ablations.name: E: is_backbone only
ablations.desc: Baseline + is_backbone (1 feature). Tests backbone/sidechain distinction value.

ablations.name: F: ru_index only
ablations.desc: Baseline + ru_index (1 feature). Tests whether redundant with PSPE monomer_index.

ablations.name: G: PSE without PSPE
ablations.desc: Remove PSPE (distance-to-chain-end, monomer-index), keep PSE. Tests whether PSE can substitute for PSPE or whether the two are complementary.

ablations.name: H: PSE with reduced RWPE
ablations.desc: Reduce RWPE from k=32 to k=16 (recovering 16 feature dimensions). Tests whether PSE enables lower RWPE dimensionality — if PSE captures what higher-k RWPE was providing, the feature budget can be reallocated.

X.compute: ~2 GPU-hours per run. 5 seeds × 8 ablations ≈ 80 GPU-hours on 11GB VRAM. Pure feature engineering — no architectural overhead, minimal compute.

positive_signals: H1-H2 confirmed (B > A by ≥0.5K): PSE improves RMSE to 34.2-34.7K. Periodicity is a genuine and previously uncaptured signal in polymer Tg prediction. This would validate the hypothesis that PerioGT's SOTA advantage is partially attributable to periodicity awareness and that explicit encoding can partially substitute for pretraining.

C (modular_position) provides most of the gain: If modular_position alone achieves 0.3-0.7K improvement, H2 is strongly supported — modular equivalence is the key periodicity signal. This single feature would be the most impactful feature-engineering addition since PSPE.

D (periodic_distance) provides independent gain: If periodic_distance adds value beyond modular_position (testable via C+D vs C), the repeating wavelength signal is independently useful — consistent with polymer physics where persistence length (related to backbone period) determines chain stiffness.

G (PSE without PSPE): If PSE w/o PSPE matches or exceeds baseline w/ PSPE, PSE captures chain-geometry information more efficiently than PSPE. This would suggest that modular structure is more fundamental than absolute chain position — a physically meaningful finding.

H (PSE with reduced RWPE): If PSE+k=16 RWPE matches k=32 RWPE, PSE reduces dependence on high-dimensional spectral encodings — suggesting that explicit structural features can replace implicit spectral features, aligning with the Simplicity Principle.

Interaction with CPA (Idea 1) and PolyBG (Idea 2): PSE is purely feature-based and orthogonal to both architectural modifications. Combined PSE+CPA and PSE+PolyBG are viable multiplicative experiments. If all three work independently, the joint improvement could reach 1.0-3.0K.
negative_signals: B ≈ A (within ±0.2K): PSE adds no value. Possible explanations: (a) PSPE (distance-to-chain-end + monomer-index) already captures all chain-geometry information, including implicit periodicity — modular_position is redundant with the combination of monomer_index and distance-to-chain-end; (b) for 3-RU polymers with only 3 repeat units, the periodicity signal may be too weak — 3 repeats barely constitute a 'periodic' structure; (c) RWPE k=32, being spectral encodings of the full graph, already captures periodicity patterns through random walk statistics.

E (is_backbone) provides zero gain: Backbone/sidechain distinction is already learnable from the combination of PSPE (backbone atoms have non-zero distance-to-chain-end) and atom features (sidechain atoms have different connectivity patterns). Explicit encoding is redundant.
F (ru_index) ≈ PSPE monomer_index: The two features are indeed redundant (correlation >0.9), confirming that ru_index adds no independent signal. This is expected but worth verifying.

PSE degrades performance: If the 4 extra features cause overfitting in the 7K-sample regime (unlikely at 46-dim vs. 42-dim, but possible if PSE features are noisy or inconsistently computed), GAT may over-rely on periodicity features that don't generalize to test polymers with different backbone architectures.
Y.gap_closure_estimate: Best case: 1.0K → 3.64K gap (22% closure). Realistic: 0.3-0.7K → 3.94-4.34K gap (6-15% closure). PSE is incremental by design — it's feature engineering, not a new architecture. But its value lies in being orthogonal to CPA and bond-graph ideas, enabling multiplicative combination.

content.risk_assessment: VERY LOW. PSE is pure feature engineering: 4 new node features, zero architectural changes, zero new parameters beyond the input embedding lookup (46 × 256 = +1K parameters). The features are computed via deterministic graph algorithms (double-BFS for backbone, shortest-path for periodic distance). The primary risk is redundancy with PSPE — but this is testable via ablation G. Even if null, PSE costs minimal compute and narrows the hypothesis space by confirming that explicit periodicity encoding does not add value beyond existing chain-geometry features. The worst-case scenario (PSE degrades) is unlikely at 46-dim input — the Day 1 finding that feature richness helps (~28K gap between basic and rich features) suggests additional informative features should help, not hurt.
day5_justification: mem_135 (PI1M SSL Dead End): Identifies PerioGT's periodicity-aware pretraining as the specific missing ingredient: 'PerioGT (30.8K SOTA) explicitly contrasts periodic vs non-periodic polymer graphs during pretraining. This captures the repeating-structure signal that monomer-vs-multimer contrast (MoMuCon) failed to capture.' PSE directly targets this signal through explicit encoding rather than contrastive pretraining — bypassing the PI1M dead end and the Identity-Property Antagonism.

mem_052 (PerioGT — Periodic Polymer Graphs): The foundational paper demonstrating that periodic graph representations improve Tg prediction from 39.83K to 37.35K. The periodic edge connecting terminal atoms of the repeat unit is an architectural periodicity encoding; PSE is a feature-level periodicity encoding. Both capture the same underlying physics — that polymer structure is fundamentally periodic — through different mechanisms. PSE is simpler and more directly interpretable.

mem_107 (PSPE — Polymer-Specific Positional Encodings): Established the pattern for polymer-specific feature engineering: explicit chain-geometry features (distance-to-chain-end, monomer-index) provide +0.50K incremental improvement over RWPE. PSE follows the same pattern: explicit periodicity features providing incremental improvement over PSPE+RWPE. If PSPE's +0.50K pattern extrapolates, PSE should provide +0.2-0.5K.

mem_131 (GNN-SSM): The Jacobian spectrum is unaffected by PSE because PSE only modifies input features — the GAT architecture, message-passing depth, and layer connectivity are unchanged. The well-conditioned Jacobian spectrum is preserved. This is the ideal kind of improvement under GNN-SSM: enrich the input signal without perturbing the architectural dynamics.

mem_132 (GPS-Lite): The +8K degradation from global attention reinforces that feature-based improvements (PSPE, now PSE) are safer than architectural modifications for small-data polymer regression. PSE continues the successful PSPE pattern rather than the failed GPS-Lite pattern.

mem_084 (ELENE Integration): The finding that structural encodings for polymers should target 'chain-level periodicity and long-range connectivity, not just local ego-network degree triplets' directly motivates PSE: modular_position and periodic_distance target exactly the chain-level periodicity that ELENE (k=1) failed to capture.

memory.abstract: GMT: Graph-level Multi-Task Training with physically-motivated auxiliary prediction heads (rotatable bond density, aromatic fraction, H-bond density, backbone ratio, branching index) to inject property-relevant domain knowledge during supervised Tg training, avoiding Identity-Property Antagonism.
memory.keyword: multi-task-training property-aligned auxiliary-prediction graph-level-targets domain-knowledge Identity-Property-Antagonism-avoidance curriculum-decay supervised

H: H1 — Property-Aligned Auxiliary Training Avoids Antagonism: The Identity-Property Antagonism (mem_137) demonstrates that contrastive SSL objectives teaching inter-polymer discrimination destroy the property manifold needed for Tg regression. The causal mechanism: NT-Xent pushes 'polymer A ≠ polymer B,' but Tg regression needs 'polymer A and polymer B share property-relevant features because both contain aryl backbones.' GMT avoids this by using AUXILIARY TASKS THAT ARE CAUSALLY UPSTREAM OF Tg: predicting rotatable bond density (flexibility → lower Tg), aromatic fraction (rigidity → higher Tg), H-bond density (inter-chain interactions → higher Tg), backbone ratio (chain linearity), and branching index (free volume → lower Tg). These auxiliary targets teach the encoder to attend to Tg-relevant features — they are property-aligned, not identity-aligned.

H2 — Joint Training vs. Pretraining: GMT uses JOINT multi-task training (shared encoder + separate prediction heads, trained simultaneously on Tg + auxiliaries) rather than pretrain-then-finetune. Joint training has two advantages: (a) the encoder learns Tg-relevant features from epoch 1, rather than first learning PI1M features then adapting them; (b) the auxiliary tasks serve as regularizers — they constrain the encoder representation to preserve property-relevant structure, preventing overfitting to Tg-specific patterns in the small training set. This is conceptually similar to multi-task learning in polyGNN (mem_071) where co-predicting 30+ polymer properties improved generalization for low-data tasks.

H3 — Non-Trivial Auxiliary Targets: Unlike simple node-level statistics (atom count, degree), the GMT auxiliary targets require GRAPH-LEVEL AGGREGATION and BACKBONE IDENTIFICATION — they cannot be computed from local atom features alone. Rotatable bond density requires identifying backbone bonds and counting rotatable ones; aromatic fraction requires counting aromatic atoms across the full graph; branching index requires computing the ratio of branch points to total backbone atoms. These tasks force the encoder to learn global graph structure, providing a graph-level signal that complements the Tg regression head. This addresses the Pretraining-Task Alignment Principle v3 (mem_135) without requiring PI1M SSL.

H4 — Curriculum Weighting: Auxiliary tasks are most useful early in training when they guide the encoder toward Tg-relevant features. Once the encoder has converged to a good representation, auxiliary losses provide diminishing returns and may compete with Tg optimization. A curriculum schedule where auxiliary loss weight λ decays from λ_max to 0 over training allows auxiliary tasks to shape the representation early while letting Tg optimization dominate late training. This prevents auxiliary tasks from becoming a distraction in the fine-tuning phase.

H5 — Relationship to Virtual Knowledge Nodes: KPGT (mem_104) injects domain knowledge through a virtual node with molecular descriptors. GMT injects domain knowledge through auxiliary prediction heads with graph-level targets. The two are complementary: a virtual node provides EXPLICIT descriptor values to the encoder; auxiliary heads force the encoder to IMPLICITLY discover descriptor-relevant features. GMT is architecturally simpler (no virtual node, no cross-attention), aligning with the Simplicity Principle.

X.name: GMT: Graph-level Multi-Task Training for Supervised Polymer Tg

architecture.encoder: Standard Day 5 best GAT: 4 layers, 256 hidden dim, 4 attention heads, NO residuals, NO LayerNorm, mean readout (256-dim graph embedding). Input: 42-dim (8 rich + 2 PSPE + 32 RWPE).
architecture.tg_head: 2-layer MLP (256→128→1) with ReLU, Dropout=0.1. Output: Tg prediction (scalar). Loss: MSE.
architecture.auxiliary_heads: Five separate 2-layer MLPs, each (256→64→1) with ReLU, Dropout=0.1, outputting scalar predictions:

auxiliary_tasks.name: Rotatable bond density
auxiliary_tasks.target: rotatable_bonds / total_bonds. Rotatable bond = single bond between heavy atoms, not in ring. Motivation: directly encodes chain flexibility. Higher → lower Tg.

auxiliary_tasks.name: Aromatic atom fraction
auxiliary_tasks.target: aromatic_atoms / heavy_atoms. Motivation: aromatic groups increase backbone rigidity and π-π stacking. Higher → higher Tg.

auxiliary_tasks.name: H-bond density
auxiliary_tasks.target: (HBD_count + HBA_count) / heavy_atoms. HBD = O-H, N-H bonds. HBA = O, N atoms. Motivation: H-bonds increase inter-chain cohesion. Higher → higher Tg.

auxiliary_tasks.name: Backbone fraction
auxiliary_tasks.target: backbone_atoms / total_atoms. Backbone = atoms on longest simple path. Motivation: higher backbone fraction = more linear chain, less side-chain plasticization. Higher → higher Tg.

auxiliary_tasks.name: Branching index
auxiliary_tasks.target: n_branch_points / backbone_atoms. Branch point = backbone atom with degree ≥ 3 in the heavy-atom graph. Motivation: branching increases free volume. Higher → lower Tg.

X.total_loss: L_total = L_Tg + λ(t) · (L_rot + L_arom + L_hbond + L_bb + L_branch) / 5, where λ(t) = λ_max · (1 - t/T_max) decays linearly from λ_max to 0 over training. λ_max = 0.3 (auxiliary weight at epoch 0). At epoch T_max, λ = 0, and only Tg loss remains. This curriculum ensures early guidance without late distraction.
X.training: AdamW (lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4), CosineAnnealingLR (T_max=300, eta_min=1e-6), batch_size=64, max 300 epochs, early stopping patience=50 on val RMSE. 5 seeds. λ_max=0.3, T_max=200 (auxiliaries phased out by epoch 200).
X.data: Tg dataset (7170 polymers, 3-RU), 72/8/20 split seed=71. Auxiliary targets precomputed offline from graph structure.

ablations.name: A: Baseline (Tg only)
ablations.desc: Standard 42-dim GAT+RWPE+PSPE, no auxiliaries. Target: 35.19K.

ablations.name: B: Full GMT (primary)
ablations.desc: Tg + all 5 auxiliaries with λ(t) curriculum decay.

ablations.name: C: Constant λ
ablations.desc: Fixed λ=0.1 throughout training. Tests whether curriculum decay is necessary.

ablations.name: D: No curriculum (λ=0.1 flat)
ablations.desc: Same as C but with explicit comparison to B.

ablations.name: E: Individual auxiliaries
ablations.desc: Tg + each auxiliary alone. Tests which auxiliaries provide the most signal.

ablations.name: F: Node-level auxiliaries (control)
ablations.desc: Replace graph-level auxiliaries with node-level statistics: total_atoms, total_bonds, mean_degree. Tests whether any auxiliary signal helps or specifically graph-level, property-aligned signals.

ablations.name: G: High λ (λ_max=1.0)
ablations.desc: Tests whether stronger auxiliary signal helps or dominates.

ablations.name: H: Auxiliaries-only pretraining
ablations.desc: Pretrain encoder on auxiliaries only (no Tg, λ=1.0, 200 epochs on Tg training set), then finetune on Tg. Tests whether auxiliary pretraining > joint training. This is a supervised pretraining variant.

X.compute: ~2.5 GPU-hours per run (5 extra forward+backward passes through small MLP heads). 5 seeds × 10 ablations ≈ 125 GPU-hours on 11GB VRAM.

positive_signals: H1-H2 confirmed (B > A by ≥0.5K): GMT improves RMSE to 34.2-34.7K. Property-aligned multi-task training provides a viable supervised alternative to PI1M SSL — injecting domain knowledge without triggering Identity-Property Antagonism. This would be a significant methodological finding: the PI1M dead end doesn't mean pretraining is dead; it means the pretraining must be property-aligned.

H3 supported (graph-level auxiliaries > node-level auxiliaries): If B > F by ≥0.3K, graph-level aggregation tasks provide genuinely useful signal beyond trivial node-level statistics. This validates the task design.

E (individual auxiliaries): Expect aromatic fraction and rotatable bond density to provide the most individual benefit (they correlate most strongly with Tg). If all individual auxiliaries provide similar benefit, the tasks are interchangeable — any property-aligned signal helps. If none provide individual benefit but the combination does, synergism exists.

H4 (curriculum vs. constant): If B > C/D by ≥0.2K, curriculum decay is beneficial — auxiliaries should guide early but not distract late. If C ≈ B, constant weight works equally well, simplifying the training protocol.

H (auxiliaries-only pretraining > joint training): If H > B by ≥0.3K, pretraining on property-aligned auxiliaries (even on the SAME dataset) is better than joint training — supporting the pretrain-then-finetune paradigm but with property-aligned rather than identity-aligned objectives. This would be a template for supervised multi-task pretraining on external polymer property datasets if they become available.

Interaction with CPA, PolyBG, PSE: GMT is a training-strategy modification, not an architecture modification. It is fully orthogonal to CPA (aggregation change), PolyBG (architecture change), and PSE (feature change). If all four ideas work, they can be combined: CPA-PolyBG-GAT + PSE features + GMT training.
negative_signals: B ≈ A (within ±0.2K): Multi-task auxiliary training provides no benefit. Possible explanations: (a) auxiliary targets are too easy — the model learns to predict them within 10 epochs and the loss saturates, providing negligible gradient signal thereafter; (b) the auxiliary heads are separate from the Tg head — the shared encoder can learn auxiliary-relevant features that are orthogonal to Tg-relevant features (the auxiliary signal doesn't 'flow' to Tg); (c) the Tg loss dominates — 7170 samples is enough to learn Tg-relevant features from scratch, and auxiliaries add noise rather than signal.

F (node-level auxiliaries) ≈ B: If trivial node-level auxiliaries match graph-level auxiliaries, the benefit (if any) comes from multi-task regularization generally, not from property-aligned signal specifically. This would weaken H1.

H (auxiliaries-only pretraining) significantly WORSE: If pretraining on auxiliaries then finetuning performs worse than joint training, the auxiliaries provide no transferable signal — the encoder learns auxiliary-specific features that don't transfer to Tg. This would suggest that joint training's benefit (if any) comes from regularization during Tg learning, not from pretraining signal.

Auxiliary tasks cause negative transfer: If some auxiliaries actively hurt (e.g., rotatable bond density is anti-correlated with Tg in some polymer families), the encoder may learn conflicting features. This would manifest as certain individual auxiliaries (E) degrading performance.

Curriculum decay degrades: If D (constant λ=0.1) > B (curriculum decay), the auxiliaries provide sustained benefit throughout training and should not be phased out. This would suggest that Tg optimization benefits from continued auxiliary regularization.
Y.gap_closure_estimate: Best case: 1.0K → 3.64K gap (22% closure). Realistic: 0.3-0.7K → 3.94-4.34K gap (6-15% closure). GMT is incremental but methodologically important: if it works, it establishes that property-aligned multi-task training avoids the Identity-Property Antagonism and provides a template for future pretraining on external polymer property data.

content.risk_assessment: LOW-MODERATE. The primary risk is that auxiliary targets are too easy — the encoder can learn to predict rotatable bond density from a few atom features without developing deep graph-level representations. If the auxiliary loss saturates in 10 epochs, it provides minimal gradient signal. Mitigation: (a) curriculum decay ensures auxiliaries are only active early; (b) λ_max=0.3 limits their influence; (c) ablation F (node-level auxiliaries) provides a diagnostic for whether any auxiliary signal helps. The secondary risk is negative transfer — some auxiliaries may correlate with Tg in unexpected ways for specific polymer families. But the small λ weight and curriculum decay limit potential damage. Even if GMT is null, the experiment is informative: it tests whether property-aligned multi-task training can substitute for PI1M SSL, a key open question from Day 5.
day5_justification: mem_137 (Identity-Property Antagonism): GMT is the direct operationalization of the Antagonism's strategic implication: 'If pretraining is revisited, it must use objectives where discrimination is between property values rather than between sample identities.' The auxiliary tasks in GMT predict Tg-relevant PROPERTY values (rotatable bond density, aromatic fraction, etc.), not polymer identities. Each auxiliary head asks 'does this polymer have high aromatic content?' — a property question — rather than 'is this polymer A or polymer B?' — an identity question. The encoder learns to attend to property-relevant structural features rather than identity-discriminating features.

mem_135 (PI1M SSL Dead End): The integration identifies supervised multi-task as one of the remaining viable paths: 'Supervised multi-task pretraining on related polymer properties (density, solubility, thermal decomposition) rather than self-supervised objectives on PI1M.' GMT implements this on a small scale using computable graph-level properties rather than external datasets — a proof of concept for the supervised multi-task direction.

mem_071 (polyGNN): Demonstrates that multi-task learning on 30+ polymer properties improves generalization, especially for low-data properties: 'Multitask learning proves essential: ST polyGNN yields negative R² for five low-data properties, while MT polyGNN achieves positive R² across all 34.' GMT adapts this principle to Tg-focused training with fewer, carefully selected auxiliary tasks.

mem_104 (KPGT): The virtual knowledge node with molecular descriptors improves masked node prediction by providing global semantic context. GMT inverts this approach: instead of injecting descriptors as input, predict descriptors as output. Both approaches inject domain knowledge — KPGT via input augmentation, GMT via output augmentation. GMT is architecturally simpler (no virtual node, no cross-attention).

mem_138 (Post-PI1M Architecture): The consensus that 'the success of any architecture depends more on data scale and training strategy than on architectural details' motivates GMT: changing the training strategy (adding property-aligned auxiliaries) may be more impactful than changing the architecture, especially when the non-pretraining architectural asymptote is confirmed at ~35K.

mem_122 (Complementary Hierarchy Principle): GMT's multi-task design embodies the Complementary Hierarchy Principle at the objective level: Tg prediction (global property) + auxiliary predictions (intermediate properties) provide complementary signals at different semantic levels. The auxiliary tasks occupy an intermediate level between atom-level features and Tg — they are graph-level properties that are causally between local structure and global Tg.

memory.abstract: Day 6 Idea Generation Synthesis: Four mutually orthogonal supervised ideas targeting the 4.64K SOTA gap — CPA-GAT (aggregation), PolyBG-Supervised (architecture), PSE (features), and GMT (training strategy) — all avoiding PI1M SSL and Identity-Property Antagonism.
memory.keyword: Day6-synthesis four-ideas CPA PolyBG PSE GMT orthogonal supervised SOTA-gap-closure Day5-grounded

content.integration_type: Day 6 idea generation synthesis — four orthogonal supervised ideas grounded in Day 5 evidence
content.design_philosophy: All four ideas obey a unified set of constraints derived from Day 5: (1) SUPERVISED ONLY — no PI1M SSL, avoiding the triple-confirmed dead end and Identity-Property Antagonism; (2) NO GLOBAL ATTENTION, NO RESIDUALS, NO LAYERNORM — preserving the proven GAT architecture whose Jacobian spectrum is naturally well-conditioned for 1D chain topology (mem_131); (3) CLEAN ABLATION MATRICES — each idea includes a diagnostic ablation that distinguishes mechanism from confound; (4) SIMPLICITY PRINCIPLE — each idea adds the minimum necessary complexity to probe a specific new inductive bias; (5) DAY 5 EVIDENCE GROUNDING — every hypothesis and design choice is explicitly justified by Day 5 readings and experimental results.

four_ideas.name: CPA-GAT: Cardinality-Preserving Message Aggregation
four_ideas.mechanism: Add sigmoid-gated unnormalized sum channel to GAT message-passing (~1% parameter overhead)
four_ideas.signal: Chain length, branching density, functional group multiplicity — all Tg-relevant signals that softmax-normalized mean aggregation discards
four_ideas.risk: LOW — ~1% parameter increase, no architectural disruption, clean supervised ablation
four_ideas.orthogonality: Modifies how neighbor information is aggregated — compatible with all other ideas

four_ideas.name: PolyBG-Supervised: Parallel Bond-Graph GAT
four_ideas.mechanism: Parallel atom-GAT + bond-GAT with concatenated readout, no cross-attention
four_ideas.signal: Backbone bond-type sequences encoding chain flexibility — bond order, conjugation, aromaticity, rotation barriers
four_ideas.key_reading: mem_115 (MolCHG bond graph), mem_125 (PolyBG-SSL bond features)
four_ideas.risk: MODERATE — bond graph may be topologically redundant for 1D chains; enriched-edge ablation provides fallback
four_ideas.orthogonality: Modifies graph representation — independent of aggregation (CPA) and features (PSE)

four_ideas.name: PSE: Periodicity-Structural Encoding
four_ideas.mechanism: 4 new node features: modular_position, repeat_unit_index, periodic_distance, is_backbone
four_ideas.signal: Modular periodicity within repeat unit — the structural equivalence of atoms across repeat units that PerioGT's pretraining captures
four_ideas.key_reading: mem_052 (PerioGT periodic graphs), mem_135 (periodicity as missing ingredient)
four_ideas.risk: VERY LOW — pure feature engineering, zero architectural changes, 4 extra input dimensions
four_ideas.orthogonality: Modifies input features — independent of aggregation (CPA), architecture (PolyBG), and training (GMT)

four_ideas.name: GMT: Graph-level Multi-Task Training
four_ideas.mechanism: Joint supervised training with 5 property-aligned auxiliary prediction heads and curriculum decay
four_ideas.signal: Property-relevant graph-level features (rotatable bond density, aromatic fraction, H-bond density, backbone ratio, branching index) — causally upstream of Tg
four_ideas.key_reading: mem_137 (Identity-Property Antagonism), mem_135 (supervised multi-task alternative), mem_071 (polyGNN multi-task benefits)
four_ideas.risk: LOW-MODERATE — auxiliary targets may be too easy; curriculum decay and low λ limit potential damage
four_ideas.orthogonality: Modifies training objective — independent of architecture, features, and aggregation

content.combination_potential: The four ideas target different components of the learning pipeline (aggregation, architecture, features, training) and are designed to be mutually orthogonal. If each provides independent signal, the joint combination (CPA-PolyBG-GAT + PSE features + GMT training) could theoretically achieve 1.6-5.5K cumulative improvement. Realistically, with partial redundancy between mechanisms, 1.0-3.0K is more likely — closing 22-65% of the 4.64K SOTA gap. The Day 6 experimental priority order: CPA-GAT (lowest risk, fastest turnaround) → PSE (lowest risk, feature-only) → PolyBG-Supervised (moderate risk, richest signal) → GMT (training change, methodological significance).
content.what_is_not_proposed: (1) No PI1M SSL in any form — triple-confirmed dead end. (2) No global attention, residuals, or LayerNorm — GPS-Lite +8K is definitive. (3) No contrastive pretraining — Identity-Property Antagonism is causal, not correlational. (4) No large architectural overhauls — the non-pretraining asymptote at ~35K is ironclad, and complexity is actively harmful (GPS-Lite, residuals in GAT). (5) No external data sources — the ideas work within the 7170-sample Tg dataset constraint. (6) No speculative mechanisms — every hypothesis is grounded in Day 5 readings and experimental evidence.
content.strategic_narrative: Day 5 established that the path to closing the 4.64K SOTA gap cannot go through PI1M SSL (dead end) or architectural complexity (harmful). Day 6 pivots to a new strategy: supervised innovations that extract more signal from the 7170 labeled samples through better inductive biases. CPA enriches the aggregation function, PolyBG enriches the graph representation, PSE enriches the input features, and GMT enriches the training objective. Each probes a genuinely new inductive bias while respecting the hard-won Day 5 constraints. If any idea works, it demonstrates that the non-pretraining asymptote can be pushed beyond ~35K through focused, principled innovation rather than brute-force complexity.

memory.abstract: CardinalGraphFormer introduces a query-conditioned cardinality-preserving attention (CPA) channel that adds a sigmoid-gated unnormalized sum alongside softmax attention in graph transformers, theoretically resolving cardinality blindness and achieving 1-WL expressivity, with consistent empirical gains across 11 molecular benchmarks under matched protocols.

content.background: Molecular property prediction is a critical proxy task in drug discovery, constrained by limited experimental labels and an immense candidate chemical space. Graph transformers with self-supervised pretraining have shown strong performance on standardized benchmarks, with Graphormer establishing the value of injecting structural biases (shortest-path distance, centrality, edge features) into global attention. However, softmax attention has a fundamental limitation: it is 'cardinality-blind.' Softmax computes a weighted average over distinct value identities, discarding information about how many copies of each value exist in the support set. This means two nodes with support sets of different cardinalities but identical empirical value distributions and matching attention profiles produce identical attention outputs. In molecular graphs, support-set cardinality correlates with chemically meaningful quantities: the number of neighbors within K hops reflects local structural density, branching patterns, and functional group clustering. Existing approaches attempt to recover this information through static centrality embeddings (binned node degree), but these capture only fixed topological properties and are static under the augmentations and masking used in self-supervised pretraining. The dynamic nature of support-set size during training — particularly under subgraph sampling, node dropout, and edge dropout used in contrastive learning — means static degree embeddings cannot fully capture the shifting cardinality signals. Zhang & Xie (2020) originally proposed cardinality-preserving attention for MPNNs by adding unnormalized sums to retain degree signals, but this was limited to message-passing architectures without query-conditioning or transformer-specific design. CardinalGraphFormer addresses this gap by integrating a query-conditioned CPA channel into transformer attention with shared support, structured sparse attention via K-hop SPD masking for scalability, and dual-objective pretraining (masked reconstruction + contrastive alignment).
content.method: CardinalGraphFormer's core innovation is the query-conditioned cardinality-preserving attention (CPA) channel, which augments standard multi-head softmax attention with a parallel unnormalized sum pathway. For each attention head at layer l, the output is: o_i = sum_j(α_ij * v_j) + g_i ⊙ sum_j(v_j), where α_ij are softmax-normalized attention weights, v_j are value vectors, and g_i = σ(W_g * q_i) is a per-head, query-conditioned sigmoid gate. The gate is learned through a linear projection W_g ∈ R^{d×d} applied to the query vector, producing head-specific scalar gates in (0,1)^d via element-wise sigmoid. This design enables dynamic, context-dependent modulation of the unnormalized channel: the model learns when and to what degree to incorporate raw cardinality signals based on the query content. Both sums use the same head-specific value projections and the same support set S(i), ensuring alignment between the normalized and unnormalized pathways. The method is grounded in theoretical analysis through three formal results. Proposition 1 proves cardinality blindness of softmax attention: under identical empirical value distributions and matching attention profiles, softmax outputs are identical regardless of support-set cardinality differences. Proposition 2 proves CPA resolves this blindness: the unnormalized sum scales with the replication factor λ, and the sigmoid gate (strictly positive) preserves this difference in output. Theorem 1 establishes that CPA-augmented attention achieves at least 1-WL expressivity: the gated sum over embedded features is injective over multisets (since g_i ≻ 0 ensures bijection), and composed with self-features via an injective function ψ, matching one WL iteration. Critically, degree-normalized CPA (dividing the unnormalized sum by |S(i)|) provably reduces expressivity since mean aggregation is not multiset-injective. The architecture uses structured sparse attention with K-hop SPD masking (K=3 in main experiments). The support set S(i) = {j | SPD(i,j) ≤ K} is precomputed, and attention is masked outside this set. Attention logits incorporate Graphormer-inspired biases: a_ij = q_i^⊤ k_j / √d_h + b_{φ(SPD(i,j))} + b_{e_ij} + b_c(j), where b_{φ(SPD)} is binned SPD bias (K+1 bins), b_{e_ij} is direct-bond edge feature embedding (active only for SPD=1), and b_c(j) is key-side centrality bias (binned node degree). After attention, static centrality is injected per-layer as u_i ← u_i + c_i. The backbone uses 12 transformer layers with hidden dimension 512, 8 attention heads, FFN dimension 2048, LayerNorm, and dropout 0.1. Pretraining combines two self-supervised objectives on ~28M molecules (ZINC20 + ChEMBL35, filtered): (1) masked modeling with 15% node and 15% edge masking, single-layer MLP decoder predicting original features; (2) contrastive learning with NT-Xent loss (τ=0.2), using three augmentations per view (random subgraph sampling 50-75% nodes, node dropout rate 0.1-0.3, edge dropout rate 0.1-0.3), with per-view SPD recomputation as the primary augmentation strategy. Total loss: L = L_mask + 0.5 * L_contrast. The CPA channel adds approximately 1% parameter overhead (~48.2M vs 47.7M parameters).
content.experiment: Evaluation spans 11 public molecular property benchmarks across three suites: MoleculeNet (ESOL, Lipophilicity, BBBP, Tox21, ClinTox), OGB (ogbg-molhiv, ogbg-molpcba), and TDC ADMET (Caco2_Wang, hERG, Clearance_Hepatocyte_AZ, Clearance_Microsome_AZ). Metrics follow dataset conventions: RMSE for regression, ROC-AUC for classification, average precision for molpcba, MAE for Caco2, Spearman for clearance tasks. MoleculeNet uses 80/10/10 Bemis-Murcko scaffold splits; OGB and TDC use official splits. The pretraining corpus comprises ~28M molecules after filtering from ZINC20 (40M sample from clean-leads) and ChEMBL35 (2.4M). Standardization uses RDKit (canonical isomeric SMILES, heavy atoms only), Lipinski-style filtering (MW≤500, logP≤5, HBD≤5, HBA≤10, removing ~30%), InChIKey deduplication, and scaffold-based benchmark decontamination (~20k removed). Pretraining uses AdamW optimizer with 2e-4 peak learning rate, 10k warmup steps, cosine decay to 1e-6, global batch size 4096, 500k optimizer steps, on 4×A100 80GB GPUs with bf16 precision (~2784 GPU-hours). All transformer-family baselines (CardinalGraphFormer, SparseGraphormer-K3, GraphMAE-K3, GraphCL, Graphormer) share identical backbone depth/width, pretraining corpus, optimization budget, and fine-tuning protocol. The primary comparison is SparseGraphormer-K3 (identical architecture minus CPA) to isolate CPA's contribution. GraphMAE-K3 uses mask-only pretraining; GraphCL uses contrast-only; Graphormer (faithful implementation) uses global attention with full SPD binning and path-edge encodings. Non-transformer baselines (D-MPNN, GIN) are reproduced with literature hyperparameters. Fine-tuning uses max 300 epochs with patience 50. Statistical significance uses paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples per task/seed) with Holm correction across 11 tasks. The ablation study is extensive (>15 variants): degree-normalized CPA, no CPA + explicit size injection (scalar N and |S(i)| appended to inputs), no CPA + scalar |S(i)|+N as additive bias, no CPA + learned |S(i)| scaling, no CPA + learned temperature, no CPA + extra FFN capacity (parameter parity), removal of per-layer centrality injection, removal of key-side centrality bias, K=2 and K=5 and K=∞ variants, mask-only pretraining, contrast-only pretraining, no pretraining (random init), reduced pretraining budgets (10%, 25% steps), sum+mean aggregation alternative, chemistry-aware augmentations (attribute masking, valency-constrained edge dropout), per-view SPD recomputation vs stable SPD, mismatched-support CPA (global sum), and gate function variants (sigmoid, linear unbounded, tanh). Size-stratified and size-shift evaluations (small N<30, mid 30≤N<50, large N≥50) with size-only baseline and explicit size controls rule out simple size shortcuts.
content.result: CardinalGraphFormer achieves consistent and statistically significant improvements over the protocol-matched SparseGraphormer-K3 baseline across all 11 benchmarks. On MoleculeNet: ESOL RMSE 0.542 vs 0.598 (-0.056, p=0.002), Lipophilicity 0.629 vs 0.658 (-0.029, p=0.015), BBBP 0.938 vs 0.918 (+0.020, p=0.008), Tox21 0.921 vs 0.908 (+0.013, p=0.032), ClinTox 0.954 vs 0.939 (+0.015, p=0.045). On OGB: molhiv 0.819 vs 0.802 (+0.017, p=0.012), molpcba 0.304 vs 0.294 (+0.010, p=0.028). On TDC ADMET: Caco2_Wang 0.241 vs 0.265 (-0.024, p=0.005), hERG 0.898 vs 0.870 (+0.028, p=0.001), Clearance_Hepatocyte_AZ 0.538 vs 0.525 (+0.013, p=0.040), Clearance_Microsome_AZ 0.621 vs 0.614 (+0.007, p=0.048). All deltas remain significant after Holm correction. The ablation study reveals several key findings: (1) CPA's contribution is substantially larger than individual static centrality components (removing per-layer c_i or key-side b_c(j) causes smaller degradation than removing CPA entirely); (2) degree-normalized CPA underperforms the unnormalized version by 0.006-0.009 AUC/AP, consistent with the theoretical prediction that normalization destroys multiset injectivity; (3) explicit size controls (scalar injection, learned scaling, learned temperature) recover only 20-30% of CPA's gain, confirming benefits beyond simple cardinality leakage; (4) the L2 norm of the gated unnormalized sum correlates positively with |S(i)| even after controlling for node degree (partial r=0.52±0.03), and this correlation persists under augmentations (r=0.48±0.04), supporting dynamic adaptation; (5) sigmoid gates provide best stability (linear unbounded gates diverged in 2/5 seeds); (6) dual-objective pretraining outperforms mask-only or contrast-only; (7) per-view SPD recomputation adds +0.005 AUC over stable SPD. Size-stratified evaluations confirm CPA maintains gains across all size strata and under size-shift conditions, while size-only baselines achieve metrics far below learned models (e.g., AUC 0.65-0.75 vs ~0.90), ruling out simple size shortcuts. hERG shows the largest CPA benefit (+0.028 AUC), attributed to the task's dependence on discriminating compounds with subtle local structural differences where dynamic support-size signals are most informative. Clearance_Microsome_AZ shows the smallest gain (+0.007), consistent with clearance depending on broader metabolic pathways where local cardinality is less relevant. For typical drug-like molecules (median N≈22), K=3 covers >95% of nodes, acting primarily as a regularizer rather than strict sparsity; genuine efficiency benefits (2.5-4.4× speedup) emerge on larger molecules (N≥35, ~15% of corpus). Limitations include K=3 potentially missing long-range effects in very large molecules, Lipinski filtering biasing the pretraining distribution toward traditional drug-like space, query-only gating (rather than per-neighbor gating), and lack of dedicated block-sparse kernel optimization.
